sens: Worthless man, unworthy, despicable
Evil person, wicked, who rejects God
Morally corrupt individual
Enemy of good, opponent of justice
H1100G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a person of little value, lacking dignity or respect. This is someone whose behavior makes them despicable in the eyes of the community. In 1 Samuel 30:22, the "worthless" men who accompanied David refuse to share the spoils with those who stayed behind to guard the baggage.
2. It then qualifies the morally and religiously evil man: one who acts wrongly intentionally, who despises the law and God Himself. The sons of Eli in 1 Samuel 2:12 are "wicked" men who "did not know the Lord," meaning they willfully reject a relationship with God.
3. It characterizes one who is inwardly rotten, whose corruption is expressed through acts of wickedness: lying, betrayal, incitement to evil. In Deuteronomy 13:13, "wicked" men seduce the inhabitants of their city by urging them to serve other gods.
4. More broadly applied, the term designates anything that opposes justice and the order established by God, like a destructive force at the heart of the community.
H1100G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning literally "without profit" or "useless." It evokes the image of a person who brings nothing good, who is a moral waste. Its meaning has enriched to become a designation of personified forces of evil. The word has sometimes been used in late Jewish tradition as an equivalent of "Satan" or as a name for a demonic power (it appears in non-biblical texts like "Belial"), although in the Old Testament it primarily designates wicked men.
H1100G.emploi: The word appears about fifteen times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the Law. It applies to concrete men who embody moral and religious evil: the sons of Eli who profane worship, Nabal who refuses hospitality, the men who conspire against David or who seduce Israel into idolatry. The word can qualify a particular individual ("a wicked man named Sheba") or groups of troublemakers. In all cases, it designates those who threaten social order and the covenant with God, which is why it is often linked to the idea that they must be eliminated to "remove the evil from the midst of Israel."
H1100G.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Bible acknowledges the existence of deeply corrupt men, not only through isolated acts but by their very hearts turned against God. It invites us not to confuse justice with naive softness: the community must discern and reject those who threaten its integrity. For us today, it is a call to examine whether our hearts are drifting away from God, and to turn to Him rather than hardening ourselves in evil.

sens: Total loss, ruin, annihilation
Character of being vain, useless, worthless
Corrupted, bad, despicable person or thing
H1100H.detail:
1. The word first designates destruction or total ruin. In 2 Samuel 22:5 and Psalms 18:5, the torrents of destruction are the waves that threaten to engulf and completely lose: the image evokes devastating waters that sweep everything away in their path.
2. It also expresses the character of what is vain, useless, or worthless — a thing or person good for nothing, who cannot produce anything good. It is the notion of nothingness or powerlessness.
3. By extension, it qualifies what is corrupted, bad, or despicable — a person or project undermined by evil or immorality. In Psalms 41:9, the one who is "dangerously stricken" is hit by a ruin that renders him unable to rise again.
H1100H.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root לִי (liy), which can mean "weakness" or "nullity." With the prefix בְּ (bə), which marks the state or condition, it forms a word that paints the idea of complete nullity, a total absence of substance or value. This image of nothingness or destruction appears in several biblical texts to express physical or moral annihilation.
H1100H.emploi: The word appears three times in the biblical text we know. Twice, it describes the waves or torrents of destruction that threaten the psalmist — this mythical image of the waters of chaos that engulf (2 Samuel 22:5 and Psalms 18:5, which is a parallel). A third time, in Psalms 41:9, it qualifies one who is afflicted by a disease so severe that he cannot rise, as if destruction had struck him full force. The word always carries a tone of extreme threat and total powerlessness.
H1100H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that destruction and ruin are the fruits of sin and evil. The psalms that use it also show that even in the face of the torrents of destruction, the believer can cry out to God to be saved — which foreshadows the deliverance that God offers in Christ against all that threatens us with annihilation.

sens: Lacking moral value, without principle
Despicable character, unworthy
Wicked, corrupt man
Evil, wicked conduct
Destruction, ruin (rare sense)
H1100I.detail:
1. The word first describes what has no value, not in a material sense but in a moral sense: a person without righteousness, incapable of good, depraved. In Proverbs 6:12, "the wicked man" is one who walks "with deceit in his mouth" — he does not have the weight of good within him.
2. It is an intrinsically evil, despicable character. In Proverbs 19:28, the "perverse witness" embodies not only lies but mockery of justice itself; his words devour iniquity instead of condemning it.
3. The word can designate the wicked act or disposition of a person: the man who conspires and prepares misfortune (Proverbs 16:27). It is wickedness put into action.
4. More broadly, it names iniquitous behavior, systematic malice: Job 34:18 speaks of proclaiming "the wickedness of kings," their manifest injustice.
5. The rare sense of destruction or ruin appears in the oldest texts, evoking moral or physical annihilation.
H1100I.origine: The Hebrew word is composed of two elements that together evoke the absence of value: "without" (בְּלִי) and a term meaning what has worth or subsists. The central idea is that of moral nothingness, of what has no weight of good. The same roots are found in other Hebrew words describing uselessness, ethical emptiness, what can only produce evil.
H1100I.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Wisdom literature (Proverbs 3 times, Psalms 1 time) and in the context of commandments (Deuteronomy). It describes either a stable moral disposition — the wicked character of a person — or a particularly iniquitous act or attitude. In Deuteronomy 15:9, it refers to a negative sentiment of the heart (refusing help out of wickedness). In Proverbs, it is almost always the man himself who is qualified: the wicked man devises evil plans (16:27) or lies in court (19:28). The word carries a strong connotation: it is not merely a passing fault, but a constitutive baseness.
H1100I.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that malice is not a passing error but a posture of the heart — which is why Deuteronomy 15:9 warns against it: it comes from within and calls for active vigilance. When reading that a man is "perverse," we understand that righteousness does not come naturally; it requires a conversion of the heart and a relationship with God that straightens what in us tends naturally toward evil.

sens: To mix intimately and work dough with hands or a utensil
To blend together, confuse several things or people
To muddle, make confusing or unintelligible
H1101A.detail:
1. Kneading is the act of working flour and oil dough to make an offering: it is the action of the baker who works the dough with his hands. The Bible constantly speaks of "fine flour kneaded with oil" in sacrifices (Leviticus 7:10; Numbers 28:9): the flour and oil blend together into a homogeneous dough.
2. To blend means to intertwine several elements in such a way that they can no longer be clearly distinguished. At the time of Babel, God said: "Let us confuse their language" (Genesis 11:7), which means He will muddle the languages of men together, just as one kneads different ingredients into a single mass, so that they can no longer understand each other.
3. To confuse in the sense of making perplexing or unintelligible: when one kneads several languages together, confusion is created. The verb expresses this muddling of meaning and mutual understanding.
H1101A.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּלַל (balal) comes from a root that expresses the idea of mixing intimately. The basic image is that of the kneading trough: one takes separate elements (flour, oil, water) and works them together until they form a uniform mass. The word has retained this concrete force even when it applies to language or people.
H1101A.emploi: The verb balal appears about forty times in the Bible. The majority of its uses (more than 30) are found in the books of Leviticus and Numbers, where it systematically describes the preparation of offerings: a dough made of fine flour mixed with oil. These references constitute the "domestic" sense of the word. But two famous uses imbue it with a broader and more dramatic meaning: in Genesis 11:7 and 11:9, the word designates God's action of "confusing" the languages at Babel, muddling mutual understanding. This passage shows that "kneading together" can also mean "to make confused and unintelligible." Hosea 7:8 uses the word figuratively to describe a people "half-baked" (image of poorly kneaded dough), symbolizing impurity and instability.
H1101A.portee: For the believer reading the laws of sacrifices, the word knead reminds that the offering to God requires work: mixing, transforming, preparing with care. It is an act of worship that engages hands and effort. The story of Babel, on the other hand, warns: mixing can also be confusion, a divine punishment. The word indicates that God even masters our communications; He is the one who "kneads" history when humanity goes astray.

sens: To supply food for an animal, particularly with fodder or provisions
To supply, nourish
H1101B.detail: 1. The word designates the action of providing food to a domestic animal, especially fodder or provisions. In Judges 19:21, the master of the house "gave fodder to the donkeys" of the travelers: it is a simple act of hospitality, feeding the beasts of his guests as one takes care of their own. 2. In a broader sense, it means to supply, to provision — the idea is to provide for sustenance, whether for animals or, by extension, for people.
H1101B.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּלַל (balal) comes from a root that evokes the action of mixing or giving to feed. It is a concrete word, linked to rural life and the care of flocks. The root also appears in other contexts related to food and the provision of nourishment.
H1101B.emploi: The verb appears only once in the provided biblical text: in Judges 19:21, where it describes the gesture of the old man offering hospitality by feeding the donkeys of the travelers. This unique use shows the word in a simple domestic context, that of welcoming and caring for the animals of guests. It is a detail that emphasizes generosity and hospitality.
H1101B.portee: This word reminds us that biblical hospitality also encompasses the care of the animals of those we receive. It is a concrete and humble gesture of kindness: welcoming the stranger also means providing for all his needs, including those of his beasts.

sens: To stop, master
To prevent from acting or speaking
To control by force
H1102.detail:
1. To restrain means to stop or master something or someone that is moving or wants to move. It is the image of the rider pulling on the reins to stop his horse: in Psalms 32:9, the psalmist compares the heart of man to a horse or mule that must be restrained by bit and bridle, otherwise they will not come near you.
2. To restrain can also mean to prevent someone from acting or speaking freely, as one stops a too spirited animal. The word carries the idea of a force that opposes, controls, or masters.
3. In a figurative sense, to restrain applies to mastering passions or instincts: one must restrain one's impulses to stay on the path of wisdom.
H1102.origine: The verb בָּלַם (balam) comes from a root that evokes the idea of braking or mastering. Its primary image is that of the brake, the bit, or the bridle that restrains an animal. This root reflects the concrete experience of the rider or the driver of a team: to control one's mount, one must restrain it firmly.
H1102.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 32:9. In this passage, the psalmist advises not to be like the horse or mule without understanding, which must be restrained by bit and bridle to obey. The context is that of wisdom and moral counsel: it is better to maintain self-control than to be carried away by blind instincts.
H1102.portee: This word invites us to reflect on self-control and the discipline of the heart. It suggests that the believer, far from being like a mindless beast dominated by its impulses, can and must cultivate restraint and control of his passions to advance on the path of wisdom and obedience to God.

sens: To take care of fig trees or sycamores, to prune and harvest their fruits
H1103.detail: 1. The verb designates the agricultural activity of caring for fruit trees, particularly sycamores (a type of coarse fig tree very common in the East). Amos, the prophet, declares to Amaziah that he is not of religious profession but an agricultural worker: "I am no prophet, nor the son of a prophet; but I am a shepherd, and I cultivate sycamores" (Amos 7:14). The word evokes humble, daily work, far from the official functions of the temple.
H1103.origine: The Hebrew verb balás comes from a root that specifically designates the fig or sycamore. It is a very concrete term, linked to the agricultural world of the East where the sycamore (a tree producing a fruit similar to the fig, but of lesser quality) was a common crop in the Mediterranean and Middle Eastern regions. The word has a simple and rustic tone.
H1103.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 7:14. Amos uses it to affirm his professional status: he is not a prophet by trade or religious dynasty, but a man of the field, a shepherd and farmer. This contrast emphasizes that his prophetic mission comes directly from God, not from a human institution.
H1103.portee: This verb reminds us that God's prophets came from all backgrounds, including the humblest. Amos, a sycamore cultivator, was called to announce a divine message as important as that of official prophets. This teaches that God does not need social or professional status to make His word heard: faithfulness and obedience are sufficient.

sens: To swallow, to make disappear in the mouth or stomach
To absorb, to completely make disappear (earth, water, fire)
To destroy, to annihilate (forces, cities, goods)
To cause the ruin or death of someone
To dissipate, to lose without return (money, goods)
To surpass, to absorb in a figurative sense (one thing consumes another)
H1104.detail:
1. In the literal sense, to swallow means to take something into the mouth and stomach to make it disappear. This is the basic image of the verb, especially when talking about swallowing food or an object. Job asks God: "You would destroy me!" (Job 10:8), using the verb to describe a complete disappearance, as if one were swallowed.

2. The earth or water can swallow: the earth opens up and swallows (absorbs) people or things, making them disappear forever. When the earth opened and "swallowed Dathan," it literally swallowed them alive (Psalms 106:17 and Numbers 26:10).

3. In the sense of destroying or annihilating: the verb describes the total destruction of something — cities, homes, kingdoms — as if fire or war swallows them. "The Lord has ruthlessly destroyed all the dwellings of Jacob" (Lamentations 2:2): everything has been swallowed, annihilated.

4. To swallow can also mean to cause the ruin of a person, to make them disappear spiritually or physically. "Those who are led astray are lost" (Isaiah 9:15): they are swallowed by lies, swallowed morally.

5. To dissipate or lose without return: money, goods, resources can be swallowed, meaning squandered, lost forever, just as food disappears when swallowed. Proverbs 21:20 speaks of one who "squanders" their goods.

6. Figuratively, one thing can swallow another when it surpasses and absorbs it: the lean ears "swallowed" the fat ears in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41:7), one visually devouring the other.
H1104.origine: The Hebrew verb balàʿ comes from a very ancient root that imitates the sound and action of swallowing something large or difficult. The basic image is that of a throat that swallows, that engulfs. The verb also appears in neighboring Semitic languages with the same meaning. The Bible uses it to describe anything that disappears, is absorbed, or destroyed irreversibly, as if death, the earth, or a superhuman power "swallowed" what disappears.
H1104.emploi: The verb balàʿ appears 48 times in the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in the Psalms (especially the psalms of trust in the face of danger) and in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs). It is also found in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea) to describe God's judgments. In a military context, to swallow describes the absorption or destruction of the people by their enemies. In a spiritual context, it speaks of the ruin caused by evil, idolatry, or lies. In the Psalms, the faithful ask God not to be swallowed by their adversaries. In the prophets, God "swallows" pride, idolatry, or rebellious cities.
H1104.portee: This verb reminds us that evil, judgment, or death can be powers that completely swallow. But the psalmists also confess: "If the Lord had not been on our side... the flood would have swallowed us" (Psalms 124:3). That is why faith consists of crying out to God not to be swallowed. At the same time, to swallow also shows God's omnipotence over sin and evil: He completely destroys them, without mercy. It is an image of human finitude and vulnerability in the face of the powers of evil, and of our absolute need to be saved.

sens: The action of swallowing, of engulfing
What is swallowed, engulfed
Ruin, annihilation (in a figurative sense)
H1105.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical action of swallowing: literally, it is what happens when something is engulfed. In Jeremiah 51:44, God says He will tear from the mouth of Bel "what he has swallowed," referring to the riches and spoils that the Babylonian god has swallowed, absorbed.
2. By extension, the word can refer to the swallowed object itself, what has been swallowed and does not return.
3. In a figurative and moral sense, it represents complete ruin and annihilation. In Psalms 52:6, the psalmist speaks of the "destruction" that a deceitful tongue brings — not just a simple word, but a discourse that carries within it the annihilation of the one who listens or falls victim to it.
H1105.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to swallow" or "to engulf." This image of engulfment, of what disappears in the mouth, has naturally led to expressing the idea of destruction: just as what is swallowed disappears, so total ruin erases everything.
H1105.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. In Psalms 52:6, it describes the devastating effect of a lying tongue — a moral and spiritual destruction. In Jeremiah 51:44, in a context of divine punishment against Babylon, it refers to what Babylon (personified through its god Bel) has swallowed and accumulated, which God will tear from it. In both cases, the word carries the idea of a definitive, complete, and irretrievable loss.
H1105.portee: This word reminds the reader that a lying word is never harmless: it "swallows" the one who believes it, destroying them from within. It is also a warning that the riches accumulated through injustice and idolatry will in turn be swallowed by God's judgment. The word invites us to be wary of what seems to "swallow" us — lies, luxury, idols — and to seek instead what builds up and saves.

sens: City of the Plain that was spared and became Zoar
Old name of Zoar
H1106B.detail: 1. Bela is one of the five cities of the Plain (the fertile region near the Dead Sea) that participated in the revolt against the four kings from the North (Genesis 14:2). Its name means "destruction" in Hebrew, but unlike the other cities of the Plain that were devastated, Bela was spared at Lot's request, who found refuge there during the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. 2. Bela is just an old name: the same city later became known as Zoar ("small"), this name reflecting the agreement that Lot obtained to escape divine judgment. The two biblical occurrences, both in Genesis 14, mention both names simultaneously to show this continuity.
H1106B.origine: The name Bela comes from the Hebrew "destruction." It is a historical city of the Plain, mentioned in the accounts of Genesis among the cities that rebelled against Kedorlaomer and his allies. The name change to Zoar ("small") marks a moment of grace: the city, although initially called "destruction," became a refuge of salvation.
H1106B.emploi: Bela appears only twice in the Bible, both in Genesis 14, in verses 2 and 8. These two occurrences describe the same battle where the kings of the Plain, including the king of Bela, stood against the four kings from the North led by Kedorlaomer. The explanatory parenthesis "which is Zoar" reminds that Bela is the old name of the city that the reader knows as Zoar. No other biblical book mentions Bela.
H1106B.portee: This small detail reveals the irony of divine grace: a city called "destruction" was the only one saved. The name change to Zoar emphasizes that God sometimes grants mercy to those who turn to Him, as Lot did. It echoes the message of Genesis: even in the midst of judgment, God reserves an escape for those who seek Him.

sens: First king of Edom according to the biblical genealogy
Son of Beor
H1106G.detail:
1. Bela is the first king mentioned as having reigned over Edom, the territory occupied by the descendants of Esau. He reigned from his city of Dinhabah (Genesis 36:32).
2. He was the son of Beor, and after his death, Jobab son of Zerah took his place on the throne of Edom (Genesis 36:33). The same information is reported in 1 Chronicles 1:43-44, confirming his role in the royal succession of Edom.
H1106G.origine: The name Bela means "destruction" in Hebrew. It appears in two distinct biblical contexts: this king of Edom, and a city of the plain that was spared during the destruction of Sodom at Lot's intercession, which received the name Zoar (or Tsoar). These two uses of the same name reflect the importance of the term in patriarchal traditions.
H1106G.emploi: Bela appears four times in the Bible, all in the royal genealogies of Edom: twice in Genesis 36:32-33, and twice in 1 Chronicles 1:43-44 (which repeats the same genealogical passage). The Bible reports nothing of his deeds; it is only known that he reigned over Edom before Jobab. These lists show that the kings of Edom existed before Israel had a king, as noted in 1 Chronicles 1:43.

sens: Man of the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
Ancient city of the plain, spared during the destruction of Sodom
H1106H.detail:
1. Bela is a clan chief of the tribe of Reuben mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Azaz and lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two: the Northern kingdom (Israel) and the Southern kingdom (Judah). The text tells us that he lived in the region of Aroer, near the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:8).
2. The name Bela also refers to one of the five cities of the plain of Sodom, which was spared during the destruction of that cursed region. This city became known as Zoar, the refuge where Lot and his daughters found shelter when the fire from heaven ravaged Sodom and Gomorrah.
H1106H.origine: The name Bela means "destruction" in Hebrew, which connects it to the catastrophic imagery of ancient Sodom. It is a significant name: the father of the clan bears a name evoking divine judgment, while the historical city of Bela symbolizes rather the escape, the remnant that was spared. The name reflects the Hebrew mentality that gives children names loaded with spiritual meaning and reminders of the history of the people.
H1106H.emploi: Bela appears only once in the provided biblical uses: in 1 Chronicles 5:8, in the midst of a genealogy of the tribe of Reuben. This passage places Bela in the succession of generations that populated the region east of the Jordan. The genealogical context places this character in the period of the divided monarchy, without recounting any particular events. It is a name preserved by the genealogical memory of Israel, a witness to a humble but real historical existence.

sens: outside of, excluding
except, unless
without, in the absence of
independently of, contrary to
H1107.detail:
1. The word denotes what is outside, separate, or distinct from something: "besides the altar of the Lord" (Joshua 22:19) means an altar built in addition to, alongside, in violation of divine order.
2. It expresses exception or what is lacking: "besides me there is no savior" (Isaiah 43:11) means that except for God, no one else can save — it is the formula of the uniqueness of salvation in God.
3. It marks the absence of consent or authorization: "without the will of the Lord" (2 Kings 18:25) means that nothing can be done against what God wants or allows.
4. It sometimes introduces a restriction or an implicit condition: the word emphasizes what is necessary, fundamental, or inevitable for something to be true.
H1107.origine: The Hebrew word בִּלְעֲדֵי (bil'adé) is composed of the preposition בְ (be, "in, with") and לְעֲדֵי (l'adé), which comes from a root expressing the idea of "side" or "separation." Its primary image is that of crossing a boundary, of being set apart. The root etymologically evokes what is rejected or left aside. It is an ancient and solemn word, frequent in solemn declarations about the uniqueness and exclusivity of God.
H1107.emploi: This word appears about 16 times in the Old Testament, mostly in contexts of solemn declarations about the power or uniqueness of God. It appears three times in Isaiah's major affirmations: "besides me there is no savior" and "besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 43:11; 44:6; 45:6), where it marks the absolute exclusivity of the God of Israel. It is also used to express the absence of consent: "without the will of the Lord" (2 Kings 18:25; Isaiah 36:10), denying that an action can be done against divine will. Elsewhere, it simply denotes a separation or an excess (Joshua 22:19). Its use is always grave and solemn, never trivial.
H1107.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the reader about the uniqueness of God and the impossibility for anyone — creature, idol, rival force — to supplant Him or act without His order. It teaches that all true security, all true salvation, rests solely on God, with no possible alternative. It is a word of trust and clarity: there is no other resource but God, and this is good news for those who submit to His authority.

sens: descendants de Béla, fils de Benjamin
H1108.detail: The Balites are the members of the family or clan descending from Bela, the son of Benjamin. Bela was one of the sons of Benjamin at the time of the Exodus and the sojourn in the desert (Genesis 46:21). His descendants formed one of the large families of the tribe of Benjamin, and during the census in the desert, they are listed among the Benjaminite families: "from Bela comes the family of the Balites" (Numbers 26:38). It is a genealogical term that designates a family group identified by its ancestor.
H1108.origine: The word "Balites" comes from Bela (בֶּלַע), whose name means "the one who swallows" or "who devours." The descendants of the same person receive in the Bible the name of that ancestor with the suffix "-ite" (or in Hebrew a similar suffix), which indicates belonging to a lineage or family group. This is a common practice in the Old Testament to identify clans and their branches.
H1108.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:38, during the census of the Israelites in the desert after the Exodus from Egypt. It is then that "the family of the Balites" is mentioned, one of the twelve families of the tribe of Benjamin. This genealogical enumeration shows how the tribe of Benjamin was organized into distinct clans, each with its eponymous ancestor and its descendants.
H1108.portee: This term reminds us that God knows each person and each family in His people, even the smallest clans. The enumeration of the families of Israel also shows how God is committed to entire groups, not just isolated individuals. It is an invitation to recognize our own belonging to the community of believers and our responsibility towards our brothers and sisters.

sens: Homme doué du don de prophétie à l'époque de la sortie d'Égypte
Devin mercenaire engagé pour maudire Israël
Prophète que Dieu a contraint à bénir Israël malgré lui
H1109A.detail:
1. Balaam is a man living at the time of the Exodus and the desert, son of Beor, from Pethor. He is a man who possesses the gift of prophecy and is sought for his power to intervene through his words in events (Numbers 22:5-6).

2. King Balak of Moab hires him to curse the people of Israel who have settled at his borders, offering him considerable gifts in exchange (Numbers 22:7, 22:17). Balaam initially agrees to travel to Balak, but the Lord forbids him to curse Israel (Numbers 22:12).

3. During his journey, God opens Balaam's eyes so that he sees the angel of the Lord who stops him, sword drawn (Numbers 22:31). Although Balak urges him to try again, Balaam is compelled by God to pronounce blessings on Israel, particularly a famous messianic prophecy (Numbers 24:15-17).
H1109A.origine: The name Balaam means "not of the people" or "strange to the people." Balaam is presented as a man living outside of Israel, endowed with knowledge of the true God, which marks him as a foreign prophet whom the Lord uses despite the malice of his mercenary heart.
H1109A.emploi: Balaam appears 56 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the account of Numbers 22-24, with later mentions associating him with the corruption of Israel. During his first encounter with Balak, he asserts that he can only act according to the command of the Lord (Numbers 22:18). God speaks to him in a dream and imposes His will. Balaam becomes an unwitting instrument of blessing: at each attempt to curse Israel, his mouth pronounces blessings, particularly an oracle about the Messiah. Although compelled to bless, Balaam later advises Balak on how to seduce Israel through idolatry and immorality (Numbers 31:16), revealing his venal heart. He dies during Israel's conquest of the South (Numbers 31:8).
H1109A.portee: The story of Balaam teaches that God is sovereign over the words and hearts of men, even those who are malicious or foreign to His people. It also shows that one who seeks to enrich themselves by opposing God, or who knows the truth without loving it, incurs divine judgment. Balaam's prophecy about the Messiah (the Star and the Scepter) becomes for believers a proof that God has guided history in favor of His people and His Anointed.

sens: Ville d'Israël en Galilée, dans le territoire de Manassé
Résidence des lévites de la famille de Kehath
H1109B.detail: Bileam is a city located in Galilee, in the region of Manasseh, assigned to the Levites of the family of Kehath (1 Chronicles 6:70). It served as a residence for the priests and temple servants, along with its surrounding lands (its "suburbs"). It is a variant or another name for the city of Ibleam.
H1109B.origine: The Hebrew name Bileam (בִּלְלְעָם) literally means "not of the people" or "strange to the people." This etymology may reflect the special role of this city: although in the territory of Manasseh, it was reserved for the Levites, which distinguished it from the rest of the territory.
H1109B.emploi: Bileam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:70, in the list of cities assigned to the Levites after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned alongside Aner, as a possession intended for the family of Kehath, the priestly branch of the people of Israel. Its unique appearance shows its administrative importance: it was part of the system of distribution of Levitical lands desired by God.

sens: Détruire complètement une terre, une ville, la rendre inhabitable
Ravager, saccager avec violence
Réduire à néant, anéantir
H1110.detail:
1. Devastate means to completely ruin a land or region, leaving it in ruins, void of life. In Isaiah 24:1, the Lord "devastates the earth and makes it desolate": this is to transform a fertile and inhabited land into a barren solitude. The image is one of total destruction affecting both buildings, crops, and the inhabitants themselves.
2. Ravage expresses this same destruction, but often with the idea of rapid violence and pillaging. In Nahum 2:11, the context speaks of plundering and devastating an enemy city: it is the work of military conquest that destroys everything in its path.
3. The word can also signify the annihilation of a reality or a people: not only do the buildings fall, but the social order collapses and hearts are broken, as shown in the verses following Nahum 2:11.
H1110.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּלַק (balaq) comes from a root expressing the idea of "emptying," "removing," "making disappear." The form used in the Bible (Poel and Pual) intensifies this meaning: it is not just a simple damage, but a systematic and complete destruction. The word belongs to the family of destruction verbs in biblical Hebrew.
H1110.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: in Isaiah 24:1 and Nahum 2:11. In Isaiah, it refers to a divine judgment upon the whole earth. In Nahum, it is the invasion and fall of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. Both uses illustrate the radical destruction of a place or a people, either by divine judgment or by military conquest. The context always emphasizes the extent of the ruin and its human consequences.
H1110.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of divine judgment: God can completely destroy what opposes Him or violates His order. It also invites reflection on the consequences of collective sin and the fragility of all human power. For the believer, it is a call to fear God and to trust in His justice.

sens: King of Moab at the time of Israel's desert crossing
The one who sought to curse God's people through the prophet Balaam
H1111.detail:
1. Balak is a Moabite king who reigns at the time when Israel arrives at the borders of his kingdom, after defeating the Amorites. He sees the power of Israel and is terrified. Balak, whose name means "devastator," makes his first appearance in Numbers 22:2 where he observes all that Israel has done to the Amorites.

2. Fearing for his people, Balak undertakes a desperate action: he hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, hoping that this curse will weaken his enemies. From Numbers 22:15 to 23:30, we see Balak repeatedly sending messengers, then accompanying Balaam to high places to pronounce the requested curse. But with each attempt, Balaam blesses Israel instead of cursing it, which fills Balak with anger and frustration (Numbers 24:10).
H1111.origine: The name Balak (בָּלָק in Hebrew) literally means "devastator" or "the one who destroys." This king certainly lives up to his warrior name, even though he cannot destroy Israel by force — hence his resort to magic and sorcery. His father is Zippor, whose name means "bird."
H1111.emploi: Balak appears about 40 times in the biblical text, almost exclusively in the account of Numbers 22-24. He is the central character in the story of Balaam: a pagan king who recognizes the power of Israel but refuses to submit to it and instead seeks to counter it with a curse. His name is later mentioned in historical reminders (Joshua 24:9, Judges 11:25, Micah 6:5) as an example of the nations' opposition to Israel. The contrast between Balak's intentions and God's actions through Balaam is at the heart of the message: even a powerful king cannot nullify God's plans for His people.
H1111.portee: The story of Balak teaches that political power and human schemes, even sophisticated ones, cannot undo God's promises to His people. Balak represents unbelief that refuses to recognize the divine hand and attempts to fight against it. For the Christian reader, this story serves as a reminder that God protects His children and that His blessings cannot be annulled by the malice of enemies.

sens: King of Babylon at the time of the empire's fall
The one to whom the prophet Daniel interpreted the miraculous writing on the wall
H1112.detail: 1. Belschatsar is the king of Babylon mentioned in the accounts of Daniel. His name means "Bel protects the king," recalling the Babylonian god Bel. In Daniel 8:1, he is presented as the sovereign who reigns at the time when Daniel receives his prophetic visions. 2. Belschatsar is most famous for the event in chapter 5 of Daniel: during a royal feast, a mysterious hand writes enigmatic words on the wall of the palace. Terrified, Belschatsar calls upon Daniel to interpret them. These words announce the end of his reign and the imminent fall of Babylon.
H1112.origine: The name Belschatsar combines Bel, the great Babylonian god, and a word denoting king or royalty. It is an Akkadian name attested in historical sources from the Babylonian period, transliterated into biblical Hebrew. It embodies the pride of an empire that believes itself invulnerable but ignores the true God.
H1112.emploi: Belschatsar appears as a historical figure in the last days of Babylon. The biblical accounts present him as a prince or co-regent in the years leading up to the conquest by Cyrus and the Medes. He represents human power in the face of divine might: proud in his royal feast, he despises the sacred vessels of the Jerusalem temple, and receives immediate divine judgment. His story illustrates how arrogant empires fall when they oppose the God of Israel.
H1112.portee: The story of Belschatsar teaches that political power, even the most dazzling, remains subject to God. His misadventure with the mysterious writing reminds the reader that God judges the powerful and that the mockery of sacred things does not escape His gaze. It is an invitation not to place trust in earthly kingdoms but to recognize the sovereignty of the eternal God.

sens: King of Babylon at the time of the fall of the Babylonian empire
Son of Nebuchadnezzar according to the Bible
The one to whom Daniel interpreted the mysterious writing on the wall
H1113.detail: Belschatsar is the last king of Babylon mentioned in the Bible. He organizes a great feast where he profanes the sacred vessels of the Jerusalem temple by using them to drink wine with his court (Daniel 5:1-2). It is during this banquet that Daniel, summoned by the frightened king, interprets the mysterious writing that appeared on the wall: "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin" — a pronouncement predicting the imminent fall of the kingdom (Daniel 5:25-28). Belschatsar reigns over the Chaldeans at the time when God humbles Babylonian pride: the text emphasizes that he did not humble his heart despite knowing God's judgments on Nebuchadnezzar, his predecessor (Daniel 5:22). That very night, he is killed, and the Babylonian empire falls (Daniel 5:30).
H1113.origine: The name literally means "Bel protects the king": "Bel" was the supreme god of Babylon, and the king bore this theophoric name to invoke divine protection. It is an Aramaic name, the language spoken in Babylon at the time of the exile.
H1113.emploi: Belschatsar appears exclusively in chapter 5 of the book of Daniel (6 verses), a decisive moment when God judges Babylon for its pride and sacrilege. The narrative first shows him in a position of absolute power, giving orders and bestowing honors (he appoints Daniel to "third place in the kingdom"), then humiliated by fear before the divine sign he cannot understand. His story illustrates the biblical contrast between apparent human power and the sovereignty of God.
H1113.portee: The account of Belschatsar teaches that neither rank, nor power, nor riches immunize against God's judgment. His inability to understand the writing, while Daniel, a mere Jewish prisoner, deciphers it, shows that wisdom and spiritual understanding come from God. The profanation of the temple vessels — an act of contempt towards the God of Israel — accelerates the fall of Babylon: it is a call not to defy the Lord, even when ruling over an empire.

sens: Man who lived during the time of the exile and return
Exile who returned with Zerubbabel
H1114.detail: Bilschan is a man mentioned in the lists of those who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, the Persian governor of Judah. He appears twice in Scripture, in Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7, where these two chapters enumerate the main leaders and families who participated in the return. His name appears among important names, alongside Joshua, Nehemiah, and Mordecai, indicating that he played a notable role in the returning community.
H1114.origine: The name Bilschan means "in calumnies" or "in defamations" (from Hebrew "bil" = in, and "shan" = calumny). It is a typical personal name from the Persian period, borne by a man from the tribe or family of Judah during the return from captivity to Babylon in the sixth century B.C.
H1114.emploi: Bilschan is named exactly twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages: Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7. These two chapters report the same events — the return of the exiles under the leadership of Zerubbabel — but with slightly varied lists of leaders. Bilschan is cited among the leaders and elders who guided the people during this decisive return. His appearance in these two accounts shows his importance in the restoration of Israel after the Babylonian captivity.

sens: negation: expresses absence or refusal
absence of something possible or expected
exception: what remains when excluding the rest
negative condition: so that it does not occur, in order that it does not happen
negative cause: due to not, because not
H1115.detail:
1. This is the simple negation: to say that something is not, does not exist, or does not happen. In Genesis 3:11, God asks Adam, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?" — the Hebrew word here means prohibition, the interdiction to eat.
2. The word also expresses deprivation or total absence: in Numbers 11:6, the people complain, "We see nothing but manna" — nothing else, just the manna. It expresses what is lacking, what disappears.
3. Sometimes it marks the exception, what remains when the rest is excluded: in 2 Kings 10:11, Jehu kills those of the house of Ahab "without letting a single one escape" — meaning "except zero, without exception."
4. It can introduce a negative condition, to avoid something: in Jeremiah 17:27, the Lord warns, "If you do not listen... not to introduce through the gates of Jeremiah on the Sabbath day," meaning "so that it does not happen."
5. The word can also express the cause: why does this happen? Because something did not happen. In Jeremiah 44:7, "so that there may be no remnant of you" — the non-fulfillment of an action produces a result.
H1115.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a very ancient root meaning negation and absence. It is related to other Hebrew forms of negation (lō, bal) but is distinguished by its particular function: it does not simply negate, it often marks a condition, a restriction, or an exception. In Greek, the Septuagint generally translates it as "mē" (μή), which carries the same conditional and restrictive nuance. It is a fundamental word in Hebrew logic and grammar.
H1115.emploi: This word appears 107 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Torah (Pentateuch) and the Prophets. It is primarily used to express a prohibition or a ban, as in Genesis 3:11 (the forbidden tree) or Exodus 20:20 ("do not be afraid"). It is also used to mark a negative totality, a completeness in exclusion: in 2 Kings 10:11 or Joshua 8:22, one kills or destroys "without leaving any survivors." In prophetic speeches (Jeremiah, Isaiah), it expresses conditions of obedience: if you do not obey, then such consequence follows. Finally, it can mark an exception or a restriction in language, as in Ruth 2:9 ("stay close to my maidens").
H1115.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God's commandments are never neutral: they demand a choice, obedience, or refusal. The constant presence of this negation in the Law shows that God does not speak vaguely but sets clear boundaries. Understanding the force of "not" in the Bible helps grasp the seriousness of sin, which is always a voluntary crossing of what has been forbidden. It is also learning to distinguish true obedience (which says "no" to evil) from mere passive abstention.

sens: Topographical elevation, mountain or hill
Platform or sanctuary built on a height for religious worship
Place where idolatrous sacrifices to foreign gods are practiced
Battlefield or site of martial victory
H1116.detail:
1. A high place is primarily a geographical height, a mountain or hill that rises above the surrounding terrain. Deuteronomy 33:29 speaks of those who "advance on the high places of the earth," referring to summits or ridges.
2. The word also refers to altars or sanctuaries built on these heights, where the people offered sacrifices. In 1 Kings 3:2, before the Temple in Jerusalem was built, "the people only sacrificed on the high places."
3. Often, these high places become sites of idolatrous worship, where sacrifices are offered to pagan gods. Leviticus 26:30 shows the Lord saying, "I will destroy your high places" where other gods are worshiped.
4. In battle contexts, the word also evokes the strategic advantage of dominating from the summit. In 2 Samuel 1:19, the parallel between "height" and martial predominance appears in a lamentation song.
H1116.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to elevate" or "to ascend." Bamah primarily describes the physical reality: a place that rises. In Israel, these heights initially served as legitimate places of worship (altars can be found at Gibeon, 1 Chronicles 16:39), but they became the symbol and seat of idol worship to Baal and other deities, hence the negative connotation of the word in most prophetic texts.
H1116.emploi: This word appears 92 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Kings and Chronicles, and among the prophets. At the beginning of the Israelite monarchy, the high places served for the worship of the true God when the Temple did not yet exist (1 Samuel 9:12-14). But as soon as the central sanctuary in Jerusalem was established, the high places gradually became synonymous with idolatrous worship and disobedience to God. Pious kings like Hezekiah and Josiah made it a goal of religious reform: they "tore down" or "destroyed" the high places (2 Kings 18:4, 2 Chronicles 34:3). The prophets, especially Jeremiah and Ezekiel, denounce them as centers of sin, where even children are sacrificed (Jeremiah 7:31). The word is thus inseparable from the spiritual history of Israel and its struggle between idolatry and faithfulness.
H1116.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that authentic worship of God cannot be divided or left to personal religious improvisation. The high places illustrate how, over time, practices that seem neutral or tolerable (offering on a mountain) can gradually become centers of idolatry and distance from God. It serves as a warning against the gradual compromise of faith and the importance of maintaining worship centered on true worship, away from religious deviations.

sens: Place name in Palestine, ancient name of Gibeon
H1117.detail: Bama is a place name in Palestine. It is another name given to Gibeon, the well-known city of the Old Testament. The name literally means "high place" in Hebrew, reflecting the topography of the region and also the use of these heights as places of worship, often idolatrous. This place appears in the context where God reminds Israel of its religious waywardness.
H1117.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew "bama," which literally means "high place" or "height" (from the root meaning "to elevate"). The term is also used in the Bible to designate the "high places" where idols were worshiped, which explains the religious imagery attached to the name of this place. It is another name for Gibeon, a famous city of Canaan.
H1117.emploi: Bama appears only once in the preserved Bible, in Ezekiel 20:29, where the prophet mentions it as an ancient name for Gibeon. In this passage, God reproaches Israel for its infidelities and idolatrous practices. The choice of this name — meaning "high place" — likely underscores the connection between this place and illicit worship on the heights, a recurring theme in the prophetic denunciation of Israel's sins.

sens: A man from the tribe of Asher in ancient Israel
H1118.detail: Bimhal is a name mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:33. He was a man who belonged to the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, and he lived before the establishment of the monarchy. He was the son of Japhleth and the brother of Pasac and Aschvath. His name appears in the genealogical list of the descendants of Asher, which traces the origins of the families of this tribe.
H1118.origine: The name Bimhal comes from Hebrew and literally means "in the circumcision" or "in the weakness by mixture." Although the meaning is uncommon, it reflects the Hebrew compound names where prepositions and spiritual or physical concepts are combined to form a person's identity. The name belongs to the genealogical heritage of the tribes of Israel.
H1118.emploi: Bimhal is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:33, in the context of a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Asher. This passage lists the descendants of Asher and places Bimhal among the sons of Japhleth. His isolated appearance in this genealogical list shows the importance that Scripture places on the transmission of generations and the rooting of families in the history of Israel, even for individuals whose notable deeds are unknown.

sens: inside of, in the midst of
toward, against (with a verb of movement or action)
by, through (instrument or cause)
in, clothed with (state or condition)
H1119.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses position or location: something is found inside a space or place. In Isaiah 25:10, the straw is trampled "in a dung pit" — this is the place where the action takes place.
2. It then designates the direction or target of an action: an arrow is shot "in the shadow" (Psalms 11:2), it is not struck randomly but toward a specific place.
3. The word can also indicate the instrument or means by which something is done: one speaks "from the mouth" or "by the mouth" (Job 16:5), one stirs "the lips."
4. Finally, it expresses a state or condition: the wild animal retreats "in" (or rather "into") its den (Job 37:8), the adjective "wild" here is a natural state of the beast.
H1119.origine: This very common preposition comes from an ancient Hebrew root expressing interiority and location. It is similar to other positional prepositions (like "in," "at"). Its basic image is that of the inside or enclosed space, from which it has derived more abstract uses to express direction, means, or state.
H1119.emploi: This preposition appears about 9 times in the cited passages, mostly from the book of Job and the Psalms. It is extremely common in biblical Hebrew and can take on different nuances depending on the context. With a place name (Isaiah 25:10), it indicates location. With an action name or a verb (shooting "in" the shadow), it expresses direction. With a body part or instrument name ("from the mouth"), it shows the means or origin of the action. It is a very flexible preposition, whose exact meaning largely depends on the grammatical and semantic context.
H1119.portee: This ordinary preposition reminds us that the Bible often speaks of the world as we experience it: real places, concrete actions, emotions that manifest through the body. It helps us visualize biblical scenes — a person pleading "from their mouth," an arrow flying "in the shadow" — and to grasp how God acts at the heart of ordinary human realities.

sens: City located on the Arnon River in Moab
Stage of the Israelites' journey in the desert
H1120G.detail:
1. Bamoth is a city located in Moabite territory, near the Arnon River. The name literally means "high places" or "great high place" in Hebrew, probably because the city was built on a height. It occupies a strategic position in the geography of the region east of the Jordan.

2. In the account in the book of Numbers, Bamoth appears as a stage in the long journey of the Israelites after their exit from Egypt. After leaving Nahaliel, the Israelites arrive at Bamoth, then continue toward the valley that extends into the territory of Moab, at the summit of Pisgah, from where they can see the desert (Numbers 21:19-20). This enumeration of stages shows the winding path taken by the people to circumvent the lands of the peoples who refused passage.
H1120G.origine: The Hebrew word ba.mot (בָּמוֹת) is the plural of bamah, which means "high place" or "elevation." This term evokes the natural heights of the terrain. In the Bible, high places are often sites of worship, but here the proper name Bamoth simply designates a city established on a hill or elevated region of Moabite territory, near the Arnon.
H1120G.emploi: Bamoth appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Numbers, chapter 21, verses 19 and 20. These two verses are part of the account of the stages of the journey of the people of Israel through the desert, after the exit from Egypt and before entering the Promised Land. Bamoth is mentioned between Nahaliel and the valley of the territory of Moab, near Pisgah, placing this city in the geography of the path taken by the Israelites to circumvent the lands of the Ammonites and Moabites.

sens: City of Moab located on the Arnon River
H1120H.detail: Bamoth-Baal is a Moabite city located near the Arnon River, east of the Jordan. Its name literally means "the high places of Baal," reflecting the religious significance of the site in the worship of the god Baal. It is from here that King Balak summoned the diviner Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22:41): from the heights of this city, Balaam could see part of the camp of Israel. The city also appears in the list of Moabite cities mentioned during the allocation of territory after the conquest (Joshua 13:17).
H1120H.origine: The Hebrew name bamot (בָּמוֹת) means "high places" or "heights." This root evokes the idea of elevated places, often associated with shrines and altars. The full name Bamoth-Baal adds "of Baal," the Canaanite god of thunder and fertility worshiped in this region. The place bears the name of this cult, indicating that this high place was dedicated to Baal.
H1120H.emploi: Bamoth-Baal appears only twice in the Bible. In Numbers 22:41, it is the place from which Balak, the king of Moab, summons the diviner Balaam to curse Israel during their march toward Canaan. From these heights, Balaam can see the camp of Israel and carry out his attempt at cursing. In Joshua 13:17, Bamoth-Baal is listed among the Moabite cities of the territory east of the Jordan. These two mentions clearly situate the city in Moab, in a mountainous region suitable for shrines.
H1120H.portee: Bamoth-Baal reminds us that Canaanite and Moabite cults competed with the God of Israel for the loyalty of the people. The account of Balaam shows how God protects His people by turning curses into blessings, even when invoked from the high places of false gods. The contrast between the power of the false gods of the place and the power of the God of Israel underscores the importance of exclusive fidelity to the Lord.

sens: young boy or adolescent, from birth until adulthood
man descended from a father, in a direct filial relationship
descendant of an ancestor, by blood or alliance
member of a people or community defined by a common bond
man in general, in a relationship of dependence or status
H1121A.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the young boy or adolescent, from the first breath to adulthood: it is the male child in his growth. Cain begets Enoch and "named the city after his son" (Genesis 4:17), marking the arrival of new life. 2. It expresses the relationship of direct filiation: one who descends from a particular father. When Scripture says that Moses sprinkled oil on Aaron "and on the sons of Aaron" (Leviticus 8:30), it refers to his male children, bearers of his house and function. 3. By extension, it designates any descendant, even distant, or a member of the community linked by a common ancestor: "seventy sons of Ahab" (2 Kings 10:1) are his heirs. 4. It broadens to denote belonging to a group or shared condition: we speak of the "sons of Eli" for his priests, the "children of Ahab" for his dynasty. 5. Finally, it can reinforce the idea of status or relationship of dependence: one may call someone "my son" to express authority or affection.
H1121A.origine: The word ben comes from an ancient Semitic root expressing the construction of a house, the extension and continuation of lineage. In Hebrew, it is at the heart of biblical genealogies that structure history: each "son" prolongs and transmits the name and covenant of his father. This notion of generational link, of passing from one life to another, unites all the uses of the word.
H1121A.emploi: Ben is the most frequent Hebrew word for designating the father-son relationship, appearing over 2300 times. It is used from the first verses of Genesis to trace the genealogies from Adam to Noah (Genesis 5), giving the Bible its genealogical structure. It is found both in the patriarch Abraham speaking of his son Isaac (Genesis 22:2-3), and in the laws of Leviticus recalling the father's responsibilities towards his son (Proverbs 29:17: "Discipline your son"). The word also applies to the descendants of a king (the sons of Ahab, the sons of Eli) to designate the house or dynasty. Its use is concrete in family relationships and abstractly in lineages and alliances.
H1121A.portee: Understanding the weight of the word ben in biblical Hebrew opens the genealogical and patriarchal dimension of Revelation: God reveals Himself as Father and commits to the sons, that is, the descendants. This prepares the reader to grasp the importance of being called "sons of God" as believers, and to recognize Jesus as the only Son, heir of all promises. The word, humble and earthly, thus becomes the bridge between natural human relationship and divine adoption.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy
H1121B.detail: Beno is a Levite mentioned in the register of priestly and Levite families during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. He was the son of Jaaziah and the brother of Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri. His name, which literally means "his son" in Hebrew, was common in the genealogies of the tribe of Levi.
H1121B.origine: The name Beno comes from the Hebrew root "ben" which means "son." In biblical genealogies, particularly among the Levites, this type of name was sometimes given to mark the filial relationship in the official records of priestly families.
H1121B.emploi: Beno appears twice in Chronicles, in chapter 24, in the list of descendants of Merari, an important branch of the tribe of Levites. These mentions are found in the register established under the reign of David to organize the temple service. Beno and his brothers are presented as sons of Jaaziah, himself a son of Merari, which establishes their precise place in the Levitical genealogy.

sens: a boy or girl, child of a father or mother
a man in the direct descent of an ancestor
the whole of the members of a people, tribe, or nation
a social group defined by a common characteristic
H1121G.detail:
1. The word "son" primarily designates the male or female child in a biological sense: one who comes from his parents. This is the simplest and most concrete usage (Genesis 50:23: "The children of Manasseh were born on Joseph's knees").

2. Beyond the first child, "son" extends to all descendants of a man, particularly the male line. This is why we say "the sons of Abraham" or "the sons of Levi" to refer to all the men who descend from him (Genesis 25:3: "The sons of Dedan were the Asshurim, the Letushim, and the Leummim").

3. The word especially designates the whole people: "the children of Israel" means all the Israelite people, regardless of age or sex. This is the most frequent usage in the Bible, particularly in Exodus and the historical books (Exodus 12:37: "the children of Israel went out from Ramses").

4. The word can also qualify a group of people united by a quality or common belonging: for example, we speak of the "sons" of a city for its inhabitants (Genesis 23:3: "Abraham rose from before his dead, and spoke to the sons of Heth," meaning the inhabitants of that region).
H1121G.origine: The Hebrew word בֵּן (ben) primarily means "son" in the strict sense. Its basic image is that of the link of filiation: one who is born of a father. The word naturally extends to all male descendants of an ancestor, and then to an entire people when seen as descendants of a founder (Israel is the "son" of Jacob). This extension of meaning reflects how the Hebrews thought of identity: not as an isolated individual quality, but as belonging to a lineage, a community, a house.
H1121G.emploi: The word "son" or "children" appears over 1,200 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is omnipresent from Genesis to name the descendants of the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob), and then the tribes of Israel ("the sons of Reuben," "the sons of Levi"). From Exodus onward, the expression "the children of Israel" becomes almost formulaic: it designates the Hebrew people in its entirety, from the day of the Exodus until the end of the historical books. The word is also used for the inhabitants of a region ("sons of Heth"), members of a profession or group. Each use emphasizes the link of belonging: to be the "son" of something or someone is to be in solidarity with it, to belong to it.
H1121G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word opens a deep understanding: Israel is not primarily a political nation, but a family, a people bound by a promise made to its fathers. The "children of Israel" are not the children of any king, but of the living God who has chosen and kept them. This familial vision of the people helps to grasp how God relates to His people: not as a distant leader, but as a father who knows each of His children.

sens: A young animal, particularly a calf, a ram, or a lamb of a few months
A young of an animal, notably the young of a lioness or lion
The young shoot of a tree, a young sprout or seedling
H1121H.detail:
1. In the accounts of sacrifice and ritual offerings, ben refers to a young domestic animal that is still young and vigorous: a calf, a ram, or a flawless lamb intended for burnt offerings. Leviticus 9:2 is a classic illustration: Aaron takes "a young calf for the sin offering" — it is an animal of a few months, chosen for its youth and purity. Numbers 29:13 also lists the prescribed offerings: "thirteen young bulls." 
2. Ben also applies to the young of a wild animal, still dependent on its mother. Job 4:11 mentions "the young of the lioness" that scatter when the lion can no longer hunt: the image emphasizes the vulnerability of the young animal separated from its mother. 
3. Less frequently, ben can refer to the young shoot or small of a tree: Genesis 49:11 mentions a donkey tied at the foot of the vine, and Psalms 114:4-6 speaks of the "young" mountains — a poetic image of a mountain compared to a young animal that leaps.
H1121H.origine: Ben comes from the Hebrew root עמט(ben), which primarily expresses the idea of "filiation" or "descent" — hence the main meaning: "child." The secondary meaning "young animal" naturally follows: any small being born, whether human or animal, can be called ben. In biblical Greek, this word is often rendered by νέος (néos, "young") or by specific words according to the animal (μόσχος for calf, νεοσσός for young bird).
H1121H.emploi: This word appears 87 times in the Hebrew Bible, heavily concentrated in the books of law and accounts of ritual offerings. The books of Leviticus and Numbers are full of it: sin offerings, burnt offerings, consecration offerings feature "young bulls" and "young rams." Genesis 18:7 recounts how Abraham hurries to his flock to take "a tender and good calf." Job 4:11 and Psalms 29:6 use it poetically to refer to the young of wild animals or fragile shoots — the meaning always remains that of young life, a new being, or one still growing.
H1121H.portee: Recognizing this word helps the Christian reader understand the sacrificial system of the Old Testament: offerings of young animals were not wasteful, but gifts of particular purity, as the most delicate and living were chosen. This also illuminates the seriousness of consecration: offering the young of one's flock truly cost, both to the animal and to the one offering it. This image of youth finally underscores the novelty and growth that God honors — important themes when considering Christ as the perfect Lamb of sacrifices.

sens: male person born of a father and a mother
member of a group, nation, or community
inhabitant of a place, characterized by origin or condition
person marked by a quality or defect
H1121I.detail:
1. The most direct meaning refers to a male child: it is the child of a father, as when Genesis 6:2 speaks of the "sons of God" who saw the daughters of men. 
2. By extension, "son" designates members of a people or community: the "sons of the captivity" (Ezra 4:1) are the Israelites returned from Babylonian exile, bound together not by direct kinship but by a shared destiny. 
3. "Son" can also characterize someone by their place of origin or social condition: the "sons of the foreigner" (2 Samuel 22:45) are men foreign to the people of Israel, defined by their non-belonging. 
4. The word also expresses belonging to a moral category or a dominant quality: in Proverbs 31:5, not to give wine to the "sons of ruin" means not to give it to those destined for destruction or misfortune.
H1121I.origine: In Hebrew, ben (בֵּן) comes from a very ancient root meaning "to build" or "to beget." The word expresses the idea of what is produced, begotten — primarily the male child, then by analogy everything that is derived, produced, or belonging to a group. The same root is found in other Semitic languages. In Greek, the word "huios" (υἱός) regularly translates ben in the Septuagint.
H1121I.emploi: The word ben appears 46 times in the provided passages, mainly to designate male children (Genesis 6:2, 6:4) and members of a community ("sons of the captivity" in Ezra, "sons of the foreigner" in Psalms and Isaiah). It is also encountered to qualify men of a particular group: the "sons" of kings (2 Chronicles 25:24), the "sons" of the righteous and the wicked (Job 5:7). In Psalms, it characterizes those who oppose the righteous. In Isaiah 56 and 61, the "sons" of the foreigner become those who turn to God. The meaning always adapts to the context: it is not always biological filiation, but belonging to a group or a moral characteristic.
H1121I.portee: Understanding that "son" in biblical Hebrew does not only mean the child of a father, but also belonging to a people, a condition, or a destiny, helps the reader grasp how the Bible speaks of human relationships beyond biology. This is important to hear that God calls foreigners to become His children (Isaiah 56:3-6), not by blood but by faith. The word also reveals that biblical identity is built through belonging to a community and a commitment to God.

sens: one who receives the inheritance of a father or master
one who continues the work or perpetuates the name of someone
in the New Testament, one who receives the promises or the Kingdom of God
H1121J.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who, legally or by natural right, receives the goods and rights of a deceased person. In Genesis 15:2, Abram thus calls Eliezer, the servant of his house who would succeed him in the absence of children: this is the most concrete meaning, that of the legal heir. 
2. By extension, it refers to one who receives a charge, a mission, or a promise: one who inherits the name or position of the one who precedes him. In this sense, the heir is one who continues the work. 
3. In the spiritual sense cherished in the New Testament, the heir is one who receives the blessings promised by God — not by mere carnal birth, but by faith. Believers in Jesus become heirs of the promises made to the patriarchs.
H1121J.origine: The word ben (בֵּן) primarily means "son" in the biological sense. To designate the heir, the same word is used, as in Israelite law it is naturally the son who inherits from the father. Biblical usage plays on this closeness: the son is by excellence the one who perpetuates the house and inherits it. This word belongs to a family of very ancient Hebrew terms, present in all Semitic dialects.
H1121J.emploi: The word ben is used more than 4,400 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and the meaning "heir" is a specialized usage, particularly visible in legal texts and succession narratives. In Genesis 15:2, Abram uses this term to designate the one who would inherit him: it reflects a man without children seeking to secure his succession. This meaning becomes important in divine promises: God promises Abram an innumerable offspring, that is, heirs of His blessings. The New Testament picks up this theme by speaking of believers as "heirs" of the Kingdom and the promises.
H1121J.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith in Jesus does not marginalize us: on the contrary, we become heirs of the promises made to Abraham, sons of Abraham by faith. It is a word of consolation — what seemed lost or denied is given to us in fullness. The New Testament sees in this the secret of our identity in Christ: we inherit not because we are born into a certain family, but because we are united to the one who is the Son par excellence, Jesus Christ.

sens: Courageous and strong man, capable of fighting bravely
Trained and experienced warrior
Person worthy of trust and respect due to moral strength
Son or descendant (sense of close filiation to the root word)
H1121K.detail:
1. The valiant is primarily a man of physical courage, able to stand up to danger and adversity without wavering. When David tells his men, "be valiant men" (2 Samuel 2:7), he calls them to show strength of heart and arm in the face of the battles ahead. It is the image of a soldier who does not retreat.

2. He is also the proven warrior, one whose exploits are known. Benaiah, "a man of valor and renowned for his exploits" (2 Samuel 23:20), embodies the perfect type of the valiant: a man whose reputation for bravery precedes his words. His courage is not merely an attitude, but a story written in actions.

3. The valiant inspires confidence through his moral strength as much as his physical strength. When Elisha speaks of the "son of a murderer" (2 Kings 6:32), he uses the word in a slightly disdainful manner, but the context shows that it is someone whose determination is feared — someone formidable.

4. Finally, the word can retain its basic sense of "son" or "man of," which simply situates the person within a lineage or category ("son of a man of Kabzeel").
H1121K.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root ben (בֵּן), which primarily means "son" or "child." The sense of "valiant" or "warrior" is derived from this: it is the robust and active man, one who has grown and acts — the opposite of the small or weak. In Hebrew, the same root also denotes construction or building, which reinforces the idea of strength and solidity. The word always retains a nuance of filiation or human connection, even when it means "warrior."
H1121K.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the provided usages, mainly in the books of Samuel and Kings, during accounts of war or military courage. David uses it to urge his soldiers to bravery (2 Samuel 2:7), Absalom to command his servants to show courage (2 Samuel 13:28), and the elders of Israel to speak of King David's feared reputation (2 Samuel 17:10). The Shunammite women use it to refer to the fifty "valiant" men capable of seeking the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 2:16). In each usage, the word retains this idea of moral or physical strength, the ability to act without weakness in the face of peril.
H1121K.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that bravery is not merely the absence of fear: it is the ability to obey and act despite danger, standing firm in one's convictions. It is also an invitation to cultivate integrity and trust in God rather than brute strength. The valiant of the Bible does not boast of himself, but draws his courage from his relationship with the Lord.

sens: number of years of life
moment of life characterized by a specific number of years
period of life marked by specific abilities or responsibilities
H1121L.detail:
1. The word designates the number of years a person has lived: "Joseph died, aged one hundred and ten years" (Genesis 50:26). It is the time elapsed since birth.
2. It also indicates a particular moment in life, defined by the number of years reached: "Noah, aged five hundred years, fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth" (Genesis 5:32). Age marks a stage in the journey of life.
3. The word serves to set age limits for religious or military responsibilities: "from the age of twenty years and above, all who are able to bear arms" (Numbers 1:30) and "from the age of thirty years and above to the age of fifty years" for service in the sanctuary (Numbers 4:23). Age determines who can and must fulfill certain functions.
H1121L.origine: The Hebrew word ben (בֵּן) primarily means "son" or "child." When it is said that a man "is the son of so many years," it indicates the number of years he has, that is, his age. It is a construction where "ben" (son) is followed by a number of years. This expression, very common in Hebrew, is one of the applications of the word ben that has produced a specific translation in French versions: "aged" or "age." The root thus evokes the idea of generation and the counting of time elapsed.
H1121L.emploi: This word, in the sense of "age," appears about 110 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis, Exodus, and Numbers. It is used to express the age of a person (Noah, Abraham, Joseph), but also to establish legal and religious criteria. In the census lists of the Book of Numbers, it sets the minimum age for military service (twenty years) or service in the sanctuary (twenty-five or thirty years depending on the function). The French Segond translations render this term as "age," "aged," "year," depending on the context and grammatical structure of the sentence.
H1121L.portee: Understanding that the Bible takes the age of men seriously invites the reader to recognize that God accompanies each stage of life. The age thresholds set for service show that God orders community life with wisdom: He places each person in their place according to their maturity and strengths. For today's Christian, this reminds us that each season of life has its function and dignity before God.

sens: A Levite porter during the divided monarchy
H1122.detail: Ben is a Levite appointed by David to guard the Ark of the Covenant. He appears in the list of musicians and temple servants responsible for transporting and protecting the ark (1 Chronicles 15:18). He is a man of God's people, chosen for a sacred task in the service of worship.
H1122.origine: The name Ben means "son" in Hebrew (it is the same word as in "Benjamin," "son of the right hand"). Here, Ben is a complete personal name, probably a nickname or diminutive common in Levitical families. Its use reflects the importance given to filiation and family identity in Israel.
H1122.emploi: Ben appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:18, where he is mentioned alongside other Levites during the organization of the transport of the ark by King David. He is classified among the "porters" (guards), and his name appears in a list of about seventeen chosen servants for this important worship ceremony. He is a minor historical figure, with no other account concerning him.

sens: To construct a structure by assembling materials
To restore, rebuild what has been destroyed
To erect, to set up gradually
To establish or form something lasting
H1124.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to assemble materials, stones, and wood to erect a building. This is the act of construction itself. In Ezra 5:4, the builders are asked for the names of those who "are building this edifice."
2. The word often takes on the nuance of "rebuild," as it refers to reconstruction after destruction. In Ezra 4:12, the Jews are reproached for "rebuilding" Jerusalem, the rebellious city, by raising its walls.
3. The verb also evokes the action of progressing step by step, advancing gradually in realization. In Ezra 5:16, the house "is being built" since the time of Sheshbazzar; it is a continuous and unfinished process.
4. Figuratively, to build means to establish or create something solid and lasting, a work that stands firm.
H1124.origine: The Hebrew root bnh evokes the image of raising or erecting. It belongs to a family of words denoting construction and edification. The corresponding noun "binyan" means edifice or building. The verb expresses both the physical action of building and the broader idea of creating or establishing a stable structure.
H1124.emploi: This verb appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the book of Ezra (16 occurrences) and once in Daniel. It is used almost exclusively to describe the reconstruction of the Temple in Jerusalem after the exile. The usages show a long and contested process: the Jews receive the order to rebuild (Ezra 5:11), the work progresses slowly (Ezra 5:16), and then is ordered by the king (Ezra 6:7). The verb emphasizes both the physical effort and the spiritual stakes of this restoration.
H1124.portee: For the Christian reader, this word speaks of reconstruction after ruin, of perseverance in God's work despite obstacles and delays. It reminds us that restoring what is broken takes time, obedience, and faith. It is also an image of renewal: when everything is lost, God allows rebuilding, not only materially but spiritually.

sens: Officer of King Solomon
Son of Abinadab
H1125.detail:
1. Ben-Abinadab is an officer appointed by King Solomon to govern an administrative region of Israel. His name literally means "son of Abinadab." He alone governed the whole region of Dor and was connected to the royal family by marrying Taphath, the daughter of King Solomon (1 Kings 4:11).
2. As his name indicates, Ben-Abinadab is the son of Abinadab, a man from the first generation after David. His existence and position testify to the administrative structure established by Solomon to effectively govern his kingdom.
