H1125.origine: The name Ben-Abinadab is composed of two elements: "ben" (son) and "Abinadab" (which means "my father is noble" or "father of nobility"). It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, combining a familial relationship and a spiritual significance. This patronym follows the Israelite custom of giving the son the name of the father or grandfather by prefixing "ben."
H1125.emploi: Ben-Abinadab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:11, where he is presented as one of the twelve officers that Solomon established to administer the regions of the kingdom. This passage is set in the context of the administrative organization of the unified kingdom under Solomon, where each officer was responsible for supplying the king and his court for one month each year. His marriage to Taphath shows how Solomon consolidated his political power by marrying his children to high officials of the kingdom.

sens: Son of pain or sorrow, first name given to Benjamin by his mother Rachel at his birth
H1126.detail: 1. Ben-Oni literally means "son of my pain" in Hebrew. Rachel, the mother of this child, gives him this name under the most tragic circumstances: she dies giving birth to her son (Genesis 35:18). The name expresses her maternal grief in the face of imminent death, marking the child with the memory of the suffering that accompanies his coming into the world.
H1126.origine: The name Ben-Oni is composed of two Hebrew words: "ben" (בֶּן) which means "son," and "oni" (אוֹנִי) which comes from a root expressing pain, sorrow, or misery. It is a meaningful name, like many biblical names that reflect the circumstances of birth or the feelings of the parents. Rachel chooses this name to perpetuate the memory of her agony.
H1126.emploi: Ben-Oni appears only once in the Bible, at the precise moment of Benjamin's birth in Genesis 35:18. Rachel, who is traveling with Jacob to Canaan, dies in childbirth after giving birth to this child. Dying, she gives him this name of pain. Immediately afterward, Jacob changes this name to Benjamin, which means "son of the right hand" or "son of my strength," a name of hope and blessing that replaces the initial sadness. This original name then disappears from the narrative, replaced everywhere else by Benjamin.
H1126.portee: This passage shows how a moment of extreme pain can mark a life, but also how God's grace transforms destiny. The name change, from mourning to hope, illustrates that our birth or painful origins do not define our future. Benjamin, despite his tragic entry into the world, becomes one of Jacob's most beloved sons, particularly cherished by his father, reminding us that God can turn sorrow into blessing.

sens: Officer of King Solomon, in charge of a region of the kingdom
Son of Geber, a man living during the united monarchy of Israel
H1127.detail:
1. Guéber was one of the twelve royal officers that King Solomon established to administer and provide for the needs of the kingdom (1 Kings 4:13). He governed the region of Ramoth in Gilead and the surrounding territories, including the towns of Jair and the region of Argob in Bashan with its sixty large fortified cities — an important charge that shows the extent of his authority and the wealth of his district.
2. The name "Ben-Geber" literally means "son of Geber" — his kinship is thus attached to his administrative identity. Nothing else is known about him other than this role in the central organization of the kingdom.
H1127.origine: The Hebrew name is composed of "ben" (son) and "Geber" (a strong man, a man of value). "Geber" (H1398) comes from a root meaning "strength" or "manliness." The name thus reads as "son of a strong man" or "son of Geber," emphasizing the family line and perhaps qualities of strength or authority.
H1127.emploi: Guéber appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:13, in the list of the twelve royal administrators that Solomon had placed in the main regions of Israel to collect the taxes and provisions necessary for the maintenance of the royal court and army. His district included the territory of Ramoth in Gilead, rich and strategic, indicating that he enjoyed a position of trust in Solomon's administration.

sens: Officer of King Solomon
Son of Déker
H1128.detail: Ben-Déker is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:9. He is one of the twelve officers that King Solomon had established to administer the various regions of the unified kingdom of Israel and to collect the taxes and provisions necessary for the royal court. His name means "son of Déker," which simply indicates his lineage.
H1128.origine: The name Ben-Déker means "son of Déker" in Hebrew. "Ben" means "son" and is a very common element in Hebrew proper names to indicate lineage. Déker, the father, bears a name that evokes the idea of piercing or stabbing (from the root דקר, daqar). No further information is given about this character or his family in the preserved biblical texts.
H1128.emploi: Ben-Déker appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:9, in the list of the twelve prefects that Solomon had placed over the districts of the kingdom. He was in charge of the region including Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-Shemesh, Elon, and Beth-Hanan. This administrative system was essential for managing the supply of the royal court and the organization of the territory.

sens: Construct a building of stone, wood, or other materials
Erect a religious or civil structure (altar, city, temple)
Establish a family or household through descendants
Restore, raise up what has been destroyed
Found, institute, or maintain durably
Build or organize in a figurative sense
H1129.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to construct materially: to assemble materials (stone, wood) to erect a building. Noah "built an altar" after the flood (Genesis 8:20); David desires to "build a house" for the ark of God (2 Samuel 7:5).
2. One "builds" religious and civil constructions: altars, temples, cities. In Babylon, they "built" the city and the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:4-5); Asa "built" Geba and Mizpah to fortify his kingdom (1 Kings 15:22).
3. A woman "builds" a house by giving children to her husband: Rachel and Leah "have built the house of Israel" (Ruth 4:11), and a barren woman could "build" her family through the children of a concubine (Genesis 30:3).
4. The word also means "to rebuild," "to restore" after destruction: they will "rebuild on ancient ruins" (Isaiah 61:4) and the returned exiles will "build" the ruined temple (Ezra 4:4).
5. In a figurative sense, God "builds" a house or dynasty for someone, meaning He establishes it durably and assures it of descendants: "I will build you a house" means an eternal lineage (2 Samuel 7:11, 7:27).
6. More broadly, "to build" means to create, organize, institute: God "forms" or "builds" the woman from the man (Genesis 2:22).
H1129.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of assembling, progressively erecting. It is related to the word for "son" (ben), as building a house also means perpetuating it through children. The root is found in several ancient Semitic languages, including Aramaic (benah). The fundamental image is that of stacking, progressively lifting materials to form a durable structure.
H1129.emploi: The verb "to build" (with its variants "to rebuild," "to construct") appears 345 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis (early chapters: altars, city), in the historical books (construction of the temple, cities, royal fortifications), and in the prophetic books (restoration after exile). Its scope extends from concrete material edification (Solomon built the temple) to the establishment of families (Ruth 4:11), to the foundation of dynasties by God Himself (2 Samuel 7:13). The figurative sense "to establish" or "to found" is affirmed when God "builds" a house for David or when one "rebuilt" the people after exile: it is to create something durable and significant.
H1129.portee: This word reminds Christians that God "builds" durably: He builds families, peoples, and especially His Church (Jesus says, "I will build my Church"). For the believer, "to build" a life of faith is to construct on the solid foundation of Christ. The word also invites us to see that every achievement—family, work, testimony—requires time, perseverance, and a stable base, like the building of a house.

sens: King of Syria in the 9th century B.C., contemporary of King Asa of Judah
H1130G.detail: Ben-Hadad was a powerful Syrian king who ruled in Damascus. The name means "son of Hadad" (Hadad being a Syrian deity). There were at least two kings by this name: the first, son of Thabrimmon, confronted King Asa of Judah in the 9th century (1 Kings 15:18), and the second, son of Hazael, waged several wars against Israel during the reigns of Ahab and Joash. Ben-Hadad led significant armies: during his conflict with Ahab, he commanded thirty-two allied kings (1 Kings 20:16), and he launched massive attacks against Israel. Despite his military power, he sometimes had to negotiate or flee from the Israelites, as when he fled on horseback after his defeat (1 Kings 20:20). The mention of Damascus, the capital of Syria, underscores that Ben-Hadad was an established and influential monarch in the Levant.
H1130G.origine: The name "Ben-Hadad" literally means "son of Hadad," where "ben" means "son" in Hebrew and Aramaic. Hadad was a Syrian god of storm and fertility, worshiped in Syria-Aram. It was common for Syrian kings to take or bear a name related to Hadad, reflecting their connection to the local religion. This name reflects the religious and political culture of the Aramean kingdom in the 1st millennium B.C.
H1130G.emploi: Ben-Hadad appears 17 times in the biblical texts, almost exclusively in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles (chapters 15 to 20), with a prophetic mention in Jeremiah 49:27. The first Ben-Hadad (9th century) is presented as a powerful king against whom Asa sends tributes and gifts to gain his support against the Northern kingdom (1 Kings 15:18-20). His successor, during Ahab's reign, becomes a major adversary: 1 Kings 20 recounts his repeated military campaigns against Israel, his negotiations, his defeats, and his flights. The texts depict a feared leader but also a politician, capable of negotiating peace with King Ahab in exchange for his life (1 Kings 20:32-34). These accounts illustrate the Syrian-Israelite wars of the 9th century B.C.

sens: King of Syria contemporary with King Asa of Judah
King of Syria son of Hazael
H1130H.detail:
1. Ben-Hadad is a king of Syria who reigned during the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel and Judah. He appears in the accounts of the prophet Elisha, where he besieges the city of Samaria in Israel (2 Kings 6:24), then falls ill and sends Hazael to consult Elisha to know if he will recover (2 Kings 8:7-9).
2. A second Ben-Hadad, son of Hazael, is also king of Syria and bears the same name as his predecessor. He represents the continuity of the Syrian royal dynasty during the Old Testament period.
H1130H.origine: The name Ben-Hadad literally means "son of Hadad," where Hadad is the name of a false deity worshiped in Syria. This name reflects the religious culture of Syria and the common practice of giving royal children names related to the gods. Ben-Hadad is a dynastic title that has been borne by at least two consecutive kings, indicating the importance of this name in the Syrian royal succession.
H1130H.emploi: Ben-Hadad appears three times in the biblical text, all occurrences found in the second book of Kings and concerning the relations between Syria and the Northern kingdom (Israel). The first Ben-Hadad besieges Samaria and seeks to heal from his illness through the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 6:24, 8:7-8). His successor, also named Ben-Hadad and son of Hazael, continues the Syrian royal tradition. These passages reveal the political and military tensions between the kingdoms of the Levant at that time.
H1130H.portee: These accounts show that even the kings of pagan nations and enemies of Israel are subject to the sovereignty of God. The prophet Elisha intervenes in the affairs of Syria not only for God's people but also to fulfill divine plans. This testifies to the universal scope of God's power that extends beyond the borders of Israel.

sens: king of Syria, son of Hazael
contemporary ruler of the king of Israel Joash
H1130I.detail:
1. Ben-Hadad is the son of Hazael who became king of Syria after his father's death (2 Kings 13:24). His name means "son of Hadad," named after a pagan deity worshiped in Syria. He represents the hostile power that God allowed against Israel during the reign of Joash, the father of Joash.
2. It is under Joash's reign that Israel begins to recover: the king of Israel defeats him three times and regains the cities that Hazael had conquered, thus showing the turning point that God works in favor of His people (2 Kings 13:25). The prophet Amos also announces him among God's judgments against enemy nations (Amos 1:4).
H1130I.origine: The name Ben-Hadad literally means "son of Hadad." Hadad was the god of storm and fertility worshiped by the Syrians. In Hebrew, "ben" means "son." This name indicates that it was believed at the time that the king derived his legitimacy from a deity, a common practice among ancient Near Eastern kings.
H1130I.emploi: Ben-Hadad is mentioned four times in the Bible, exclusively in the context of the political history of Israel and Syria around the 9th century B.C. He appears mainly in 2 Kings 13, which recounts the military relations between Syria and the Northern Kingdom (Israel) under Joash. The prophet Amos also cites him to predict God's judgment against Damascus, the Syrian capital. The passages show a powerful Syrian king ultimately defeated by God's grace, which uplifts Israel.
H1130I.portee: Ben-Hadad illustrates how God controls the history of nations and even turns hostile powers to serve His purposes. The transition from oppression (under Hazael and at the beginning of Ben-Hadad's reign) to Joash's victory shows that God never leaves His people without hope and that faithfulness to His covenant bears fruit, even if late.

sens: Man of the Jewish community during the exile and return
Head of a family among those who returned with Zerubbabel
Assistants in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem
H1131G.detail: Binnuï is the name of a man belonging to the generation of exiles who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. He is mentioned in Nehemiah 7:15 as the head of a family of 648 people who returned with Zerubbabel. His name literally means "built" or "edified," evoking the image of a house or a built work. This man bore the same name as a Levite contemporary of Ezra, indicating that several people shared this name among the exiles returning from captivity.
H1131G.origine: The name Binnuï comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to build" or "to construct." Its literal meaning, "built" or "edified," was a common symbolic name among the Hebrews, evoking an established and founded family or lineage. Other similar forms of the name, such as Bani, were also borne by members of the Jewish community upon their return from exile.
H1131G.emploi: Binnuï is mentioned only once in the Bible according to the Segond translation: in Nehemiah 7:15, among the list of family heads who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. This passage enumerates the families that formed the first wave of returnees, and Binnuï is listed with his large descendants of 648 people. This historical mention is set in the context of the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Jewish community after captivity.

sens: Levite during the time of Ezra, father of Noadiah
H1131H.detail: 1. Binnuï is a Levite who lived at the time of the return from exile, under the reign of King Artaxerxes. He is mentioned only as the father of Noadiah, a Levite who helps weigh and record the gold, silver, and sacred objects brought from the temple in Babylon during the return to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:33). His son Noadiah works alongside other officials for this sacred mission of restoring the temple's goods.
H1131H.origine: The name Binnuï literally means "built" or "edified" in Hebrew, deriving from the root that evokes the idea of building, erecting. It is a meaningful name, common for Levites of that time, reflecting a faith in the reconstruction of the people and the temple after exile.
H1131H.emploi: Binnuï appears only once in the biblical texts, in Ezra 8:33, where he is identified as the father of Noadiah. He is among the important Levites of the return from exile, at the end of the sixth century B.C. The mention of his son in this official responsibility suggests that he came from a respected and trustworthy family of Levites for temple affairs.

sens: Levite during the time of Ezra who had married a foreign woman
H1131I.detail: 1. Binnuï is a Levite who lived at the time of the return from exile, under the reign of King Artaxerxes. He appears in the list of men who had taken foreign wives and who had to repudiate them to comply with God's law (Ezra 10:30).

No other details about this man are provided by Scripture.

sens: Levite during the time of Ezra who took a foreign wife

He appears in the list of men who acknowledged having married non-Israelite women and who committed to correct this situation (Ezra 10:38). H1131J.origine: The name means "edified" or "built" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the action of building. It is a Levite name from the time of the return from exile, borne by several men at that time.

This passage is part of the record of families who transgressed the marriage law during the return from exile to Jerusalem.

sens: Man who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
H1131K.detail: Binnuï is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile. Son of Henadad, he worked to repair a section of the wall, between the house of Azariah and the corner of the city (Nehemiah 3:24). His name means "built" or "edified," which is particularly fitting since he himself participated in building.

H1131K.emploi: Binnuï appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:24. He is presented as a worker on the reconstruction project of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's direction, likely after the return from Babylonian exile. His inclusion in this list of builders of the wall shows that he was a trustworthy man, capable of leading a team on an important section of the restoration work of the holy city.

sens: Levite contemporary of Ezra and Nehemiah, active in the restoration of the temple and the Jewish community upon returning from exile
H1131L.detail: 1. Binnuï is a Levite who appears in the lists of religious leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Ezra and Nehemiah. In Nehemiah 10:9, he is among the Levites who sign the solemn covenant of the people with God, a solemn commitment to uphold the Law of Moses.
H1131L.origine: The name Binnuï literally means "built" or "established" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the action of building. His name appears without additional biographical details, which is typical of these administrative and religious lists from the return from exile.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H1132.detail: Ben-Zoheth is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible within a genealogy. His name literally means "son of Zoheth," and he is presented as the son of Ishi and the brother of Zoheth (1 Chronicles 4:20). He appears in the list of descendants of Judah, with no particular event from his life reported in the Bible.

H1132.emploi: Ben-Zoheth appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20, where the genealogies of Judah are listed. The Bible provides no information about his life, actions, or historical significance; he is simply named among the descendants of Judah during the divided monarchy.

sens: Man of the united monarchy in Israel

Ben-Hur held an important position at Solomon's court: he was one of the twelve officers responsible for providing for the needs of the king and his household. He was specifically in charge of the mountainous region of Ephraim (1 Kings 4:8), which shows that Solomon had divided his kingdom into administrative districts, each assigned to an officer.
H1133G.origine: The name "Ben-Hur" is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ben" (בֶּן), which means "son," and "Hur" (חוּר), whose etymology evokes whiteness or purity. H1133G.emploi: Ben-Hur appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:8. sens: Prince or chief appointed by King Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in the cities of Judah
H1134.detail: Ben-Haïl is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once, during the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were separated. He was one of the princes or chiefs that King Jehoshaphat sent to the cities of Judah to teach the book of the Law of the Lord to the people (2 Chronicles 17:7). His role was therefore educational and religious: to contribute to the instruction of the people in the knowledge of God.
H1134.origine: The name Ben-Haïl literally means "son of strength" or "son of power" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "ben" (son) and "haïl" (strength, power, vigor). This type of name reflects the importance or vigor expected of the character, a common practice in Hebrew onomastics.
H1134.emploi: Ben-Haïl appears only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:7. He is cited among the religious leaders that King Jehoshaphat of Judah mobilized for a national campaign of teaching and evangelization. This mission took place during a period of religious reform and a return to obedience to God under the reign of this pious king. His mention in this context indicates that he was a respected authority figure, capable of instructing the populations.
H1134.portee: This character illustrates how God uses spiritual and civil leaders to convey His Word to future generations. Ben-Haïl reminds us that religious education is not solely the responsibility of the temple or the priest, but can be entrusted to local authorities. His example, though brief, demonstrates the biblical importance of spreading the knowledge of God through systematic teaching.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H1135.detail: Ben-Hanan is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 4:20. He is presented as the son of Shimon and the brother of Amnon, Rinna, and Tilon. His name means "son of favor" in Hebrew, composed of ben ("son") and Hanan ("favor" or "grace"). Although little known, he belongs to the genealogy of Judah, placing him during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel.
H1135.origine: The name Ben-Hanan is composed of two Hebrew elements: ben ("son") and Hanan ("grace, favor"). The name expresses the blessing of a son received as a divine favor. He is listed among the descendants of Shimon, alongside his brothers Amnon, Rinna, and Tilon. sens: Gadite warrior during the time of King David
H1137G.detail: Bani is a man of the tribe of Gad, enrolled among the mightiest warriors of David. His name appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:36, where he is mentioned as part of the thirty "mighty men" of the king.
H1137G.origine: The name Bani means "built" or "established" in Hebrew, suggesting perhaps the idea of solidity or strength. It is a simple and common name in Israel during the time of the monarchy, with no particular etymological link to the warrior context.
H1137G.emploi: Bani appears only once in Scripture: in 2 Samuel 23:36, where he is listed among the mighty warriors of David. He is presented as originating from Gad, one of the tribes east of the Jordan known for its formidable warriors. This brief mention fits into the role that the Gadites played as elite soldiers in the service of the kings of Israel.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, ancestor of Ethan the musician
Man of the tribe of Gad, one of David's mighty warriors
Man of Judah, from the lineage of Perez
Head of a family whose descendants returned from captivity
Levite during the time of Nehemiah
H1137H.detail:
1. Bani is a Levite from the line of Merari, mentioned as the ancestor of Ethan, who was one of the musicians in the temple during the time of David. He appears in the genealogy of the Levites in 1 Chronicles 6:46.

2. Another Bani was a man of the tribe of Gad and one of David's renowned warriors, those who joined the royal army.

3. A Bani from Judah was part of the lineage of Perez, one of the prominent families of this tribe.

4. After the Babylonian exile, descendants of Bani were among the repatriates who returned with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple and Jerusalem.

5. During the time of Governor Nehemiah, there were several Levites bearing this name who played a role in the religious restoration of Israel.
H1137H.origine: The name Bani literally means "built" in Hebrew, derived from the root that denotes the action of building. This name was borne by several important men in the history of Israel, particularly among the Levites and warriors. The repetition of the name across different generations and contexts indicates that it was a common and esteemed name in the families of Levi.
H1137H.emploi: Bani is the name of several different men in the Old Testament, living at different times. The primary biblical usage places him in the Levitical genealogy in 1 Chronicles 6:46, where he appears as the son of Shamer and father of Amzi, in the direct line of Merari leading to the musician Ethan. The Bible also mentions Bani among David's warriors, among the men of Judah, and among those who returned from exile. The context of the genealogies in Chronicles shows the importance given to the lineages of the Levites in temple service.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah at the time of the Exile and the Return
H1137I.detail: 1. Bani is a man of Judah mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 9:4, where he appears in a genealogy: he is the ancestor of Imri, from whom Uthai descends. This passage lists the first inhabitants who settled in Jerusalem after the return from captivity, showing that Bani is among those who contributed to the rebuilding of the people.
H1137I.origine: The name Bani literally means "built" or "constructed," derived from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of building. It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, often expressing a form of trust in God. Several individuals bear this name in Scripture, but this one is identified as a man of the lineage of Perez, in the tribe of Judah.
H1137I.emploi: Bani appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:4, in a post-exilic genealogical context. He is named as the ancestor of Imri, who is the father of Uthai. This passage is part of a list of descendants of Judah who were among the first to return and inhabit Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. This mention highlights the importance of the people's return and the transmission of genealogies as proof of the continuity of God's people.

sens: Man of the time of the Exile and the Return
Name meaning "he who has built"
H1137J.detail: 1. Bani is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:34, among the men who had married foreign women and had to separate from them upon returning from exile. The text lists his sons: Maadai, Amram, and Uel. 2. His name means "he who has built" in Hebrew, derived from the root בנה (bana), which means "to build." Although few details are given, this name reflects the values of reconstruction that characterize the time of the Return after the Babylonian exile.
H1137J.origine: The name Bani comes from the Hebrew root בנה (bana), which means "to build." The same root appears in words like בַּיִת (bayit, "house"). This name evokes the action of building, creating a lasting structure. It is an appropriate name for a time of national and spiritual reconstruction after the Babylonian exile.
H1137J.emploi: Bani appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:34. The context is that of Ezra's reform, when the repatriates from Babylon are urged to send away their foreign wives to preserve the purity of God's people. Among the descendants of this Bani are three sons: Maadai, Amram, and Uel. Although the text does not specify further who Bani himself was, his name appears in this official list of men affected by this drastic measure.

sens: Man of Judah at the time of the Exile and the Return
H1137K.detail: Bani is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:38, among the men who had taken foreign wives and who repudiated them at Ezra's command after the return from captivity.
H1137K.origine: The name Bani means "built" in Hebrew, derived from the root bny which means "to build." It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, but several people bear this name at different periods in Israel's history.

sens: Man of Judah at the time of the Exile and the Return
Father of Rehum, a Levite
H1137L.detail:

sens: Levite teacher and spiritual leader in Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah

His repeated appearance in these accounts shows that he was a respected and active figure in the reconstruction of the Jewish community and its worship in Jerusalem.

sens: A man from the time of Exile and Return
Leader of the people of Judah who signed the covenant

H1137N.origine: The name Bani means "he who has built" in Hebrew, derived from the root banah which means "to build." It is a meaningful name in the context of the Return: the people were in the process of rebuilding the temple and the community after the devastation of the exile.
H1137N.emploi: Bani is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:14, where he is listed among the leaders of the people who affix their seal to the covenant. Here, in Nehemiah, he is a leader who plays a public role in the spiritual restoration of Jerusalem.
H1137N.portee: This character reminds us that the return from exile was not just a material reconstruction of the temple, but a renewal of the covenant between God and His people. By signing this covenant, Bani represents the personal commitment of the leaders to guide the people in obedience to the Law and faithfulness to God.

sens: Man of the time of the Exile and the Return
Levitical leader in Jerusalem
Father of Uzzi

His role was to oversee the Levites responsible for liturgical services at the house of God, indicating that he was a man of trust and responsibility in the reconstruction of Israel's religious life.

sens: Character from the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem

H1137P.emploi: Bani is mentioned in Nehemiah 10:13 as one of the important Levites of Nehemiah's time. sens: man of the line of Judah who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel
father of a family whose descendants returned from exile

His sons or descendants played an important role during the return: some of them are mentioned as having to repudiate their foreign wives at the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:29), which shows that his family had ties to the restoration of the Judean community.

sens: Levite during the time of Nehemiah

His role is that of a religious leader participating in this public and solemn prayer.

sens: Levite during the time of Nehemiah who signed the covenant with God

sens: City in the territory of Israel assigned to the tribe of Dan

sens: construction or erected work
architectural structure of a building
set of walls and framework of a house
H1140.detail:
1. The word refers to a construction, a structure built with solid materials (stone, wood). In Ezekiel 41:13, it refers to measuring the building of the temple, that is, its total structure in length, the walls, and everything that composes it.
2. By extension, it can refer to the work or the edifice itself in its architectural entirety — here, the built space of the temple with its dimensions and material proportions.
H1140.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "bnh" (to build, to erect). Biniah is the name of the concept of construction, the action of building transformed into an object: what has been built. This root is very common in Hebrew (it is found in binah, understanding, and in ben, son — one who is "built" by his parents). The word characterizes the finished work of the builder.
H1140.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 41:13, where the prophet describes the measurements of the temple rebuilt after the exile. It is a technical term in the architectural and priestly context: it precisely designates the built structure of the temple, distinguishing between the empty space (the place) and the constructed mass (the building itself with its walls). The unique usage does not allow for nuances of meaning, but the context shows that it is a term of measurement and sacred geometry.
H1140.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us of the importance of God's house and its concrete materiality. God does not dwell only in the abstract or the spiritual: the Bible precisely describes the dimensions and structure of His temple. This teaches that God sanctifies space and matter, and that the orderly construction of the temple reflects divine order and beauty.

sens: Military leader under David and Solomon, son of Jehoiada
H1141G.detail: Benaja is a major historical figure during the reign of David and the beginning of Solomon's reign. Son of the priest Jehoiada, he is first the chief of the royal guard (the Cherethites and Pelethites), then becomes commander-in-chief of the army in place of Joab after Solomon's ascension. He is known for his military exploits: in 2 Samuel 23:20-22, the text reports that he killed two Moabite warriors and a lion in a pit, which earned him great renown. During the Davidic succession, he remains loyal to Solomon against the rebellion of Adonijah, which explains his promotion. He regularly appears alongside the priests and prophets at key moments of royal power, notably during Solomon's coronation in 1 Kings 1:38-44.
H1141G.origine: The name means "the Lord has built" or "Yahweh has erected" — composed of "Yah" (God) and "to build." This name expresses trust in divine construction, common among theophoric Hebrew names. Several other individuals bear this same name in the Old Testament, indicating its popularity.
H1141G.emploi: Benaja is named about 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. These references first show him as a renowned warrior among David's thirty mighty men (2 Samuel 23), then as a trusted officer in sensitive political operations during Solomon's reign: it is he whom the king sends to execute Joab (1 Kings 2:29) and Shimei. In 1 Chronicles 27, he is mentioned as the chief of a division of the army. His role evolves from warrior to political officer and then to administrator of the kingdom, embodying the continuity between David's reign and Solomon's.
H1141G.portee: Benaja illustrates rewarded loyalty: having remained loyal to Solomon during a succession crisis, he receives the highest military charge in the kingdom. His example shows that God elevates those who serve Him with integrity, but also that the politics of power entails serious and sometimes violent responsibilities. For the Christian reader, his story reminds us of the importance of remaining attached to the order established by God and to those He places in authority.

military officer commanding a division
man from the clan of Ephraim

sens: Man from the tribe of Simeon during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H1141I.detail: 1. Benaja is a man from the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of family leaders of his tribe (1 Chronicles 4:36). His name appears among the descendants of Simeon at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms.

sens: A Levite during the time of King David, musician and priest

He appears in the accounts of the organization of worship of the Lord, notably during the solemn procession of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. He held two important roles: musician, playing the lyre on "alamoth" (1 Chronicles 15:20), and priest-trumpeter, sounding the trumpet before the Ark (1 Chronicles 15:24; 16:6). Benaja was part of the musical team led by the chief Asaph (1 Chronicles 16:5), where he worked alongside other Levitical musicians.
H1141J.origine: The name Benaja means "Yahweh has built" or "The Lord has constructed." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ben" (son, servant) and the divine name with a verb expressing building. In 1 Chronicles 15:24, he is designated as a priest sounding trumpets. Finally, 1 Chronicles 16:5-6 mentions him as a member of the permanent choir established by David before the Ark, confirming his role as a musician and priest in the daily worship of the Lord.

sens: Military officer in the service of King David, chief of his personal guard and commander-in-chief of the army of Israel
H1141K.detail: Benaja is best known as one of the most famous warriors of David. The son of the priest Jehoiada, he was first appointed by the king to lead his personal guard, that is, his elite soldiers tasked with protecting him. Later, he reached the highest military position by becoming commander-in-chief of the kingdom's army. In 1 Chronicles 27:34, he is mentioned as one of the king's advisors alongside the scribe Ahithophel and the priest Abiathar, which shows the importance and prestige he enjoyed at court. His name means "Yahweh has built" or "Yahweh has established," which emphasizes that his position and strength were seen as a gift from God.
H1141K.origine: The name Benaja is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ben" (son of) and "Yah" (Yahweh), completed by the verb "bânâ" (to build, to establish). It expresses the idea that God has built or established something solid and enduring. This name was borne by several men throughout the history of Israel, but the most renowned remains the warrior during the time of David and Solomon.
H1141K.emploi: The most famous Benaja is mentioned only once in the Bible at 1 Chronicles 27:34. However, the Hebrew Bible speaks elsewhere of other Benaja: notably the "Pirathonite," a warrior among David's thirty valiant men, and several Levites and priests during David's time or later. These different men bearing the same name illustrate its popularity in Israelite families, particularly among priests and warriors of the kingdom. The Benaja who is chief of the army proved faithful to Solomon during the attempted coup by Adonijah, which earned him the retention and even expansion of his power.
H1141K.portee: Benaja's role reminds us that in God's design, military power and authority are placed in the service of the elected king. His rise shows how a man of faith and valor can ascend in dignity; his integrity in the face of political crises invites believers to remain faithful to the true leaders established by God, even in uncertainty. His name also proclaims that all strength and all building come from God, not from men.

sens: Character from the time of the Divided Monarchy, father of Zechariah
Levite from the family of Asaph, ancestor of the prophet Jahaziel
H1141L.detail:
1. Benaja is an ancestor mentioned in the genealogy of the prophet Jahaziel, who received the Spirit of the Lord during the assembly of the people in the time of King Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:14). He is a figure from the lineage of the Levites, descendants of Asaph.
2. His name means "the Lord has built" or "Yahweh has constructed," reminding us that it is God who builds the families and generations of His people. Although he is only briefly mentioned in Scripture, he is part of the lineage through which God raised up prophets and servants.
H1141L.origine: The name Benaja comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to build, to establish." The full name expresses the belief that the Lord builds and establishes—not only houses and families but also His people and His purposes. It is a chosen name that reflects faith in divine providence.

This indicates that he lived during the time of the Divided Monarchy and belonged to the musical and prophetic lineage of the temple in Jerusalem. Although not detailed, this lineage shows how God maintains a continuity of service through generations.

sens: Character mentioned in the Bible
Man from the time of the divided monarchy
H1141M.detail: Benaja is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament. The provided reference shows him active during the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah, where he served in the administration of the Temple alongside other Levites under the leadership of Conaniah and Azariah. The name means "Yahweh has built" or "Yahweh has established," expressing divine construction or edification.

H1141M.emploi: Benaja is a name borne by several important figures in Israel's history. According to sources, the name also designates one of David's mighty warriors, who later became the commander-in-chief of the army in place of Joab, showing that bearers of this name held positions of responsibility, both civil and religious, within the Israelite community.

sens: Man of Israel who took a foreign wife during the time of Ezra

Benaja is the name of an Israelite living at the time of the return from exile, mentioned in the list of men who had married foreign women and had to send them away according to Ezra's order. His appearance in the register in Ezra 10:25 places him among those who transgressed the law by contracting these mixed unions.
H1141N.origine: The name Benaja means in Hebrew "Jehovah has built" or "The Lord has constructed," formed from "Ben" (son) and "Yah" (Jehovah). It is a name borne by several important figures in the Old Testament—most notably the valiant warrior of David, son of Jehoiada, commander of the army—but the Benaja of Ezra 10:25 is a simple Israelite from the time of the Restoration.
H1141N.emploi: Benaja appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Ezra 10:25, in the list of Israelites who returned from Babylonian captivity and had committed the sin of taking wives from foreign peoples. This list, drawn up by Ezra, marks the critical moment when the people returned from exile had to purify themselves by sending away these wives to preserve separation from the pagan nations. Benaja is one of the seven sons of Parosh specifically mentioned in this communal purification.
H1141N.portee: The case of Benaja reminds us that even believers returning from captivity, having experienced the judgment of exile, remain exposed to spiritual compromises. His name present in this list invites us to contemplate how God restores His people not only through geographical return but through the call to repentance and obedience to His Word, even at the cost of painful sacrifices.

sens: Man living during the time of exile and return
One of the mighty warriors of King David
Military chief who became commander-in-chief of the army

H1141O.emploi: The name Benaja designates several distinct individuals in the Old Testament, indicating that it was a fairly common name in Israel. The most famous person is the son of Jehoiada, a major military figure and trusted man of the kings. The other Benajas are known only through brief mentions: the Ephraimite warrior, the Levitical musicians, the men during the time of Ezra. In Ezra 10:30, the only provided usage, Benaja is one of the sons of Pahath-Moab who had to send away their foreign wives to comply with the law.

sens: An Israelite during the time of Ezra who had married a foreign woman

sens: Camping site of the Israelites in the desert
Group of springs or wells in the region of Beit Jala
H1142G.detail:
1. Bené-Jaakan is a place where the people of Israel stopped and set up camp during their journey through the desert after leaving Egypt. The name literally means "sons of the flexion" or "sons of the twist," which may refer to a rugged terrain or winding water sources. It is a stop on the long march of the people toward the Promised Land, mentioned in the exact itinerary of the encampments (Numbers 33:31-32).
2. The term may also refer to a group of springs or wells (as indicated by its variant "Beeroth-bené-jaakan," literally "wells of the sons of Jaakan"), which explains why this place was chosen as a stop: it provided the necessary water for the Israelites and their flocks.
H1142G.origine: The Hebrew name "Bené-Jaakan" is composed of two elements: "bené" (בְנֵי) means "sons of" and "Jaakan" (יַעֲקָן) is a proper name whose etymology refers to Hebrew roots evoking bending, twisting, or undulation. This nominal composition is typical of place names in Hebrew, particularly those associated with water sources or remarkable geographical sites. The parallel with "Beeroth-bené-jaakan" ("wells of the sons of Jaakan") shows that the place was identified by its water resources.
H1142G.emploi: Bené-Jaakan appears twice in the Bible, only in the record of the stages of the desert journey in Numbers 33. It appears in the official itinerary of the encampments of the people, between Moseroth and Hor-Guidgad (Numbers 33:31-32). This mention in an administrative and geographical list indicates that it was a recognized and important landmark for the journey. This place remains one of the many poorly detailed stops of the Exodus, with no account of particular events that occurred there.
H1142G.portee: This name reminds the reader that the journey of the people through the desert was a succession of well-planned stages, where God provided for their needs for water and resources. It is an invitation to see divine faithfulness in the concrete details of believers' lives, and to recognize that even the unremarkable stopping places are part of God's plan.

sens: Camping site of the Israelites in the desert
H1142H.detail: 1. Jaakan is a place where the people of Israel set up camp during their journey in the desert after leaving Egypt. The full name is Beeroth-Bené-Jaakan, which means "the wells of the sons of Jaakan" — a place where there were water sources, essential for the survival of the people on their way to the Promised Land. It is at this stage that the high priest Aaron died and was buried, before his son Eleazar took his place.
H1142H.origine: The name literally means "sons of Jaakan" or "sons of the tortuous" (jaakan being related to the idea of twisting or winding). The term "Beeroth" that accompanies it means "wells" in Hebrew, designating the water points in the desert. This composite geographical name reflects the reality of the journey in the desert: the stages were named after natural features (sources, wells) and often attached to family or clan names.
H1142H.emploi: Jaakan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 10:6, as one of the stops in the journey of the Israelites in the desert after their departure from Egypt. This summary itinerary of the desert camps is given to geographically and spiritually situate the death of Aaron, a major event during the desert stay. The context shows the religious importance of the place: it is not just a stop, but the place where the ministry of Israel's first high priest comes to an end.
H1142H.portee: This place reminds us that the journey of the people of Israel toward the Promised Land was marked by precise stages, marked by God's acts and events. The mention of Aaron's death at Jaakan illustrates that even the greatest servants of God face an earthly end, and that ministry is passed down from generation to generation — a lesson on humility and the continuity of divine service.

sens: To place oneself or move in the space that separates two conflicting groups
To step out of the ranks to stand alone against the opponent
To act as a champion, representing one's army in single combat
H1143.detail:
1. The word specifically denotes the action of positioning oneself in the space that separates two armies facing each other. It is the neutral ground between the lines of battle, the no man's land where a man can stand isolated. Goliath "advanced between the two armies" in 1 Samuel 17:4, leaving the Philistine ranks to stand alone before the Israelites.
2. More precisely, the one who acts this way is a man who steps out of the ranks to challenge the enemy in single combat. It is a challenge: rather than having two entire armies clash, a warrior would step out to fight alone against a chosen warrior from the other camp. This is what Goliath does in 1 Samuel 17:23 when he "advanced between the two armies, out of the ranks of the Philistines." 
3. By extension, this term refers to the warrior who takes this position, the champion who represents his people. Goliath thus becomes "the man of the space between the two armies," the one who dares to face all opponents alone.
H1143.origine: The Hebrew word bénaïm comes from the root "ben" (between, space between two things) and fundamentally describes a passage or a defined space. This image of the man standing alone in this space has given rise to a warrior reality known in antiquity: the duel of champions, where a single warrior represented his entire army. The word captures both the place (between) and the function (champion).
H1143.emploi: This word appears twice, exclusively in the account of Goliath in 1 Samuel 17. Both occurrences describe Goliath who "advances" to leave the Philistine camp and stand alone before the Israelites: first in 1 Samuel 17:4 when he presents himself for the first time, and then in 1 Samuel 17:23 when he repeats his challenge. The term emphasizes that he voluntarily leaves the ranks of his army to occupy this liminal space where he will fight alone. It is an act of bravery and provocation: Goliath places himself forward, alone and isolated, which makes his eventual defeat by David even more symbolic.
H1143.portee: This account shows that a single man, armed with faith in God, can defeat a giant even when standing alone against him. David does not have Goliath's armor, but he advances in the name of the Lord. For the Christian, this image teaches that when one stands alone in the face of a trial or opposition, faith in God compensates for any physical or human strength. Like David, one can be victorious not by the power of the world, but by trust in the one who sends us.

sens: The youngest son of Jacob and Rachel, brother of Joseph
H1144G.detail: 1. Benjamin is the youngest son of Jacob and his beloved Rachel. His Hebrew name means "son of the right hand," which evokes a position of honor and favor. Rachel initially named him "Ben-Oni" ("son of my sorrow") as she died during childbirth, but Jacob changed this name to Benjamin (Genesis 35:18). He is the full brother of Joseph, with whom he shares their father Jacob's special love.
H1144G.origine: The name Benjamin is composed of two Hebrew elements: Ben ("son") and Yamin ("right hand"). This composition reveals how Jacob viewed the birth of his youngest son: a child of the right hand, meaning blessed, favored, preferred. In Semitic culture, the "right" symbolizes strength, blessing, and dignity. The name thus expresses the father's joy and hope despite the tragic death of the mother.
H1144G.emploi: Benjamin appears more than 150 times in the Bible, first as an individual character in Genesis, particularly in the story of Joseph: Jacob long refuses to let him go down to Egypt with his brothers, fearing he would lose him just as he lost Joseph (Genesis 42:4, 36; 43:14). After Joseph's revelation in Egypt, Benjamin becomes a link of reconciliation between the patriarch and his beloved son. Subsequently, Benjamin designates the tribe that descends from him: it receives territory around Jerusalem (Joshua 18), participates in Israel's wars, notably in the terrible civil war recounted in Judges 20-21. The tribe of Benjamin remains an important part of the southern kingdom after the division, and several notable figures come from it, including King Saul and the Apostle Paul.
H1144G.portee: Benjamin embodies a father's preferential love and how divine grace operates through the most tender family bonds. His story shows that loss and mourning are not final: Jacob, who believed Benjamin lost like Joseph, finds both alive. For the Christian, this speaks of trust in God beyond suffering, and how God restores what we believed to be irretrievably lost.

sens: Son of Bilhan, grandson of Jediael, living during the divided monarchy
H1144H.detail: 1. Benjamin is a man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. He is the son of Bilhan and the grandson of Jediael, as indicated in the only passage that explicitly mentions him: 1 Chronicles 7:10. He has several brothers: Jeusch, Ehud, Kenaana, Zethan, Tarsis, and Achishachar.
H1144H.origine: The name "Benjamin" literally means "son of the right" or "son of the right hand" in Hebrew. This name evokes both a position of honor (the right) and filiation. In the Old Testament, this name was first borne by Jacob and Rachel's youngest son, who became the ancestor of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The character of this entry is a distant namesake, living many centuries after the founding of the tribe.
H1144H.emploi: Benjamin appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, in the genealogy of the descendants of Jediael, son of Benjamin (according to 1 Chronicles 7:6). It is a simple genealogical mention, without narrative or particular action. His name appears in the list of Bilhan's children, likely compiled during the writing of the Chronicle, which recorded the genealogies of the great tribal families of Judah and Israel after the exile.

sens: A man from the time of the Exile and the Return, mentioned only in Ezra 10:32
H1144I.detail: Benjamin is a man who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return to Jerusalem, in the time of the prophet Ezra. He is mentioned in Ezra 10:32 among the sons of Harim who had married foreign women and who, at the governor's order, had to separate from them to comply with the Law. This is the only passage where this specific man is mentioned in the Bible.
H1144I.origine: The name Benjamin means "son of the right hand." In Hebrew, bin means "son" and yamin means "right." It is a common family name in Israel, carrying the idea of strength, blessing, and divine favor—the "right hand" being the symbol of power and honor. The name also carries a historical weight: Jacob named his last son this way, born of Rachel, which has marked the entire tradition of Israel.
H1144I.emploi: This Benjamin is a man of the people of Israel who, during the return from Exile to Babylon under Ezra's leadership, was in Jerusalem. According to Ezra 10:32, he belonged to the family of the sons of Harim. Like many Israelites upon returning from Exile, he had committed the grave sin of marrying a foreign woman, that is, a non-Israelite. In response to the prophet Ezra's call to repentance and separation from these unions forbidden by the Law, Benjamin was led to end this marriage, as required for the restoration of the holy people.

sens: A man from the time of the Exile and Return
Son of Bilhan, great-grandson of Benjamin the patriarch
A Benjamite who took a foreign wife during the time of Ezra

He works on the repair of the wall with Haschub, each building in front of his own house (Nehemiah 3:23). 2. The name "Benjamin" literally means "son of the right hand" — it evokes blessing and strength. This man bears the same name as one of Jacob's twelve sons, but is simply a member of the people who returned from exile to help rebuild the desolate Jerusalem. 3. Unless he is a direct descendant of the patriarch Benjamin through the line of Bilhan, he represents one of those simple workers whom the Bible celebrates for their faithfulness to the restoration of Israel, without providing further details about his life.
H1144J.origine: The name Benjamin comes from the Hebrew "ben" (son) and "yamin" (right, strength): literally "son of the right" or "son of strength." In the Old Testament, this name is primarily associated with the youngest son of Jacob and Rachel, blessed for his position as the favored youngest. The name carries the idea of blessing and divine favor, one who is born at the father's right hand, the side of honor and power.
H1144J.emploi: Benjamin appears only once in Nehemiah 3:23, during the account of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. At that time, two men named Benjamin (or two generations bearing this name) are mentioned: one works on the wall with Haschub, the other is the son of Bilhan and great-grandson of the patriarch Benjamin. The Bible provides no details about this man other than his work for the common good of the restored community.

sens: A man who lived during the Exile and Return

H1144K.emploi: Benjamin appears only once in Nehemiah 12:34, among the leaders of the Levites who ascend the wall of Jerusalem for the dedication ceremony after the reconstruction. He is not otherwise identified in this passage, and no additional details are given about his life or specific role. His name in this list suggests that he was a respectable figure in the religious community of the Return.

sens: Entry gate of Jerusalem, on the north side
Access to the territory of Benjamin
H1144L.detail: 1. A monumental gate located in the northern enclosure of Jerusalem, through which one could access the city from the north. It likely derives its name from its proximity to the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. In Jeremiah 20:2, it is at this gate that the priest Pashhur imprisons Jeremiah; it is also where the commander Jireijah captures him in Jeremiah 37:13, and where King Zedekiah stands in Jeremiah 38:7.
H1144L.origine: The name "Benjamin" literally means "son of the right hand" in Hebrew (ben = son, yamin = right), a classic biblical image of strength and favor. This gate of Jerusalem was named as such because it opened directly to the north, from where the territory of Benjamin came, the border tribe between Judah and Israel.
H1144L.emploi: The gate of Benjamin appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Jeremiah, during its last days of freedom before the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Pashhur uses it as a detention place for the prophet; then Jireijah positions himself there to check the passage of people and arrests Jeremiah; finally, King Zedekiah resides there for a time while Jeremiah is in prison. These three accounts show the gate as a strategic and monitored location in Jerusalem.

sens: A gate of Jerusalem, located to the north of the city
H1144M.detail: The gate of Benjamin was an entrance to the fortified Jerusalem, oriented towards the north, in the direction of the tribe of Benjamin. In the prophetic vision of Zechariah, it marks one of the boundaries of the transformed and elevated city (Zechariah 14:10), serving as a geographical landmark in the description of the future Jerusalem.
H1144M.origine: The name comes from Benjamin, whose meaning is "son of the right hand" — that is, the beloved son. Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob, and the gate that bears his name was located on the side where the tribe of Benjamin settled in the territory of Israel, to the north of Jerusalem.
H1144M.emploi: The gate of Benjamin appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 14:10, where it is listed among the geographical landmarks in the prophetic description of the transformed Jerusalem at the end of times. It marks a northeast boundary of the city, between Geba and Rimmon to the south, up to the gate of the angles and the tower of Hananel to the west.

sens: A person from the tribe of Benjamin
Man or woman belonging to the people of Benjamin in Israel
H1145.detail:
1. A Benjamite is a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob (also called Israel) and Rachel. His tribe settled in the central region of Canaan, north of Judah. Several important figures in Scripture are Benjamites: Saul, the first king of Israel (1 Samuel 9:21), Ehud the deliverer (Judges 3:15), and later the apostle Paul.

2. The term also broadly refers to any citizen or inhabitant of the territory occupied by this tribe. After the division of the kingdom, the Benjamites generally followed the king of Judah. In the provided usages, we see Benjamites reacting to the politics of their king (1 Samuel 22:7) or moving to meet him (2 Samuel 19:16).
H1145.origine: The name Benjamin comes from Hebrew and means "son of the right hand" or "son of the south." Benjamin was named so by his father Jacob in memory of his mother Rachel's death at his birth (Genesis 35:18). The word "Benjamite" (ben-yemini in Hebrew) is a derivative that literally means "one who belongs to Benjamin." This name reflects the tribal organization of Israel, where each tribe bore the name of its founding ancestor.
H1145.emploi: The word "Benjamite" appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings) and in the book of Esther. It is used to identify a person's tribal origin or to designate a group within the people of Israel. In Judges 3:15, it characterizes Ehud, the judge who delivers Israel from Moab's oppression. In 1 Samuel 9:21, Saul identifies himself as a Benjamite, highlighting the humility of his origin: Benjamin was a small tribe. In 1 Samuel 22:7, Saul addresses the Benjamites as his compatriots and close advisors. The term can also mark a distinction or even tension: in 2 Samuel 16:11, David speaks disdainfully of Shimei as a "Benjamite" who curses him.
H1145.portee: For the Christian reader, the Benjamites remind us that God often chooses the small and humble to accomplish His purposes. Saul, Ehud, and later Paul, all Benjamites, played decisive roles in the history of Israel and the Church. This term also shows us that our identity and human origins matter in God's economy, but they do not ultimately define us: it is divine will that prevails.

sens: Construction, edifice, built structure
Wall, partition of a construction
Architectural work in its entirety and organization
H1146.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a construction, a real edifice: it is a built structure composed of walls and rooms, such as the chambers and galleries of the temple described in Ezekiel 42:5.
2. It can also refer to the wall itself, the fundamental element of any construction: in Ezekiel 40:5, the outer wall surrounding the house is measured as an essential part of the building.
3. More broadly, the word is used to speak of a complete architectural work, with its dimensions and various parts organized together: in Ezekiel 41:15, the building is measured in its total length with all its galleries.
H1146.origine: The Hebrew word binyan comes from the root bnh ("to build, construct"), the same root that gives "ben" ("son", in the primary sense of "built"). It is a noun of action or result: the building is what has been built, the product of construction. The Aramaic equivalent binyan follows the same formation and is used in the Aramaic parts of the Bible.
H1146.emploi: The word appears six times, all in the book of Ezekiel, in chapters 40 to 42, where the prophet describes in detail the temple and its structures. It always refers to constructions or parts of the temple: walls of precise measurements, stacked chambers, galleries. The context is strictly architectural and technical — the verbs "measure" recur constantly. The word has no particular figurative or religious value in these passages: it is a concrete and practical term for discussing the spatial organization of the edifice.
H1146.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that the Bible describes the temple with precision and realism. These measurements, these chambers, these walls are not vague or symbolic: God cares about the solidity, order, and concrete beauty of His dwelling. It is an invitation to see that faith is not abstract — it is embodied in places, forms, and correct proportions.

sens: Construction, building intended for a specific use
In a figurative sense, the entirety of a structure or organization
H1147.detail:
1. The word designates a construction, a material building that is erected. In Ezra 5:4, the Persian authorities ask for the names of the men who are building the edifice of the temple: they refer to the physical structure being erected.
2. By extension, the word can evoke anything that is built or constituted progressively, in a literal or figurative sense — a constructed work, an established organization.
H1147.origine: The Aramaic word binyan comes from the common root in Semitic languages meaning "to build, construct." It also appears in Hebrew (bin.yan בִּנְיָן) with the same meaning. The family of words derived from it all refer to the act of construction and the result of that act.
H1147.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Ezra (Ezra 5:4). It arises in the context of the reconstruction of the temple after the exile: the Persian officials question the builders about the names of the master builders. It is a technical and concrete term used to discuss the construction site of the temple in Jerusalem.
H1147.portee: This word reminds us that the temple was not an abstraction but a concrete structure, rebuilt stone by stone. It also illustrates the continuity of the people after the exile: despite obstacles and questions from foreign authorities, the work of reconstruction progresses.

sens: Levite who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah upon the return from exile
H1148.detail: Beninu is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during Israel's return from exile in Babylon. He is among those who signed the solemn covenant made under Nehemiah's leadership to commit to obeying God's Law. His name appears in the list of signatories, alongside other religious and lay leaders of Israel (Nehemiah 10:13).
H1148.origine: The name Beninu literally means "our son" in Hebrew, formed from "ben" (son) and the possessive pronoun "nu" (our). It is a theophoric name typical of the exile and return period, where names often expressed belonging to God's community or the hope of a restored new generation.
H1148.emploi: Beninu appears only once in Scripture, in Nehemiah 10:13. He is cited among the Levites who affixed their seal to the covenant document that Nehemiah and the leaders of Israel signed to commit to respecting the Lord's Law, not profaning the Sabbath, and not contracting mixed marriages. This list bears witness to the religious and moral reorganization of Israel after the return from captivity.

sens: To experience intense irritation, a fury that disrupts reason
To express one's indignation through violent words or actions
H1149.detail:
1. To experience intense irritation, a fury that disrupts reason: the word describes the emotional state of a person seized by anger, a strong passion that disturbs their judgment. In Daniel 2:12, King Nebuchadnezzar "became angry" when the wise men could not interpret his dream: it is an immediate and powerful reaction to frustration.
2. To express one's indignation through violent words or actions: anger is not just an internal feeling; it is expressed through behaviors: the king does not merely feel irritation; he "became violently angry" and ordered an execution, showing that his anger generates drastic actions.
H1149.origine: The verb בְּנַס (benas) belongs to the family of Semitic roots that express agitation and fury. In Aramaic, this verbal form (the imperfect of the verb) literally means "to be set in motion" or "to become enraged." The word evokes the image of a person agitated, disturbed from within, who cannot be controlled. It is the emotional language of characters in a state of passionate excitement.
H1149.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:12. It is a characteristic word of the context of Daniel, written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew. In this unique passage, it paints the reaction of King Nebuchadnezzar to the impotence of his wise men: the royal anger that triggers a deadly decree. The context shows that this anger is not a mere annoyance, but a passion that leads to serious and immediate consequences.
H1149.portee: This word reminds us how anger, especially in one who holds power, can lead to terrible and thoughtless acts. For the Christian reader, it serves as a warning: uncontrolled anger becomes destructive. It also shows how God protects His own (Daniel and his companions) in the face of the decrees of furious kings.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H1150.detail: Binea is a distant ancestor of King Saul, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. His name appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as the son of Motsa and the father of Rapha, Eleasa, and Atsel (1 Chronicles 8:37).
H1150.origine: The name Binea means "fountain" in Hebrew, evoking a source of water. It is a typical name of the Benjaminite heritage, passed down from generation to generation within this family line.
H1150.emploi: Binea is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles: in 8:37 and 9:43. These two passages provide the same Benjaminite genealogy, placing Binea in the lineage of Jonathan, the son of King Saul. He appears in genealogical lists intended to establish the tribal and royal heritage of Israel.

sens: son of Lot and his younger daughter, ancestor of the Ammonites
H1151.detail: Ben-Ammi is the son that Lot's younger daughter had by her father during the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. Born in the mountains where Lot had taken refuge with his two daughters after the catastrophe, Ben-Ammi became the father and founder of the Ammonite people, who inhabited the region east of the Jordan and played an important role in the history of Israel (Genesis 19:38).
H1151.origine: The name literally means "son of my people" in Hebrew: "ben" means "son" and "ami" means "my people." It is a name that emphasizes the kinship with Israel: the Ammonites and the Israelites are descended from Lot, Abraham's uncle, and thus share a common patriarchal origin.
H1151.emploi: Ben-Ammi appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 19:38, during the account of Lot's last days in Sodom. This single verse recounts his birth and establishes his role as the founder of the Ammonites, a people that the Bible frequently mentions later in the historical and prophetic books as neighbors and sometimes adversaries of Israel.
H1151.portee: The name Ben-Ammi reminds us that even peoples foreign to Israel had known ancestors and a history linked to that of God's people. His existence shows how God weaves the destinies of nations, even in the darkest and most unexpected circumstances.

sens: Man from the time of the Exile and Return, father of Meschullam
H1152.detail: Besodia is a Jew mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the exiles return to Jerusalem and rebuild the city's walls under the leadership of Nehemiah. His son Meschullam appears among those who repair the old gate of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:6). Besodia himself is known only through this lineage: he is never named as a direct participant in these works.
H1152.origine: The name Besodia literally means "in the counsel of the Lord" or "in the secret of the Lord." It expresses the idea that this man or his family acts under divine guidance or protection. It is a typical name from the post-exilic period, where many names carry a confession of trust in God.
H1152.emploi: Besodia appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 3:6. He is simply the patronymic of Meschullam, one of the men who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the Return from Babylonian exile. His inclusion in this list shows that his family played its part in the restoration of the holy city, even though he himself remains in the background.

sens: Name of a group of temple servants who returned from exile
H1153.detail: Bésaï is the name of a family of servants attached to the temple of Jerusalem. This family returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel during the restoration of the temple and worship in Jerusalem (Ezra 2:49). The same group is mentioned again a few decades later in Nehemiah's list (Nehemiah 7:52), showing that these servants established themselves durably in restored Judea.
H1153.origine: The name Bésaï means "my treading" or "my footstep" in Hebrew, evoking an action of treading, possibly an image of service or work. In the lists of the return, Bésaï is listed among the descendants of the temple servants (nethinim), a category of workers dedicated to the service of the sanctuary since ancient times.
H1153.emploi: Bésaï appears twice in the Bible, in the two major lists of those who returned from exile (Ezra 2:49 and Nehemiah 7:52). These lists enumerate the family groups that accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from Babylon, around 538 BC. Bésaï is classified among the temple servants, an important religious and social function.

sens: Bunch of immature, green, and sour grapes picked before maturity
Figuratively, insufficient fruit or deprived of its natural development
H1154.detail:
1. The word refers to small green grapes that are not yet ripe: fruits that have not had time to fully form and accumulate their sugar. In Job 15:33, the vine is described as "stripped" of these green grapes, meaning emptied, rid of all its still immature fruits — an image of destruction and total loss.
2. The word is used figuratively to evoke an incomplete result, an unfinished work, or a benefit that has not had time to mature. The green grapes that fall symbolize what cannot reach its fulfillment.
H1154.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "greenness" and immaturity. There is a more frequent graphic variant (בֹּסֶר, boseɾ) in the Hebrew text. The basic image is that of the green, sour, and underdeveloped fruit — the complete opposite of the ripe and sweet grape that represents blessing and abundance.
H1154.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Job 15:33). It is used in a discourse where Job's friend describes the ruin of the wicked: the perverse man will see his vine completely stripped of its green fruits, just as an olive tree loses its flowers — a double image of sterility and complete destruction. The context is that of divine punishment that removes from the guilty all hope of harvest and prosperity.
H1154.portee: This word reminds us that God alone controls time and fulfillment. It invites us to patiently await true maturity rather than seeking to harvest prematurely. For the believer, it is also a warning: the fruit that has not had time to mature remains sour and worthless — a lesson on the importance of perseverance and completeness in spiritual life.

sens: Unripe grape, still sour
Food that causes an unpleasant physical reaction
Image of the wrongs committed by parents whose children suffer the consequences
H1155.detail:
1. The green grape is an unripe grape, still hard and very sour. In Isaiah 18:5, the text speaks of the flower that becomes a "grape" that ripens, showing the natural progression of the fruit.
2. Eating a green grape causes an unpleasant sensation: the teeth become "agitated," meaning they are irritated and become sensitive, as if they are contracting. This is a very tangible physical experience, well known to all.
3. In Jeremiah 31:29 and 30 and in Ezekiel 18:2, this sour fruit becomes an image: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" expresses the idea that the sins committed by one generation lead to suffering for the next. But the context adds that each will answer for their own actions, not for the actions of others.
H1155.origine: The Hebrew word bôser literally designates the immature grape, the fruit before its maturation. It is a concrete word, an image of incomplete development. The related verb (form besar) refers to this immaturity. This term paints a visible agricultural reality in a wine-producing region like Palestine, where green grapes contrast sharply with ripe and sweet grapes.
H1155.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular or in agricultural context. Three occurrences form a popular proverb (Jeremiah 31:29 and 30, Ezekiel 18:2) illustrating how ancient Israelites thought about the transmission of the consequences of sin. One occurrence in Isaiah 18:5 describes the natural cycle of the grape that ripens, an image of Judea in the process of maturation. The basic meaning (immature fruit) remains constant, but the proverb imbues the word with a moral and theological significance.
H1155.portee: This word reminds us that our actions have consequences that can affect others. But it also teaches that God judges each person personally for what they have truly done, not for the faults of others. It is a call to individual responsibility and divine grace.

sens: Address a request to someone
Actively seek, in search of something or someone
Address God to implore His grace, mercy, or help
Urgently ask, solicit insistently
H1156.detail:
1. Address a request to someone: this means making known one's desire or need to a person capable of fulfilling it. Daniel "prayed" the king to appoint others to oversee Babylon (Daniel 2:49): he submits an official, respectful request to him.
2. Actively seek: the word denotes the quest, the effort to find or reach something. When the wise men of Babylon "sought" Daniel to put him to death (Daniel 2:13), they were searching for him to locate and arrest him.
3. Address God in supplication: this is the most serious meaning. Daniel "prayed" to his God every day (Daniel 6:11), not to make an ordinary request, but to implore His grace, forgiveness, and help. The three young men "implore" the mercy of the God of heaven (Daniel 2:18) in the face of the danger of death.
4. Urgently ask or seek an opportunity: the word expresses persistence, intention. Daniel's enemies "sought" an opportunity to accuse him (Daniel 6:4), scrutinizing his actions to find a flaw.
H1156.origine: It is an Aramaic verb whose root evokes the idea of addressing someone, seeking their attention or help. The word belongs to the small corpus of biblical Aramaic (the Aramaic sections of the book of Daniel). The context of Daniel primarily reveals the meaning of praying, supplicating, especially when it involves turning to God in the face of danger or adversity.
H1156.emploi: This verb appears twelve times in the book of Daniel, making it one of its key terms for prayer and request. In Daniel 2, it first refers to the mourning of the wise men and the supplication of the three young men to God (verses 13, 18, 23). Daniel himself uses it to address a request to the king (2:49). In Daniel 6, the word recurs five times around Daniel's prayer despite the king's edict, and then in the account of his deliverance. The meaning varies: seek (to locate someone), pray (to implore God), ask (request to the king). This flexibility shows that the verb covers the entire spectrum of respectful and urgent address to the one who can act.
H1156.portee: For the reader, this word shows prayer not as a passive and distant act, but as a living, urgent request made face to face. In the account of Daniel, to pray is to "seek" God's grace, not to flee the world: it is to act in front of the king, in the face of danger, with frankness and persistence. It teaches the Christian that authentic prayer is a concrete request, motivated by a real need, brought confidently before the one who can help.

sens: through or by the action of
behind, at the back of
around, all around
