in the name of, in place of, on behalf of
because of
H1157.detail:
1. **Through or by the action of**: this word expresses the passage, the means by which one acts. When Noah is in the ark, "the Lord shut the door for him" (Genesis 7:16): the door closes around him, protecting his passage to the new creation.
2. **Behind, at the back of**: the image of what is located behind oneself, closed. When Ezekiel says, "a hand took me for my hair" (Ezekiel 8:3), the hand seizes from behind. This is also the meaning when one closes a window or when Samson's servant saw him "sitting behind the door" (Judges 16:27).
3. **Around, all around**: that which surrounds, encircles. "The darkness will cover me, the night becomes light around me" (Psalms 139:11): the light encircles the night.
4. **In the name of, in place of, on behalf of**: most often figurative, designating intercession, the one who pleads for another. "Do not intercede on behalf of this people" (Jeremiah 11:14): this means to speak in place of another, to take their side. Samuel says to Saul: "I will pray to the Lord for you" (1 Samuel 12:23), interceding on their behalf.
5. **Because of, for the sake of**: expresses the reason, the motive. "When they call on me because of their misfortune" (Jeremiah 11:14): their crisis drives them toward God.
H1157.origine: It is a Hebrew preposition formed from the root עד (*ad*), which originally meant "side, flank." With the prefix ב (*be*, "in, by"), it takes on the meaning of "by the side of, around." In Aramaic, it is used in a similar way. This root is related to the idea of movement that goes around, passes by something, or crosses it.
H1157.emploi: This word is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (82 occurrences). It is mainly found in contexts of intercession and prayer: Samuel prays for Israel, David for his sick child, the priests offer sacrifices "for" the people. It is also a very ordinary preposition in spatial language: "behind" the tent, "around" the walls. In the Psalms and Jeremiah, its figurative use predominates (intercession, cause); in the narratives (Samuel, Kings), the spatial or causal meaning is more common. Its uses are concentrated in the historical and prophetic books.
H1157.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp the power of intercession in the life of prayer: to pray "for" someone is to spiritually place oneself in their position, surrounding them with one's supplication. It also shows how Christ Himself intercedes "for" us — the New Testament will see an echo of this. In daily life, seeing that God "protects" means understanding that He surrounds us with His grace.

sens: ask someone to explain
make gush or boil
swell, bulge out
be searched, be uncovered
H1158.detail:
1. Interrogate means to ask someone a question to know the truth, or to ask them to account for something. In Isaiah 21:12, the watchman says to those who interrogate him about the night: "If you want to interrogate, interrogate," meaning: ask your questions, seek to understand.
2. The word can also describe the action of making gush or boil, like water boiling over a fire. In Isaiah 64:1, the prophet evokes water that "boils," comparing God's power to a fire that makes steam rise.
3. Boiling extends to the idea of swelling or bulging: something that exceeds or comes out of its usual place, like a breach in a wall that bulges out and threatens to collapse (Isaiah 30:13).
4. The word also takes on the meaning of being searched or laid bare: when the treasures of Edom are searched and discovered, it means they are actively sought to be seized (Obadiah 1:6).
H1158.origine: This Hebrew root first evokes an action of gushing, swelling, or surging with force. The primary image is that of water boiling or something inflating. From there derives the meaning of interrogating, in the sense of "drawing something out" — drawing the truth or an answer from a person. The same root can mean to seek, examine, or search.
H1158.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the prophecies of Isaiah and in Obadiah. Each use shows a nuance: asking questions (Isaiah 21:12), boiling literally (Isaiah 64:1), bulging or swelling like a breach (Isaiah 30:13), and being searched or uncovered (Obadiah 1:6). The context is always one of revelation, an action that brings to light what was hidden.
H1158.portee: This word reminds us that God, in His judgment, brings to light all that is hidden. It also invites the believer to interrogate, to seek to understand divine will with honesty and sincerity. The search for truth and acceptance of divine judgment involves sincere questioning.

sens: Request, supplication addressed to someone
Prayer addressed to God in religious life
H1159.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a request or supplication presented to someone, particularly to a king or authority. It is a formal, respectful request. In the account of Daniel, the officials of the kingdom ask King Darius to issue a decree prohibiting the presentation of "prayers" (petitions, requests) to any god or man for thirty days (Daniel 6:7) — an attempt to trap Daniel.
2. In Jewish religious life, the word specifically applies to prayer, that is, the supplication addressed to God. When Daniel continues to make his "prayer" three times a day despite the king's prohibition (Daniel 6:13), it refers to his usual prayers, his intimate conversations with God. This liturgical, spiritual sense predominates in Jewish usage.
H1159.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to ask" or "to seek." It is formed to express the idea of a request presented with respect and insistence. In Jewish religious language, this term has specialized to designate cultic prayer, the supplication addressed to God in worship.
H1159.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, both in the book of Daniel and in passages related to the same episode: the decree of King Darius against Daniel. In Daniel 6:7, it refers to the formal requests that a subject can present to an authority (a god or a king). In Daniel 6:13, it takes on the specific meaning of religious prayer, Daniel's daily practice of turning to God three times a day. It is an administrative term that becomes spiritual depending on the context.
H1159.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage illustrates faithfulness in prayer despite opposition and threat. Daniel does not give up his dialogue with God in the face of a royal prohibition: this shows that prayer is a need of the soul, stronger than fear. It is an encouragement to maintain one's personal prayer life regardless of obstacles.

sens: Father of Bela, king of Edom
Father of Balaam the diviner
H1160G.detail:
1. Beor is the father of Bela, who reigned over Edom before the kings of Israel ruled over their people (Genesis 36:32). Bela governed from the city of Dinhabah.
2. Beor is also mentioned in the Bible as the father of Balaam, the diviner whom King Balak wanted to curse Israel (although this second usage is not included in the references provided here, biblical tradition reports it).
H1160G.origine: The name Beor means "burning" or "the burn" in Hebrew. It is an ancient name, attested since the time of the patriarchs. It designates an ancestor of Edom, the brother nation of Israel descended from Esau.
H1160G.emploi: Beor appears twice in the Bible, in the same places: Genesis 36:32 and 1 Chronicles 1:43. These two passages describe the genealogy of the kings of Edom and mention Beor as the father of Bela, the first king of Edom whose name has been preserved. The context is that of ancient genealogical lists from the Levant region. Beor thus lived during the time of the Hebrew patriarchs, but in the lineage of Esau, Jacob's brother.

sens: Father of the diviner Balaam
Father of Bela, king of Edom
H1160H.detail: Beor is the father of the diviner Balaam, mentioned for the first time when the king of Moab sends for him to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5). Balaam is presented as "son of Beor," which emphasizes his identity and origin. The name means "burning" or "the one who burns," perhaps suggesting fervor or passion. Beor is also the father of Bela, the first king of Edom, according to the genealogy texts.
H1160H.origine: The Hebrew name בְּעוֹר (Beor) literally means "the one who burns" or "burning" (from the root עוּר, to be inflamed). This patronym appears as a simple family designation in biblical texts. The recurring mention of "Balaam, son of Beor" highlights the importance of tracing the lineage of powerful or renowned figures in the ancient Near East.
H1160H.emploi: Beor appears 8 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the expression "Balaam, son of Beor." He is first mentioned in Numbers 22:5, when the ambassadors of the king of Moab seek to bring Balaam from Pethor. His name recurs in Balaam's oracles (Numbers 24:3 and 24:15) to establish the authority of the prophet. He is cited at the time of Balaam's death during the battle against Midian (Numbers 31:8), and again recalled in the reproach addressed to Israel for listening to Balaam (Deuteronomy 23:4). Joshua 13:22 and 24:9 also mention this event. His name finally appears in Micah 6:5, where God Himself remembers Balaam's temptation.

sens: Intense and sudden fear
Fear inspired by God
Manifestation of divine anger
H1161.detail:
1. Terror is a violent and overwhelming fear, a fright that paralyzes. In Job 6:4, the psalmist says that the terrors of God array themselves against him like an enemy army that overwhelms him — it is the image of an organized, systematic fear that assails him from all sides.
2. These terrors come specifically from God: they are not ordinary fears, but those that God provokes in the one suffering under His hand. In Psalms 88:17, they appear alongside divine fury, as if God Himself would inspire this destructive fright in the one who cries out to Him.
3. Terror manifests God's anger in action. It is not only physical suffering but the spiritual experience of feeling abandoned or attacked by the Almighty — an inner annihilation that accompanies punishment.
H1161.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to frighten, to disturb." It is related to the idea of being seized by a fear that disorganizes, that deeply troubles. It is a noun that designates the state or event of terror rather than the one who is afraid. The word evokes the visceral experience of fright — the moment when fear seizes you and paralyzes you.
H1161.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in contexts of extreme suffering. In Job 6:4, a righteous man overwhelmed by illness speaks of the terrors of God that confront him. In Psalms 88:17, the psalmist — the one who cries out to the Lord with the most distress in the Psalms — evokes the divine terrors that destroy him. In both cases, these are not abstract terrors, but concrete and overwhelming experiences related to the apparent absence of divine compassion. The word always emphasizes the extreme emotional aspect of suffering under God's hand.
H1161.portee: This word speaks to those going through a crisis of faith, when God seems distant or hostile. It validates the real experience of spiritual terror — the Bible does not hide that suffering can include intense fright in the face of God. But by placing this word in the mouths of those who cry out to the Lord nonetheless, it shows that even this terror is not the end: one can name it and continue to pray.

sens: Man of Judah, wealthy and righteous relative of Elimelech, who became the husband of Ruth
Left pillar of the porch of Solomon's temple
H1162G.detail:
1. Boaz was a powerful and wealthy man from the tribe of Judah, related to Elimelech (Ruth 2:1). He lived during the time of the Judges, before the monarchy, and became the redeemer of Ruth, the Moabite widow of Machlon, one of Elimelech and Naomi's sons: he married her and thus became the protector of the family and the heir to the land (Ruth 4:9-13). He is an ancestor of King David.
2. Boaz is also the name of the bronze pillar placed on the left side of the porch of the temple built by Solomon (1 Kings 7:21). It measured 18 cubits high and stood opposite the right pillar, named Jakin.
H1162G.origine: The name Boaz literally means "swiftness" or "strength." Its precise root in Hebrew is unknown, but the name evokes vigor and efficiency. The historical figure Boaz bears a name that reflects his character: a man of power and action, capable of solving problems and showing justice. The pillar of Boaz, like that of Jakin, bore a symbolic name recalling the power and stability of the temple.
H1162G.emploi: The story of Ruth mentions Boaz 21 times, focusing the intrigue of the book on him. We first encounter him as the wealthy owner with whom Ruth gathers grain (Ruth 2:1-3). Boaz notices Ruth, inquires about her identity, and treats her kindly, offering her water and food (Ruth 2:5-14). He understands the situation of this unprotected foreigner and shows generosity, allowing her to glean until the end of the harvest (Ruth 2:23). Later, Boaz acts as a legal redeemer: he negotiates with a closer relative for the right to acquire Elimelech's land and marry Ruth, thus ensuring the continuity of the family (Ruth 4:1-13). The narrative reveals a man of justice, moral courage, and piety. As for the pillar, it is simply mentioned in 1 Kings 7:21 and 1 Chronicles 2:11 as an architectural element of the temple.
H1162G.portee: Boaz embodies the righteous and benevolent redeemer, one who acts with integrity to save and restore. His story shows how God guides righteous hearts through ordinary circumstances, and how quiet faith—expressed through actions—changes lives. For the believer, Boaz is a figure of God's own character, who cares for the marginalized and fulfills His promises through faithful men.

sens: Name of the left column of Solomon's temple
H1162H.detail: Boaz is the name given to the bronze column on the left that stood at the entrance of Solomon's temple. This monumental column measured 18 cubits high (approximately 9 meters) and formed a pair with its right twin, named Jakin. These two columns adorned the porch and solemnly marked the access to the holy place.
H1162H.origine: The name literally means "in him is strength" or "swiftness." It comes from a Hebrew root evoking power and vigor. These two columns had already existed at the temple in Jerusalem long before Solomon, but it was under his reign that they were cast in bronze and permanently installed as major architectural elements.
H1162H.emploi: Boaz appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 3:17, where the text reports their erection during the construction of Solomon's temple. These columns, one on the right (Jakin) and the other on the left (Boaz), constituted an important symbolic element of the sanctuary, marking the transition between the profane and the sacred. Their naming reveals the religious and architectural significance of the temple in the life of Israel.
H1162H.portee: These columns remind us that Solomon's temple was designed as the heart of Israel's worship, a structure of majesty and power meant to signify God's presence among the people. They invite the reader to meditate on the splendor of ancient worship and what it represented for the faith of the Israelites.

sens: To kick, to rear up
To reject with contempt, to trample underfoot
To rebel against God's authority
To refuse to obey with insolence
H1163.detail:
1. The literal sense is that of an animal kicking: Israel, "grown fat," has reared up like a donkey under the yoke (Deuteronomy 32:15). It is the gesture of violent refusal.
2. The verb extends to the contempt of sacred things: "trampling underfoot" the sacrifices and offerings means rejecting them disdainfully (1 Samuel 2:29). One tramples underfoot what one despises.
3. To rear up against God means to rebel against Him: it is to reject His authority like a horse that refuses to obey. The image shifts from the physical to the moral.
4. Rearing up is an act of insolence: one who rears up stands against his master, refuses his yoke, refuses to serve. It is the rebellion of the heart expressed by the gesture of the foot.
H1163.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the sudden movement of the foot— to kick, to thrust. The image is that of a horse rearing up or an animal kicking. In Hebrew, this verb primarily paints a violent gesture of the foot, from which the figurative sense of "refusing," "rejecting," "rebelling" has developed.
H1163.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first occurrence (Deuteronomy 32:15) is the clearest: Israel, satisfied and prosperous, has reared up against God—this is the rebellion of one who, forgetting where his wealth comes from, stands against his liberator. The second (1 Samuel 2:29) applies it to the sacrifices: Eli and his sons trample underfoot the offerings of the Lord, rejecting them with contempt. In both cases, the verb expresses the violent refusal to obey, the insolent contempt for the received order.
H1163.portee: This word highlights the seriousness of the sin of rebellion. To rear up is not simply to "disobey" passively: it is to actively stand against God, to reject Him with arrogance. Israel, sated, has forgotten that every blessing comes from the Lord; Eli has despised divine commandments to favor his sons. The rearing up reveals a heart that believes itself above God's authority—a particular danger for one who has received much.

sens: Domestic animals, particularly cattle and herds raised for work, food, or wealth
All the livestock belonging to a person, family, or people
H1165.detail:
1. The word refers to domestic animals that are raised: cattle, sheep, goats, and other beasts of burden or draft animals. It is a concrete term for the creatures that man feeds and exploits. Joseph tells his brothers to load their livestock to go to Egypt (Genesis 45:17); Moses must bring water from the rock to quench both the people and their livestock (Numbers 20:8, 20:11).
2. By extension, the totality of the animals one possesses becomes a measure of wealth and sustenance. When a man lets his livestock graze in another's field, he must compensate the owner (Exodus 22:5). The livestock of the people can also be struck by divine plagues, as when the Lord abandons the livestock to hail (Psalms 78:48).
H1165.origine: The Hebrew word בְּעִיר (be'ir) comes from an ancient root simply designating domestic animals, the tamed and useful creatures. It stands in contrast to wild animals. The word appears in various contexts where possession, raising, or the economic burden of a human group is discussed, reflecting the importance of livestock in ancient life.
H1165.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the provided texts, primarily in narrative prose and law. It always describes concrete domestic animals: those loaded for a journey (Genesis 45:17), those whose grazing rights must be respected (Exodus 22:5), those that must be kept alive during a desert crossing (Numbers 20:4, 20:8, 20:11), or those that can be lost through divine plagues (Psalms 78:48). The context shows that livestock is a vital resource: it is fed, protected, and for which one is responsible, and its loss is a serious deprivation.
H1165.portee: In the Bible, livestock represents man's dependence on creation and the resources that God entrusts to him. It reminds us that our possessions and means of subsistence do not belong to us outright: we are stewards of them. When the Bible mentions livestock with the people, it emphasizes that God provides for all needs, even material ones—the animals must also be watered, fed, and protected.

sens: Symbolic name given to Jerusalem
H1166G.detail: In the prophetic vision of Isaiah, Jerusalem receives the name Beutla, which means "bride" in Hebrew. This name expresses that the city, once abandoned and lonely, will be reunited with God like a bride to her husband (Isaiah 62:4). It is an image of restoration and regained happiness.
H1166G.origine: The Hebrew word בָּעַל (ba'al) comes from a root that means "to be married" or "to take as a wife." It is a name given to Jerusalem to symbolize its restored relationship with God. In this prophetic context, the word evokes the intimate and permanent union between the city and its God.
H1166G.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 62:4, where the prophet announces the restoration of Jerusalem after exile. The context shows that Jerusalem, which had borne the name "Forsaken" (אֶזְבֶּל in Hebrew), will receive the name Beutla, thus expressing the change in the city's destiny and its return to divine favor.
H1166G.portee: This prophetic name reminds us that God never permanently abandons His people and that His promise of restoration is certain. For the Christian reader, it illustrates how God transforms desolation into joy and establishes a lasting covenant with His own.

sens: To exercise authority, power over someone or something
To be the master, the lord of someone
To reign over a people or territory
H1166H.detail:
1. The verb expresses the idea of exercising authority or power over someone or something. It is the action of commanding, directing, mastering. In 1 Chronicles 4:22, some men "dominated over Moab," meaning they exercised their authority over this neighboring people.

2. The word can also refer to the relationship of the master to his subjects, the idea of being lord or chief. It is the position of one who reigns and possesses authority. This is particularly the image of marriage, where one dominates or governs the other.

3. Finally, to dominate means to reign over an entire people or territory: it is the exercise of political or royal power. In Isaiah 26:13, the prophet says that other masters have "dominated over us," thus expressing the oppression and control of a foreign nation.
H1166H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be master" or "to possess." This root evokes the idea of domination and control. It is closely related to a common name in Hebrew, "Baal," which designates a master or owner, and in a religious context, a god or false god. The same root appears in several forms that all revolve around the idea of reign and possession.
H1166H.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Bible according to the provided usages. In 1 Chronicles 4:22, it describes how some men of Judah exercised their military or political domination over the kingdom of Moab, a neighboring people. In Isaiah 26:13, the prophet uses it to express how foreign powers oppressed the people of Israel before they turned to the Lord. In both cases, the verb speaks of a relationship of force or power: the one who dominates is above, the one who is dominated is submissive.
H1166H.portee: This word reminds the believer that all human power is limited and temporary. Only the Lord truly reigns and reigns forever. When the Bible speaks of domination among men, it also evokes a reality of sin: men seek to dominate one another. This invites the Christian to reflect on his own relationship to power and authority, and to recognize that true freedom comes from obedience to God alone.

sens: To take a woman as a wife, to enter into a marital relationship with her
To be married to someone, to be the husband of
To possess, to have authority over something or someone
To appropriate, to make one's own
H1166I.detail:
1. To marry primarily means to take a woman as a wife: it is the act by which a man establishes a marital union. In Deuteronomy 24:1, the verb describes the man who "marries a woman"; the act of marriage is thus the moment when the man takes the woman for himself.

2. Next, it designates the state of being married, being bound by marriage: "you will die because of the woman you have taken, for she has a husband" (Genesis 20:3) — the husband is the one who possesses this exclusive relationship with the woman. It is the permanent state that results from the act of marriage.

3. The word also carries the idea of possessing, dominating: the husband is the one who has authority over his wife, who "reigns" over her. This nuance appears clearly in Isaiah 54:5, where the Lord is presented as the "husband" of Israel — He is the master, the one who has power and responsibility.

4. More broadly, to marry can mean to appropriate or possess something: to be bound to something as to a wife, to have mastery over it.
H1166I.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "master," "lord." It expresses both possession and authority: the one who "marries" a woman becomes her master, her possessor in a legal and marital sense. The same word can designate the master of a house, the owner of a thing. This is why the verb encompasses several related meanings: to marry, to possess, to dominate — all imply a relationship of mastery.
H1166I.emploi: The verb "to marry" appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the laws of Deuteronomy and in the prophets. In Deuteronomy 22:22 and 24:1, it designates the act or state of marriage according to the Law: it is a legal term. In Proverbs 30:23, it describes the woman who takes a husband. In the prophets, particularly in Isaiah 54:1 and 54:5 and in Jeremiah 3:14, the verb is used figuratively: the Lord "marries" Israel or Judah, an image of the covenant and divine love. The meaning oscillates between ordinary marital reality and God's spousal love for His people.
H1166I.portee: This word sheds light on the nature of marriage in biblical thought: to marry is not a simple contract, but a relationship of authority, mutual belonging, and responsibility. It also shows how the Bible uses the marital image to describe the covenant between God and His people: God is not distant, but bound to Israel as a husband to his wife, with tenderness and authority. For the believer, this reveals that marriage is not a superficial relationship, but a deep bond of benevolent mastery and mutual fidelity.

sens: One who possesses something, owner
One who commands in a household, husband
Inhabitant of a city or region
Chief, lord who exercises authority
H1167G.detail:
1. The master is primarily one who possesses a property, who is its owner. Exodus 21:28 speaks of the "master" of an ox that has killed someone: it is the one to whom the animal belongs. In Job 31:39, the former "masters" of a land are mentioned, those who owned it before us.
2. The master is also one who commands in the house, the husband. It is a relationship of domestic authority: one who leads his wife and family.
3. The term designates the "inhabitants" of a city, the citizens or local lords who exercise some responsibility there. Judges 9:2 calls upon the "inhabitants" of Shechem; Judges 9:46 mentions the "inhabitants" of the tower of Shechem seeking refuge.
4. Finally, the master is the chief, the lord, one who reigns or commands. Isaiah 1:3 shows the ox that knows its master, meaning: the one who has authority over it, the one it must serve.
H1167G.origine: The Hebrew word ba'al comes from a root meaning "to possess" or "to govern." It is a very ancient word, attested throughout the Near Eastern antiquity. In the Bible, it designates one who has authority: the owner of land or livestock, the head of a household, the citizen who counts. The word is also used, unfortunately, in idol worship: Baal is the name of a Canaanite deity, which shows that this word was associated with power and sovereignty.
H1167G.emploi: Ba'al appears 31 times in the Bible. It is very common in the laws of the Pentateuch (Exodus 21-22), where it designates the owner of an animal or property who must legally answer for what he possesses. In the accounts of Judges 9, the word repeatedly refers to the inhabitants or masters of Shechem, those who participate in the political events of the city. The context determines the meaning: when it concerns an ox or land, it is the owner; when it concerns a city, it refers to influential citizens or chiefs; when speaking of the ox and its master in Isaiah 1:3, it is a relationship of dependence and knowledge.
H1167G.portee: This word reminds believers to recognize God's sovereignty: God is the true master of all things. Conversely, it teaches us that we have responsibilities toward what we possess and those who depend on us. Understanding ba'al also helps grasp the seriousness of idolatry: to worship Baal is to acknowledge a false master in place of the true God.

sens: Man united to a woman by marriage
Owner or master of something
Inhabitant or citizen of a place
Lord or master in a general sense
H1167H.detail:
1. The husband is the man with whom a woman lives in marriage and under whose authority she places herself. This is the most common meaning of the word in the Bible. Uriah's wife "wept for her husband" when she learned of his death (2 Samuel 11:26), and the book of Proverbs speaks of a woman whose "husband's heart trusts in her" (Proverbs 31:11).
2. The word also designates one who possesses or controls something: one can say "the husband of the house" for its owner, or "the husband of the donkey" for its master. It is a relationship of possession or domination.
3. It can also mean inhabitant or citizen: for example, "the husbands of the city" are those who live there and are part of it.
4. More broadly, it expresses a relationship of power or authority: a lord, a chief, one who has authority over someone or something.
H1167H.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of possessing, commanding, dominating. That is why it primarily means owner, then master, then husband — the man who has authority in the couple according to biblical conceptions. This word has also given rise to the name of the god Baal worshiped by pagan nations: Baal literally means "lord" or "master," and idol-worshiping peoples called him this as their master-god.
H1167H.emploi: The word appears fourteen times in the historical and wisdom books of the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in the laws of the Pentateuch (notably in Exodus 21 and Deuteronomy 21-24), where it designates the husband as one who exercises legal authority over his wife — for example, it is to him that a fine must be paid if his pregnant wife is harmed (Exodus 21:22). The book of Proverbs also uses it to show the trust and esteem that a wise woman inspires in her husband (Proverbs 31:11, 28). Joel 1:8 even uses the expression "the husband of her youth" to refer to the lost life companion.
H1167H.portee: This word reminds the reader that marriage in the Bible is not a contract between equals, but a covenant where the husband exercises authority and responsibility. For the modern Christian, it invites reflection on the nature of marriage: both an intimate union ("one flesh") and a structure of authority that reflects Christ's love for the Church. It is an opportunity to revisit what the Bible says about the husband's role in light of the sacrificial love taught in the New Testament.

sens: Owner or possessor of something
Husband or spouse
Inhabitant of a city or region
Any person (man, individual)
Lord or chief having authority
H1167I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of owner: the person who possesses something, a house, goods. It is one who has control and responsibility over it. In Judges 19:22, the "master of the house" is mentioned, the one who is its owner and host.

2. The word also designates the husband, the spouse in the marital context — one who has authority and responsibility within the family. It is a link of possession or established relationship.

3. It signifies inhabitant or citizen of a city: the people who dwell and live together in the same place. In 1 Samuel 23:11-12, "the inhabitants of Keilah" refers to all those living in that city.

4. More broadly, the word can simply refer to a man, a person, any individual without particular nuance of status.

5. By extension, it can express the idea of a lord or chief having authority and power over others, one who commands and directs.
H1167I.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to possess" or "to dominate." The primitive root expresses the idea of mastery, possession, and control. The word is used to describe all those who have a power of possession or authority — first the owner of a house or property, then by extension any man in a position of responsibility or power. It is a fundamental word for expressing relationships of authority and possession in Israelite society.
H1167I.emploi: This word appears about thirteen times in the provided texts, especially in the narrative passages of the Old Testament. It is used for the owner of a house (Judges 19:22), for the inhabitants of a city (Judges 9:24; 1 Samuel 23:11-12; 2 Samuel 21:12), and in other contexts where it is necessary to designate a responsible person or one endowed with authority. The word is also present in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, often to speak of one who possesses goods or acts as a responsible person. Its meaning varies slightly according to the context: sometimes it emphasizes possession (the master of the house), sometimes social status (an inhabitant, a citizen), and sometimes simply the quality of a responsible man or authority.
H1167I.portee: This word reminds the biblical reader that there are responsibilities linked to possession and authority — one who is master of something is accountable. It also sheds light on how the Bible views human relationships: based on bonds of possession, mutual responsibility, and authority. For the Christian, this word invites reflection on what he truly possesses and how he uses it, and to recognize that all authority, in marriage or community, comes with duties.

sens: one who possesses something
one who exercises authority over someone
one characterized by a quality
the holder of a position or function
H1167J.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is one who possesses or holds something: "one who possesses it" in Proverbs 16:22, where wisdom is the object possessed. It reflects the relationship of ownership or belonging.
2. By extension, the master is one who exercises authority or control over someone else — a husband over his wife, a lord over his subjects, as indicated by the expression "bound to him" in Nehemiah 6:18, where people are in a relationship of dependence on someone.
3. The word can also characterize someone by what defines or marks them: "clothed in hair" in 2 Kings 1:8 literally means "master of hair" or "one whose hair is the distinguishing mark." This is a Hebrew way of describing a visible quality.
4. Finally, it designates one who holds a charge, a force, or a capacity — the "wicked" in Ecclesiastes 8:8 is literally one who is "master of wickedness," meaning who possesses it as a weapon or a dominant trait.
H1167J.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning fundamentally "to possess" or "to have." It is an active noun: one who possesses, dominates, masters. The word expresses the idea of an asymmetrical relationship — between the possessor and the possessed, between the master and the one who obeys him. This root has given rise in Hebrew to many compounds and expressions where it marks the relationship of control or belonging.
H1167J.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the provided passages with nuances of meaning depending on the context. In Proverbs (16:22, 17:8, 7:12), it describes one who possesses wisdom, emphasizing possession as a precious good. In Nehemiah 6:18, it indicates the relationship of dependence or vassalage to a superior. In 2 Kings 1:8 and Isaiah 41:15, it is used to characterize someone by a distinctive trait ("clothed in hair," "adorned with spikes"). In Ecclesiastes 8:8, it designates one who masters or possesses a force. In Daniel, it describes the horned animal as dominant. The word thus plays on the central idea of possession, authority, and characterization.
H1167J.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible speaks of power and possession relationships. It shows that wisdom, virtues, and abilities are seen as goods that one possesses, not just states that one knows. This invites the believer to consider their relationship to God not as mere knowledge, but as belonging — that of a creature to the master who possesses and governs it.

sens: Owner or possessor of something
Husband, spouse
Inhabitant, resident of a place
One who excels in a field, specialist
Opponent, enemy
Lord, person of power or authority
H1167K.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who possesses or controls something: an owner or a master of slaves. This is the oldest and most concrete meaning of the term.

2. It also applies to the husband in the couple: one who has authority in the household. This is a natural relationship of dominance in the society of the time.

3. The word extends to the inhabitants or residents of a city or region (Numbers 21:28, the "inhabitants" of the heights of Arnon), showing that it can mean "one who belongs to" or "who dwells in."

4. A "master" can also be one who excels in an art or practice: in Ecclesiastes 12:13, the wise man gives his words "through one master," meaning someone who masters wisdom. In Genesis 37:19, "dreamer" (literally "master of dreams") describes Joseph by what characterizes him.

5. The term takes on a nuance of hostility when it designates the opponent or personal enemy (Isaiah 50:8: "Who is my adversary?"), one who opposes you.

6. More broadly, it expresses any form of authority, lordship, or power: a chief, a leader, someone who commands.
H1167K.origine: The word comes from an ancient Semitic root expressing the idea of possession and mastery. In Hebrew, the root also generates derived terms to express domination and control. The word appears in several Semitic languages with similar nuances. Historically, "Baal" has also crystallized as the name of a Canaanite deity (literally "the Master"), but the simple word baal retains its fundamental meaning of owner or master in biblical texts.
H1167K.emploi: This word is very commonly used in the Old Testament, with about 13 significant occurrences in the provided passages. It appears in various contexts: social (husband, owner), geographical (inhabitants), moral (characterization of people by what they master), and conflictual (opponent). In Genesis 37:19, Joseph's brothers nickname him "dreamer" to mock him for his habit of reporting his dreams. In Proverbs 24:8, "man full of malice" literally translates as "master of malice," meaning one who excels or indulges in evil. The word thus plays on the contrast: it can valorize (the wise is master of wisdom) or devalue (the wicked is master of malice). This flexibility of use reflects the importance of the concept of mastery and authority in biblical life.
H1167K.portee: This word sheds light on the biblical view of authority and responsibility. To be "master" of something is to have charge of it and to be accountable for it. For the Christian reader, this raises questions: over whom or what do we have authority? How do we exercise this authority? The word also reminds us that everyone is "master" of what truly characterizes them — our actions, our thoughts — and that we bear moral responsibility for it. Finally, it invites reflection on authority relationships in daily life in light of the Gospel.

sens: supreme god of the Phoenicians and Canaanites
idol worshiped by unfaithful Israelites
idolatrous worship opposed to the God of Israel
H1168A.detail:
1. Baal is the main god of the Phoenician and Canaanite pantheon, a masculine deity associated with fertility and the forces of nature. The name means "lord" in Hebrew, and this god had a major religious influence in the ancient Levant.

2. Baal becomes the emblem of idolatry in Israel: it is by serving the Baals that the Israelites abandon the one true God and commit the sin that God hates the most. Judges 2:11 reports that "the children of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and they served the Baals."

3. The worship of Baal involves elaborate rituals — offerings, incense, devotions — that rival the worship of the true God. In 1 Kings 18:26, the priests of Baal call upon their god from morning until noon without receiving an answer, while God responds with fire to the prophet Elijah. This opposition shows that Baal is merely a vain chimera in the face of the living God.
H1168A.origine: The Hebrew word בעל (ba'al) literally means "lord" or "master" (it appears in compound names like Baal-Zebub, "lord of the flies"). It was originally a generic title for a local Canaanite deity, but it becomes the proper name of the principal Phoenician god. The Bible uses it as the name of Israel's religious enemy, symbolizing everything that diverts the people from the covenant with the Lord.
H1168A.emploi: Baal appears 76 times in the Hebrew Bible (58 times in the singular, 18 in the plural), primarily in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the prophets (Jeremiah, Hosea, Zephaniah). The word refers both to the god himself and to the worship rendered to this god. The Israelites succumb to the worship of Baal especially after the arrival of unfaithful kings: Ahab introduces the worship of Baal on a large scale (1 Kings 16:31-32), and Jehu leads a bloody purge against the worshipers of Baal (2 Kings 10). Jeremiah denounces the extent of this plague: "You have as many gods as you have cities, O Judah" (Jeremiah 11:13). Hosea also cries out against this devastating worship. Baal represents Israel's continual tendency to turn away from the Lord towards the religions of the surrounding nations.
H1168A.portee: Baal embodies in the Bible the constant trap of religious unfaithfulness: the temptation to replace the living and unique God with attractive but hollow idols. Each generation of believers must remain vigilant against the call of the "false gods" of the moment — which, for a Christian, means identifying and rejecting anything that claims to usurp the place of Christ and the Lord in the heart. The resounding defeat of Baal before God in 1 Kings 18 teaches that only the true God listens and acts.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
H1168B.detail: 1. Baal is a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of King David and King Solomon (the united monarchy of Israel). He appears twice in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles, which enumerate the ancestors and descendants of important families of God's people. His name literally means "Lord" or "master" in Hebrew.
H1168B.origine: The name Baal comes from the Hebrew root baal, which literally means "lord" or "master." It is a common name in the Old Testament to designate an owner or head of a family. It should not be confused with Baal (or Baalim in the plural), the false deity worshiped by the pagan nations neighboring Israel: here, it is simply a personal name given to an Israelite man.
H1168B.emploi: Baal is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles in chapters 8 and 9, in passages that list the genealogies of the families of Benjamin. These two lists seem to be two versions of the same genealogical record. Baal is presented as a son of Abiel and as the brother of Kish, Ner, Abdon, Zur, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth. His role in the history of God's people is not developed; he simply appears among the ancestors listed in these genealogies.

sens: Man of the tribe of Reuben during the time of the divided monarchy
H1168G.detail: Baal is a man of the tribe of Reuben, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Reaja and the father of Béera, both listed in the genealogy of the descendants of Reuben in 1 Chronicles 5:5.
H1168G.origine: The name Baal means "lord" in Hebrew. It is a common word that designates a master or owner. The name was borne by this man of Reuben, although the same word also became famous as the name of a foreign deity that the Israelites sometimes worshiped to their detriment.
H1168G.emploi: Baal is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:5, in a genealogical list of the sons of Michah. This genealogy traces the descent of the tribe of Reuben. He is simply named as the son of Reaja and father of Béera, with no events or actions concerning this individual reported in the Bible.

sens: city in the territory of Simeon
H1168H.detail: 1. Baal is a city located in the territory of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the Old Testament. It is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:33 as one of the localities in the southern part of the land of Canaan where the Simeonites lived. This city is likely identical to Baalath-Beer, a locality of the same name mentioned in the Segond 1910.
H1168H.origine: The Hebrew word "Baal" literally means "master" or "lord." In biblical geography, it is a proper name that designates this specific city. It should not be confused with Baal the pagan god worshiped by the neighboring nations of Israel: here, it is solely a place name.
H1168H.emploi: Baal appears only once in the Hebrew Bible according to the Segond 1910, in 1 Chronicles 4:33, in the list of cities and villages in the territory of Simeon. The genealogical context shows that it is a precise location of the dwellings of the Simeonites. The mention occurs in the phrase "and all the villages around these cities, as far as Baal," indicating its role as a geographical landmark for the settlements of this tribe.

sens: Fortified city of Moab, located on a high plateau
Place from which a vast territory can be observed
High place of worship for the god Baal in antiquity
H1168I.detail:
1. Bamoth-Baal is a city located in the region of Moab (east of the Jordan), probably identical to Baalath-Beer. Its name means "the high places of Baal": "bamoth" means heights, elevated plateaus. It is a strategic site, placed at a high altitude (Numbers 22:41).

2. The Bible mentions it as a place from which one can see far across the territory. It is from Bamoth-Baal that the diviner Balaam was brought to observe the people of Israel, which shows the strategic advantage of this elevated position (Numbers 22:41).

3. The name also reveals that this place was a center of idolatrous worship: homage was paid to Baal, the false deity worshiped by the Canaanite peoples. It was a "high place" of religion, where the peoples offered sacrifices to their gods.
H1168I.origine: The Hebrew word "baal" literally means "master" or "lord." Combined with "bamoth" ("heights"), it designates a sanctuary erected on a hill. Baal is the name of a Canaanite deity associated with fertility and storms, worshiped by the neighboring nations of Israel. The "high places" of Baal were altars built at high altitudes, away from official temples.
H1168I.emploi: Bamoth-Baal appears twice in the Bible, in the context of territories east of the Jordan. In Numbers 22:41, Balak, king of Moab, brings the diviner Balaam there to curse Israel from this strategic height. In Joshua 13:17, it is listed among the cities of Moab and Hesbon during the land distribution after the conquest. It is a border place, disputed between Moab and the lands of Israel, and a symbol of the prevailing idolatry at that time.
H1168I.portee: This city reminds readers that the people of God were surrounded by idolatrous cults and false religions. The contrast is striking: where Balaam attempted to curse Israel from a "high place" of Baal, God turned curses into blessings (Numbers 23-24). It is a lesson on God's sovereignty in the face of threats, even religious ones, that surround His people.

sens: One who exercises authority and command over a region or province
Administrative chief appointed by royal power to govern a territory
H1169.detail:
1. The term refers to a political official invested with official authority. In the book of Ezra, Rehum bears the title of governor of the region beyond the river (Ezra 4:8), making him the highest local administrative official. It is a position of power delegated by the central authority, in this case, the Persian king Artaxerxes.
2. The governor exercises effective command over his territory and coordinates the actions of other officials. Rehum acts jointly with the secretary Shimshai (Ezra 4:9), which shows that the governor is the head of a structured administration, capable of corresponding directly with the king on matters concerning the territory (Ezra 4:17).
H1169.origine: It is Aramaic, meaning literally "master" or "lord," formed from a root that expresses power and dominion. This Aramaic term is used in the Aramaic portions of the book of Ezra (chapters 4 to 6) and the book of Daniel, where it translates the administrative reality of the Persian empire. It comes from the same family as the Hebrew word baal (master), but here in its Aramaic form used by the scribes and authorities of the Persian era.
H1169.emploi: The word appears three times in the book of Ezra, in Aramaic, always to designate Rehum and his official authority in the province beyond the river. All occurrences are found in chapter 4, in the official correspondence between local authorities and King Artaxerxes regarding the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8, 4:9, 4:17). The context shows a governor acting as a representative of royal power and enjoying sufficient authority to correspond with the king on matters of his region.
H1169.portee: This word reminds the reader that, even in exile, under foreign domination, the administrative structure maintains officials who report to the supreme power. It also emphasizes that the events of the return from exile occur within a real political framework, where God's plans pass through negotiation with established human authorities.

sens: Canaanite deity worshiped as a god of the covenant or contract
H1170.detail: 1. Baal-Berith is a god of the Philistines and Canaanites, whose name literally means "Lord of the covenant." Contrary to what his name might suggest, he was not a true god establishing a covenant with his people, but a false deity that the Israelites began to serve after the death of Gideon (Judges 8:33), abandoning the living God for idols. This god had a temple with treasures, as indicated by the mention of a house of Baal-Berith in Shechem (Judges 9:4) where offerings and the wealth of the faithful were stored.
H1170.origine: The Hebrew name בַּעַל בְּרִית combines two words: בַּעַל (baal, "lord" or "master") and בְּרִית (berith, "covenant" or "pact"). Baal was the generic name for Canaanite deities and those of the Levant; berith indicates here the specificity: a baal associated with the idea of contract or sacred bond. This god was particularly venerated in Shechem in Canaan, reflecting how false gods appropriated sacred concepts — here that of the covenant — to seduce worshipers.
H1170.emploi: Baal-Berith appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Judges. After the death of Gideon, the Israelites turn away from the living God and adopt Baal-Berith as their deity (Judges 8:33), marking a return to idolatry shortly after Gideon's miraculous victories. The name reappears a few verses later in the story of Abimelech: Shechem has a temple of Baal-Berith with a house filled with treasures from which the money to finance Abimelech's mercenaries comes (Judges 9:4). These two mentions illustrate the context of spiritual decline and civil unrest that characterize the period of the Judges.
H1170.portee: The mention of Baal-Berith reminds the reader of the danger of idolatrous seduction and how easily God's people can abandon the living Lord for false gods. The very name of the god — "Lord of the covenant" — is a perverse counterfeit: true gods promise an authentic covenant, while these idols merely capture the imagination and drain the resources of worshipers. This rapid decline after Gideon shows that even the most spectacular miracles do not guarantee lasting faith if the heart is not rooted in faith in the one true God.

sens: City in northern Canaan, place of worship for Baal
Northernmost point of Joshua's conquests
Location at the foot of Mount Hermon, in the valley of Lebanon
H1171.detail:
1. Baal-Gad is a city in northern Canaan named after the Canaanite god Baal, associated with fertility and fortune — the name literally means "lord of fortune." It was a high place of idolatrous worship, typical of the Canaanite cities that the Israelites conquered.

2. This city marked the northern limit of Joshua's victories: it served as a geographical reference point to delineate the conquered territory, from Baal-Gad in the north to Seir in the south (Joshua 11:17 and 12:7). It indicates the maximum extent that Joshua reached in conquering the land.

3. Baal-Gad was located at the foot of Mount Hermon, in the valley of Lebanon, at the northernmost edge of the Israelite territory (Joshua 13:5). It constituted a natural and visible landmark, serving to define the borders of the promised land.
H1171.origine: The name Baal-Gad combines two Hebrew words: Baal ("lord" or "master") and Gad ("fortune" or "luck"). The word Baal designated in Canaanite religion the deity of rain, fertility, and prosperity. This city bore the name of a Canaanite idol, reflecting its character as a pagan religious high place before its conquest by Israel.
H1171.emploi: Baal-Gad appears three times in the book of Joshua, always to mark the boundaries of the conquered lands. In Joshua 11:17 and 12:7, it delineates the northern point of Joshua's victories beyond the Jordan. In Joshua 13:5, it is listed among the lands still to be possessed, marking a northern limit of the territory that God had promised to the Israelites. Its name persists in the biblical text despite its character as a place of idolatrous worship.
H1171.portee: For the believer, Baal-Gad serves as a reminder that God leads His people to conquer lands dominated by idolatry and the worship of false deities. The mention of this city emphasizes that Joshua's victory was not limited — it extended to the farthest regions, demonstrating God's power that surpasses boundaries and obstacles. It invites recognition that God alone is the true Lord, beyond all the false gods to whom peoples render worship.

sens: Woman who manages a household, owner or head of an estate
Woman who invokes the dead, necromancer
H1172.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a woman who is in charge of a household or estate, one who has authority and responsibility over it. In 1 Kings 17:17, the woman with whom the prophet Elijah stays is called "mistress of the house": she is the one in charge, the one who reigns there.
2. The word can also refer to a woman who practices necromancy, that is, one who claims to summon the dead and communicate with them. In 1 Samuel 28:7, Saul seeks "a woman who invokes the dead": these are the same words in Hebrew. These women claimed supernatural powers to consult the beyond, a practice strictly forbidden by the Law of Moses.
H1172.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "master" or "lord" (Baal). The feminine "mistress" is derived from it naturally. This root evokes the idea of domination and possession: a master is one who possesses and governs. The same root appears in several words in the Old Testament to designate the owner, chief, or husband.
H1172.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice it primarily means the woman who manages a household (1 Kings 17:17), and this meaning aligns with that of "owner" or "leader." However, the word is also used, and perhaps primarily, to refer to women who claimed to communicate with the spirits of the dead: this is the case in 1 Samuel 28:7, where Saul explicitly seeks them out. In Nahum 3:4, the word qualifies a sorceress associated with witchcraft and seduction. These three uses show that the term has taken on a dark meaning: the woman who dominates becomes one who exercises forbidden powers.
H1172.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible takes seriously the reality of occult practices and witchcraft, while firmly condemning them. Saul, king of Israel, transgresses the Law by consulting a necromancer, which shows how spiritual despair can lead one to reject God's commands. For the Christian reader, the word warns: seeking to communicate with the dead through occult means is to turn away from the living God and fall under His judgment.

sens: Mountain or place name in Judah
Border landmark between the territory of Judah and that of the Philistines
H1173G.detail: 1. Baala is a mountain or geographical site located in the territory of the tribe of Judah. The name means "mistress" in ancient Hebrew, probably because this prominent place was considered a major height. 2. In the account of Joshua 15:11, Baala serves as a reference point for tracing the borders of Judah: the boundary passes through this mountain and then extends to Jabneel and the sea. It was a strategic landmark for delineating the territory of Judah from that of the Philistines to the west.
H1173G.origine: The name Baala comes from the Hebrew baal (בַּעַל), which means "master" or "lord." In the feminine form, ba'alah (בַּעֲלָה) means "mistress." This term was often used for prominent or dominant places. This place name should not be confused with other sites bearing a similar name in Canaan.
H1173G.emploi: Baala appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:11, during the precise description of the borders of the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah. It is mentioned alongside other landmarks like Ekron, Shicron, and Jabneel, which allowed the ancient Israelites to clearly identify the limits of their lands. It was a well-known and recognizable site at the time of the conquest and division of Canaan.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H1173H.detail: Baala is a small locality located in the southern territory of Judah. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land (Joshua 15:29), where it is listed among the cities of this district. The Hebrew name suggests the idea of mistress or sovereign, but for this city, it is simply an identifiable geographical location within the territory of Judah.
H1173H.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew root בעל (ba'al), which means "master" or "lord," from which the feminine "baala" (mistress) is derived. This same word is used for the false god Baal worshiped in Canaan. For this site, biblical sources also mention the alternative names Balah and Bilhah, indicating that this city could be referred to by several forms of its name.
H1173H.emploi: Baala is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:29, in the context of the division of lands among the tribes of Israel. This verse lists the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah, particularly those in the south (the Negev). Baala appears among a list of minor settlements, indicating that it was a locality of little importance, with no specific history recounted in the Scriptures.

sens: City in the region of Judah, seat of the ark of God before David
H1173I.detail: 1. Baala is a fortified city of Judah, located at the border of the tribal territory. It first appears as a geographical landmark in the description of the borders of the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:9-10), where it marks a significant turn in the southern boundary of the territory. 2. The city is best known as the place where the ark of God rested before King David had it transported to Jerusalem. It is from Baala (also called Baalé-Judah) that David organizes the solemn transfer of the ark (2 Samuel 6:2; 1 Chronicles 13:6), a major event in Israel's history that marks the strengthening of the royal and religious power of the young king.
H1173I.origine: The name Baala means "mistress" in Hebrew. The city is also known as Kirjath-Jearim, which means "city of forests." These two names refer to the same place. The name "Baalé-Judah" (a variant appearing in 2 Samuel 6:2) literally means "lords of Judah" or "masters of Judah," perhaps highlighting the religious or administrative significance of the site.
H1173I.emploi: This city appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. First in Joshua 15:9-10, where it is listed as a boundary marker during the description of the tribal borders of Judah. It gains major religious significance during the story of David: in 2 Samuel 6:2 and 1 Chronicles 13:6, it is from Baala (also named Baalé-Judah and Kirjath-Jearim) that David and all Israel set out to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem. These last two passages, which recount the same event, show the centrality of this site in the consolidation of David's religious power.
H1173I.portee: Baala reminds us of the importance of the ark of the covenant as a living symbol of God's presence among His people. The transfer of the ark to Jerusalem under David marks a turning point in Israel's history: the centralization of worship and the stability of the kingdom. For the believer, it is an illustration of how God draws near to His people and strengthens His covenant with mankind.

sens: Vineyard of King Solomon mentioned in the Song of Songs
H1174.detail: Baal-Hamon is the name of a vineyard owned by King Solomon. The passage from the Song of Songs shows us that Solomon entrusted this vineyard to caretakers who harvested its fruits, each required to bring a thousand shekels of silver for their portion (Song of Songs 8:11). It is the image of a prosperous royal property, where grapes were cultivated and wealth was shared according to a strict organization.
H1174.origine: The name literally means "Master of Abundance" or "Lord of the Multitude." The word "Baal" (master or possessor) designated in the ancient Semitic world an owner or chief; "Hamon" refers to the idea of crowd or abundance. This vineyard bore a name that reflected its wealth and productive capacity, characteristic of the prosperity of Solomon's reign.
H1174.emploi: Baal-Hamon appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Songs 8:11. Solomon is presented as the owner of a vineyard managed by caretakers to whom he entrusted its management. This detail illustrates both the king's wealth and his economic organization: the managers each brought a thousand shekels of silver in exchange for their share of the vineyard's fruits. Although the exact location is uncertain, this passage immerses us in the world of Solomon's royal properties and his system of taxation or revenue sharing from agriculture.

sens: City in the southern region of Judah
H1175.detail: Bealoth is a fortified city in the territory of Judah, listed among the cities of this region in the inventory of Joshua 15:24. It is mentioned again in 1 Kings 4:16 as part of the administrative district of the governor Baana during the reign of Solomon. The same location is also known as Baalath-Beer.
H1175.origine: The name Bealoth means "mistresses" or "ladies" in Hebrew, derived from the word baal which designates a master or lord. It is a plural feminine form. This name reflects an ancient sanctuary or locality associated with the worship of Baal, a Canaanite deity. The site is sometimes referred to as Baalath-Beer ("Baal of Beer"), an alternative designation for the same place.
H1175.emploi: Bealoth appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in the list of cities in the southern region of Judah enumerated in Joshua 15:24, during the land distribution after the conquest of Canaan. It is then mentioned in 1 Kings 4:16 in an administrative context: it is part of the governmental district of Baana, son of Hushai, who was responsible for the region of Asher during the reign of Solomon. This double mention suggests that Bealoth was an important locality in the territorial and fiscal system of the united kingdom.

sens: Pagan deity worshiped by the Philistines at Ekron
Idol consulted for oracles about the future and healing
H1176.detail:
1. Baal-Zebub is a false deity, a god of the Philistines worshiped in the city of Ekron. The name literally means "lord of the flies," which likely designates a deity responsible for diverting harmful insects or healing wounds. It is to this god that King Ahaziah turns when he falls ill (2 Kings 1:2).
2. This god was consulted as an oracle to know the future and obtain healing. When Ahaziah sends messengers to inquire of Baal-Zebub about his illness, the prophet Elijah intervenes: the Lord reproaches him for consulting this idol instead of turning to the God of Israel, for there is a living God in Israel whose word can be consulted (2 Kings 1:3, 1:6, 1:16).
H1176.origine: The name comes from two Hebrew words: "Baal" (master, lord, owner) and "Zebub" (fly). It was probably a Phoenician or Philistine deity with the status of "lord" or "master" and associated with flies — either to combat them or to send them as a plague. The worship of Baal in its various forms was widespread in Mesopotamia and Phoenicia before and during the period of the Israelite and Judean kingdoms.
H1176.emploi: Baal-Zebub is mentioned four times in the Bible, exclusively in 2 Kings 1, during an incident in the reign of Ahaziah, king of the North. This king of Israel, after a fall, sends his servants to consult Baal-Zebub at Ekron to find out if he will recover. The prophet Elijah intervenes four times (in verses 2, 3, 6, and 16) to condemn this consultation: it constitutes a betrayal of the Lord, a failure to recognize the living God of Israel. Each mention reinforces the idea that turning to idols is an act of disobedience that invites divine judgment — in this case, the death of Ahaziah.
H1176.portee: Baal-Zebub represents the danger of superstition and idolatry: seeking answers and help elsewhere than from the true God. For a Christian, this story serves as a reminder that there is a living God, the only one worthy of trust, and that it is vain and dangerous to seek counsel from false sources — whether ancient idols or modern equivalents of divination.

sens: An ancient king of Edom, son of Achbor
H1177G.detail: Baal-Hanan is the name of a king who ruled over Edom, the territory to the south and east of the Dead Sea. He is a figure from ancient times, predating the monarchy of Israel. He succeeded King Saul (another king of Edom, sharing the name with the first king of Israel) and was himself succeeded by Hadar. His father is named Achbor, and his wife is Mehetabel. The genealogical lists in Genesis (36:38-39) and Chronicles (1:49-50) mention this king without detailing his deeds: these texts primarily preserve the succession of Edomite kings to situate the history of Israel in a broader context.
H1177G.origine: The name Baal-Hanan literally means "Baal is gracious." Baal is the name of a deity honored in the ancient Levant; Hanan means "to be gracious, merciful." The name reflects a common religious confession among Canaanite and Edomite peoples: attributing a positive divine quality to the main deity of the group. It is a typical theophoric name from the ancient world.
H1177G.emploi: Baal-Hanan appears four times in the Bible, exclusively in two parallel passages: the list of kings of Edom in Genesis 36:38-39 and its repetition in 1 Chronicles 1:49-50. These genealogical lists enumerate the kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had a king. The text mentions his father Achbor, his death, and his successor Hadar (or Hadad), as well as the name of his wife Mehetabel and that of his city (Pau or Pahi). No details about his reign or actions are provided: he simply appears in the order of Edomite dynastic succession.

sens: Officer of King David, responsible for managing the olive groves and sycamores
H1177H.detail: Baal-Hanan is a man who served King David during the divided monarchy of Israel. His name means "Baal is gracious." He was from Geder and was responsible for overseeing and managing the olive groves and sycamores belonging to the king in the plain. These crops were valuable for the production of olive oil, an essential commodity in the daily and religious life of Israel. Baal-Hanan thus represents a trusted officer, in charge of important royal assets.
H1177H.origine: The name is composed of two elements: "Baal" (master, lord) and "Hanan" (to be gracious, show kindness). This theophoric name, where the divine is named, was common in antiquity. It expresses the idea that the deity manifests its favor. Although not frequently used in the Bible, this name reflects the naming conventions of the time.
H1177H.emploi: Baal-Hanan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:28. The text mentions him as one of the twelve administrators that David had established over his estates. Each of these officers supervised a type of asset or a region. Baal-Hanan specifically had charge of the olive groves and sycamores in the plain, as well as the oversight of olive oil provisions. This mention illustrates the sophisticated administrative organization of the Davidic royal court and the importance of agricultural resources in the kingdom.

sens: City located on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin
Place where Absalom owned a sheep farm
Site of Amnon's murder
H1178.detail: Baal-Hatsor is an ancient Palestinian city, situated at the boundary of the territories of Ephraim and Benjamin. Its name means "lord of the village" or "master of the village." It is here that Absalom, son of King David, owned an agricultural property: a sheep farm where he had his sheep sheared (2 Samuel 13:23). This location becomes the setting for a dramatic event in royal history: the assassination of Amnon, another son of David, carried out by Absalom's servants to avenge their sister Tamar's honor.
H1178.origine: The Hebrew name Baal-Hatsor combines two elements: "Baal" (lord, master) and "Hatzor" (village, fortified enclosure). This compound indicates that the city was a fortified regional center or an agricultural domain of some significance. Cities bearing the name Baal were numerous in Canaan, each marking a notable locality.
H1178.emploi: Baal-Hatsor appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 13:23. The text specifically mentions it as the setting where Absalom invited all the king's sons to a sheep-shearing feast. This context shows that it was a prosperous agricultural domain capable of hosting a significant family gathering. The place becomes memorable in royal family history as the site of Amnon's murder, one of the most dramatic events of David's reign.

sens: Geographical location situated on or near Mount Hermon, in northern Israel
Northern boundary of the territory of Israel during the time of the judges
Site associated with the worship of Baal, the Canaanite deity
H1179.detail: 1. Baal-Hermon is a locality in northern Israel, located on or very close to Mount Hermon, the highest peak in the region. The name literally means "lord of Hermon" and designates a place where the worship of Baal, the god of the Canaanites, was practiced (Judges 3:3). 2. This place marks an important boundary of the territory occupied by the Israelites: it serves as a landmark to define the northern limits of the land they controlled during the time of the judges (Judges 3:3). 3. The region was also occupied by the sons of Manasseh, who lived in the territory extending to Baal-Hermon and the surrounding mountainous areas (1 Chronicles 5:23).
H1179.origine: The name is composed of "Baal" (בַּעַל), meaning "lord" or "master" in Hebrew, and "Hermon" (חֶרְמוֹן), the name of the sacred mountain of Lebanon. The Canaanites often gave religious names to their places, associating the name of their gods. Here, Baal-Hermon indicates a sanctuary dedicated to Baal on or near Mount Hermon, a mountain renowned and revered in ancient Levantine culture.
H1179.emploi: Baal-Hermon appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, only in texts situated during the time of the judges and the united kingdom. In the book of Judges, it is mentioned as the northern boundary of the Canaanite nations that the Israelites could not drive out at the beginning of the judges' period (Judges 3:3). It reappears in Chronicles as a geographical landmark marking the northern limit of the lands occupied by the half-tribe of Manasseh (1 Chronicles 5:23). Its usage is purely geographical and administrative: it serves to delineate the borders of the Israelite territory.
H1179.portee: Baal-Hermon reminds readers that the northern boundary of Israel passed through regions where Canaanite religion remained alive and influential. It is a name that signals the ongoing tension between the Israelites and their neighbors, and how the places themselves bore the traces of this complex religious coexistence at the beginning of the settlement in Canaan.

sens: Deity honored in the Northern Kingdom
Name given to God by His unfaithful people
H1180.detail:
1. Baali is a form of the name "Baal," a deity honored in the Northern Kingdom of Israel. It was a god worshiped by the Canaanite peoples and that some Israelites also revered, instead of the true God.

2. In Hosea 2:18, God declares: "you will no longer call me Baali." The word literally means "my lord" or "my master." God reproaches Israel for having called Him by this title borrowed from idol worship: the unfaithful people gave God the same name as the false gods. God promises that in the future, Israel will call Him "my husband" (Ishi), which expresses a restored covenant relationship rather than mere dominion.
H1180.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew "baal" (בעל), which means "master" or "lord" in the sense of owner or chief. It is the same term that designates the Canaanite deity Baal, worshiped to ensure the fertility of the land. In Israel, some prophets and faithful criticized the use of this title to speak of God, as it confuses the God of Israel with the idols.
H1180.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Hosea 2:18). The prophet Hosea uses it to show how Israel, in its unfaithfulness, has given God a name of master borrowed from idolatry, rather than recognizing Him as their God and husband. It is a term of prophetic reproach, highlighting the people's confusion between the worship of the true God and that of false deities.
H1180.portee: This passage reminds us that the true relationship with God is not that of a slave to an impersonal master, but that of a wife to her husband — based on covenant, love, and mutual faithfulness. It invites Christians to reject any form of superficial religion or one mixed with worldly values, and to seek a true intimacy with God.

sens: Son of King David and an unspecified mother, born in Jerusalem during the period of the united monarchy
H1182.detail: Beéliada is one of the many sons of King David. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 14:7 among the children born in Jerusalem. His name appears in two forms in the Bible: "Beéliada" and "Eliada" (which is a shorter variant of the same name), both designating the same person.
H1182.origine: The name Beéliada means "the Lord knows" or "the Master knows." It is composed of two elements: "baal" (the Lord, the master) and "yada" (to know). It is a typical theophoric name from the Israelite royal period, expressing a confession of faith in divine knowledge.
H1182.emploi: Beéliada appears in the genealogy of David's children born in Jerusalem. He is cited in 1 Chronicles 14:7, where he is listed among the twelve sons of the king. Elsewhere, he is referred to by the shortened name "Eliada." These genealogical mentions reflect the importance that the Bible attaches to the royal lineage of David, the first house of Israel.

sens: Benjamite who rallied to David at Ziklag
mighty warrior in David's service
H1183.detail: Bealia was a man from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David during his stay at Ziklag, before he became king of Israel. He was among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 12:5), meaning he was one of those highly valued fighters who followed him faithfully.
H1183.origine: The Hebrew name Bealia means "Jehovah is master" or "Jehovah reigns." It is composed of two elements: Baal (master, lord) and Yah (short form of the divine name Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a statement of faith in God's lordship.
H1183.emploi: Bealia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:5. This passage lists the Benjamite warriors who came to strengthen David at Ziklag when Saul was pursuing him. This event dates back to the period of the divided monarchy and illustrates the gathering around David of faithful fighters awaiting his accession to the throne.

sens: King of the Ammonites at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar
H1185.detail: Baalis is an Ammonite king who reigns at the time of the fall of Jerusalem. He appears only once in the Bible when men warn Gedaliah that Baalis has hired Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, to kill him (Jeremiah 40:14). He is a political adversary of the Judeans weakened after the destruction of the kingdom.
H1185.origine: The name literally means "Lord of the banner" or "Lord of joy," composed of Baal ("lord, master") and an element related to the banner or joy. It is a typically Ammonite name from the late royal period.
H1185.emploi: Baalis is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Jeremiah 40:14. He reigns over the Ammonites at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C. In this context of political chaos, he seeks to eliminate Gedaliah, the Judean governor appointed by the Babylonians, likely to avoid Judean influence at his borders or to strengthen his own power in the region.

sens: City in Transjordan, in the region of Reuben and Moab
H1186.detail: Baal-Meon is a city located in Transjordan, initially occupied by the tribe of Reuben, and later becoming Moabite. Its name literally means "Lord of the Dwelling" or "master of the habitation." It is mentioned alongside Nebo and is among the important border cities of the territory (Numbers 32:38; Joshua 13:17). In the time of the prophet Ezekiel, it belongs to Moab and is described as part of the ornament of the land, alongside Beth-Jeshimoth and Kirjathaim (Ezekiel 25:9). It is a strategic location on the Transjordan plateau, east of the Dead Sea.
H1186.origine: The Hebrew name בַּעַל מְעוֹן (Baal Meon) consists of two elements: בַּעַל (baal, "lord" or "master") and מְעוֹן (meon, "dwelling" or "habitation"). This root meon designates a place of habitation or refuge. The word Baal, very common in the geography and mythology of the Levant, simply refers to an owner or master of a place. The name reflects the importance of this site in the occupation of the Transjordan territory.
H1186.emploi: Baal-Meon appears four times in the Bible. It is first mentioned in Numbers 32:38 as a city that the Reubenites rebuilt and renamed. It appears in the territorial lists of Joshua 13:17 as part of the cities of Reuben in the plain. In 1 Chronicles 5:8, it marks the eastern boundary of the territory inhabited by the descendants of Bela. Finally, Ezekiel 25:9 includes it in his oracle against Moab, where it is presented as an important city and a jewel of the Moabite land. These occurrences show that the city changed hands over the centuries, passing from Reuben to Moab.

sens: a Canaanite deity worshiped at Peor
the idolatrous cult associated with this god, involving immoral practices
H1187.detail:
1. Baal-Peor is the name of an idol worshiped by the Canaanite peoples at Peor, a region of Moab. It is a "baal" (lord or master) associated with a geographical location. The Bible does not precisely describe what this cult was, but the contexts indicate that it involved immoral and carnal practices: in Numbers 25:3-5, Israel "attached itself" to Baal-Peor and participated in its sacrifices by eating food sacrificed to idols, which provoked severe punishment from God.
2.
