The cult of Baal-Peor symbolizes in the Bible spiritual infidelity and immorality: in Hosea 9:10, the prophet reproaches Israel for having "gone to Baal-Peor" and for "consecrating itself to the infamous idol." This is not just a religious error, but a forsaking of the covenant with God to embrace evil under the guise of religious worship. Psalm 106:28 explicitly links this cult to eating sacrifices to the dead, reinforcing the deeply corrupting nature of this practice.
H1187.origine: The name literally means "Baal (lord) of Peor." Peor is a geographical location, probably a mountain or region of Moab. "Baal" is a common Semitic word meaning an owner or master, often used for local gods. Each Canaanite deity bore the name of the place where it was worshiped, hence names like "Baal-Berith" or "Baal-Zebub." Baal-Peor represents the very type of local false god that the Canaanite nations honored before Israel's conquest.
H1187.emploi: Baal-Peor appears 5 times in the Bible, concentrated in three key passages. The major episode is in Numbers 25:1-5: at the end of the desert, the Israelites befriend the Moabites and worship Baal-Peor, which triggers God's anger and a deadly plague (24,000 dead). Moses orders the judges to kill the guilty. In Deuteronomy 4:3, this terrible memory is recalled as a lesson: God destroyed those who followed him. Psalm 106:28 revisits this event in a confession of Israel's sins. Hosea 9:10 takes up the theme: while Israel was like fresh fruit in the desert, it engaged in idolatry. This cult embodies the very type of spiritual infidelity that Israel committed and of which the prophets remind them of the punishment.
H1187.portee: Baal-Peor reminds the Christian reader that idolatry is never a private matter: it taints the entire people and provokes God's judgment. This episode shows how the allure of worldly customs (here, the immoral practices of the Canaanites) can seduce even a people saved and called by God. It is a permanent warning against compromise with sin, even when it bears a religious name.

sens: Place of David's victory over the Philistines
Mountain near Jerusalem
H1188.detail: Baal-Peratsim is the name of a place where David achieved a decisive victory over the Philistines. The name literally means "Master of the Breaches" or "Lord of the Breaks," as it is there that God scattered David's enemies "like waters that flow" — the image evokes a breach that lets out torrents (2 Samuel 5:20). It is a geographical location not far from Jerusalem, where David fought after becoming king, and this site is also called Mount Peratsim.
H1188.origine: The Hebrew name combines "Baal" (Master, Lord) and "Peratsim" (breaches, breaks), from the verb "parats" which means "to break through" or "to spread out." David named this place to commemorate how the Lord "scattered" his enemies — like a breach releases waters. This place carries the memory of the defeat of the Philistines before Israel.
H1188.emploi: Baal-Peratsim appears twice in Scripture: in 2 Samuel 5:20 and in 1 Chronicles 14:11, in the account of the same event. David wins a victory there against the Philistines shortly after his anointing as king of unified Israel. Each time, David explains the name of the place by linking it to God's action: the Lord "scattered" his enemies. This is a key moment in the consolidation of David's power.
H1188.portee: This place reminds us that God fought alongside David and granted him victory. The very name Baal-Peratsim invites the believer to meditate on the power of God that breaks down obstacles — an encouraging image for those facing resistance: God can "scatter" the enemy like water breaks through a dam.

sens: Landmark in Egypt located near the Red Sea, where Pharaoh caught up with the Israelites during the Exodus
H1189.detail: 1. Baal-Tsephon is a location in Egypt near the Red Sea, mentioned as a geographical landmark during the flight of the Israelites. It is where Pharaoh and his army caught up with the Hebrew people camped near the sea (Exodus 14:9), before God destroyed the Egyptians by closing the waters over them.
H1189.origine: The name Baal-Tsephon literally means "Lord of the North" or "Master of the North": "Baal" means "lord" or "master" in Hebrew, and "Tsephon" means "north." It was probably a place of worship or a site dedicated to an Egyptian deity of the North. By designating this place with this name, the Bible reminds us that it names places according to the religious context of ancient Egypt.
H1189.emploi: Baal-Tsephon appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the account of the Exodus and its related lists. In Exodus 14:2, God commands Moses to instruct the people to camp before Baal-Tsephon, between Migdol and the sea. In Exodus 14:9, it is toward this same place that Pharaoh pursues the Israelites with his chariots and army. Finally, in Numbers 33:7, during the enumeration of the stages of the journey in the desert, Baal-Tsephon is mentioned as a landmark of the path taken. This location holds historical and theological significance as the theater of divine punishment inflicted on Pharaoh.
H1189.portee: This place reminds readers that God controls historical and geographical events, and that He delivers His people even when they seem cornered. The repeated mention of Baal-Tsephon emphasizes that God's salvation occurs in the face of the very forces of this world and its rival deities.

sens: Location in Ephraim, situated near Gilgal
H1190.detail: 1. Baal-Schalischa is a town or village in the region of Ephraim, in northern Israel, near Gilgal. It appears only once in the Bible, when a man from this place brings Elisha bread made from barley and fresh ears of grain as a gift — a gesture of respect towards the prophet and trust in his power to bless (2 Kings 4:42).
H1190.origine: The name Baal-Schalischa literally means "master of the triple" or "lord of the triple." Baal means "master" or "lord" in Hebrew, and schalischa evokes the number three. The exact meaning of this "triple" remains uncertain — perhaps three water sources, three heights, or three fields — but the name reflects a remarkable geographical or agricultural characteristic of the area.
H1190.emploi: Baal-Schalischa appears only once in Scripture, in 2 Kings 4:42. A local resident comes to meet the prophet Elisha and brings him the first fruits of his harvest: barley bread and fresh ears of grain. This act of generosity, despite the modesty of what is offered, shows the respect the prophet inspired and the people's trust in his ability to multiply or bless the gifts. The context suggests that it was a common gesture to bring the first fruits to the prophet, just as they were brought to God.

sens: City of the tribe of Dan in Canaan
H1191G.detail: Baalath is the name of a city assigned to the tribe of Dan during the division of the promised land. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua distributes to Dan, alongside other locations such as Eltheke and Gibbethon (Joshua 19:44). It is a territorial possession recorded in the divine inheritance of the people of Israel.
H1191G.origine: The name Baalath comes from a Semitic root meaning "mistress" or "lady," a feminine word derived from Baal. In biblical geography, place names often receive divine or symbolic names that reflect the worship or characteristics of the site. This name does not imply pagan worship but simply designates the locality by its ancient appellation.
H1191G.emploi: Baalath is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:44, in the description of the borders and cities of the tribe of Dan. It is one of the many localities listed during the division of Canaan among the twelve tribes, to establish the territory that each group of Israelites was to occupy and govern under Joshua's leadership.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of the tribe of Dan
H1191H.detail: 1. Baalath is a city that King Solomon built and fortified within the territory of Dan, in Israel. It is among the strongholds and garrison towns he established to consolidate his kingdom (1 Kings 9:18; 2 Chronicles 8:6).
H1191H.origine: The Hebrew name Baalath literally means "mistress" or "lady" (from Baal, the term for "master" or "lord"). This type of place name may evoke a sanctuary or a place of significance, although the Bible does not specify further the origin of this name.
H1191H.emploi: Baalath appears twice in the Bible, both in accounts related to King Solomon. In 1 Kings 9:18, it is mentioned as one of the cities that Solomon built during his reign. In 2 Chronicles 8:6, it is listed among the cities he fortified, serving notably as storage and bases for his chariots and cavalry. These two passages show that Baalath was a strategic place in the defensive and logistical system of the united kingdom.

sens: City in the territory of Judah, in the southern part of the country
H1192.detail: Baalath-Beer is a city assigned to the tribe of Simeon during the division of Canaan. It was located in the southern part of Judah and was also known as Ramath-Negeb ("height of the south"), as specified in the text of Joshua 19:8.
H1192.origine: The name literally means "mistress of the well" in Hebrew. It combines two words: "Baalath" (mistress, lady) and "Beer" (well or water source). This type of name, formed from two geographical or descriptive elements, was common for places in Palestine that were distinguished by a remarkable natural feature, in this case, an important source or well.
H1192.emploi: Baalath-Beer appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:8. It is mentioned in the list of cities given to the tribe of Simeon during the division of the territory of Canaan after the conquest. The text indicates that it is identical to Ramath-Negeb (or Ramath of the south), suggesting that these two names referred to the same place, known by two different appellations.

sens: Location near Gibeah in Benjamin
H1193.detail: 1. Baal-Thamar is a geographical location near the city of Gibeah, in Benjamin. Its Hebrew name means "master of the palms" or "lord of the palms," suggesting that there were significant palm trees in this region. The place appears in the account of the Israelites' war against the Benjaminites, when the men of Israel reorganize militarily to confront Gibeah and prepare an ambush.
H1193.origine: The name consists of two Hebrew terms: *ba'al* ("master," "lord") and *tamar* ("palm"). In biblical place names, *ba'al* is often used to designate a recognizable or important place, while *tamar* refers to those beautiful trees that marked the landscape of Canaan. This type of geographical name describes a striking characteristic of the territory.
H1193.emploi: Baal-Thamar appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 20:33, during the battle of Israel against the tribe of Benjamin. The Israelites, gathered to punish the violence committed at Gibeah, leave their battle position and gather near Baal-Thamar, from where an Israelite ambush launches to encircle the Benjaminites. The place serves as a strategic landmark in this serious internal conflict.

sens: City of the tribe of Reuben, in Transjordan
H1194.detail: Beon is a city located in the region that would be assigned to the tribe of Reuben, east of the Jordan. It is mentioned in Numbers 32:3 as one of the cities that the Reubenites request Moses to conquer and inhabit. The name "Beon" literally means "in the dwelling" or "habitation," which corresponds to its role as an urban center in the Reubenite region. This same city is also called Baal-Meon, a longer name that emphasizes its religious or administrative importance.
H1194.origine: The name Beon comes from a Hebrew root meaning "dwelling" or "habitation." It is an abbreviated form of Baal-Meon ("Lord of Meon"), a double name common in the ancient Near East where "Baal" designates the master or lord of a place. The name reflects the importance of this locality as a center of habitation and possibly of worship in the Reubenite territory.
H1194.emploi: Beon appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 32:3. It is cited among the cities that the tribes of Reuben and Gad covet after the conquest of the Transjordanian lands. These cities, listed in a catalog, were to be the bases of their settlement and inheritance. Although mentioned only once under this short name, Beon is an important landmark for understanding the establishment of the Reubenites east of the Jordan.

sens: Administrative officer of King Solomon, responsible for the supply of a region of the kingdom of Israel
H1195G.detail: Baana is one of the twelve commissioners that King Solomon appointed to administer different parts of his kingdom and collect the taxes and provisions necessary for the maintenance of the royal court. He was the son of Achilud and had authority over a vast region that included several cities and valleys in northern Israel: Taanach, Megiddo, Beth-Shean, and the surrounding territories up to Jokmeam, near the Jordan Valley. His role was that of a regional administrator responsible for economic organization and resource collection.
H1195G.origine: The name Baana means "in affliction" or "in misery" in Hebrew. This theophoric name expresses a situation of distress from which God was to deliver. It is a classic Hebrew patronymic from the first millennium B.C., borne by several important figures in the kingdom of Israel during the times of the kings.
H1195G.emploi: Baana appears in the Bible only in 1 Kings 4:12, in the list of Solomon's twelve administrative officers. This list enumerates the regional leaders responsible for the administration and supply of the kingdom. Baana held the most northern position and covered the most strategic territory, highlighting his importance within Solomon's administration. His name is listed among the great servants of the king.

sens: Officer of Solomon responsible for the supply of the kingdom
H1195H.detail: Baana is a man who lived during the time of the united kingdom of Israel under the reign of Solomon. He was the son of Hushai and served as the officer responsible for supply (or food management) in Asher and Bealoth, regions in northern Palestine (1 Kings 4:16). His role was part of the central administration that Solomon established to govern his vast kingdom and ensure the regular supply of the royal court and the army.
H1195H.origine: The name Baana literally means "in affliction" or "in tribulation" in Hebrew. It is a compound name that expresses a condition of distress or need. In the ancient Near East, names often carried a religious or circumstantial significance reflecting the conditions of family life at the time of birth.
H1195H.emploi: Baana appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:16. He is mentioned in the context of Solomon's administrative organization, where the text lists the royal officers responsible for different regions of Israel and their surrounding territories. His specific title was to manage the supply for his region, a crucial function in maintaining the prosperity and stability of the kingdom.

sens: Father of Zadok, who helped in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
H1195I.detail: Baana is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:4. He is identified as the father of Zadok, who participated in the repair work of the wall of Jerusalem during the return from exile. Zadok worked alongside other workers and leaders on this significant reconstruction project of the holy city's wall.
H1195I.origine: The name Baana literally means "in affliction" in Hebrew. This name may reflect a difficult period or a context of trial during his life. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including an officer of Solomon, but the Baana of Nehemiah 3:4 is distinguished by his connection to Zadok and his role in the restoration of Jerusalem.
H1195I.emploi: Baana appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:4. He is mentioned solely as the father of Zadok, one of the builders who participated in the repair of the wall of Jerusalem after the return of the exiles. The context shows that his family played a role in this crucial reconstruction work for the Jewish community returned from Babylon.

sens: Assassin of Saul's son, executed by David
H1196G.detail: Baana is one of the two brothers (with Recab) who killed Ish-Bosheth, the son of Saul, taking advantage of his midday nap (2 Samuel 4:5-6). David, whose political enemy was Ish-Bosheth, refuses to accept this murder as a gift and condemns Baana and his brother to death, considering the act a betrayal rather than a service. Their bodies are then mutilated and displayed near Hebron.
H1196G.origine: The name Baana means "in affliction" in Hebrew. He is a historical figure from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.
H1196G.emploi: Baana appears only in the account of 2 Samuel 4, where he is identified as the son of Rimmon of Beeroth and brother of Recab. The passage details how the two brothers enter Ish-Bosheth's house during his nap (2 Samuel 4:5-6) and kill him. David learns of the murder and, despite his hostility towards Ish-Bosheth, orders the execution of Baana and Recab (2 Samuel 4:9-12), as he refuses to benefit from a crime.

sens: Warrior of David, father of Heled
H1196H.detail: Baana is a Netophathite, meaning a man from Nethopha, a locality near Bethlehem. He is known as the father of Heled (also called Heled), who is one of the renowned warriors of King David, a member of his elite army. The text in 2 Samuel 23:29 and 1 Chronicles 11:30 mentions him in the lists of the mighty warriors who served David, where Heled is clearly identified as his son and recognized for his valor.
H1196H.origine: The name Baana means "in affliction" in Hebrew, composed of ba ("in") and anah ("affliction"). This name reflects a difficult situation at the time of birth, but it was borne by several important men in the history of Israel during the period of the united monarchy and after the exile.
H1196H.emploi: Baana appears twice in the Bible, always in the contexts of David and his mighty warriors. In 2 Samuel 23:29, he is mentioned as the father of Heled, a warrior of David from Nethopha. In 1 Chronicles 11:30, the same Baana and his son Heled are listed in the parallel account of David's army. These two parallel passages confirm his role as a warrior in the king's entourage.

sens: Leader of the exiles returning from Babylon with Zerubbabel
Prominent member of the restored community
H1196I.detail:
1. Baana is one of the leaders who guided the Israelites during their return from exile in Babylon, alongside Zerubbabel and Joshua. His name appears at the top of the list of the people's leaders who organized this restoration (Ezra 2:2).
2. He is mentioned again in the parallel record of the book of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:7), confirming his role as an important leader in the community of returning exiles, who were to rebuild the temple and restore religious and civil life in Jerusalem.
H1196I.origine: The name Baana means "in affliction" or "in distress," evoking the trials endured during the Babylonian exile. It is a symbolic name that reflects the collective experience of the people at that time. In the Old Testament, several men bore this name, but this one is specifically the leader returning with Zerubbabel, a few decades after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.
H1196I.emploi: Baana appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of the return of the exiles: in Ezra 2:2 and in Nehemiah 7:7, which offer the same account of the return under Zerubbabel in the 6th century B.C. His name is listed among the family leaders who led the people during this historic return. He represents one of the figures of restored authority in the post-exilic community.
H1196I.portee: Baana embodies the role of leader in the restoration of faith and community after the judgment of exile. His appearance in the return lists reminds us that God does not abandon His people: even after the trial of captivity, He raises up leaders to gather and rebuild them. It is a promise of restoration and renewal.

sens: Leader of a family of exiles returned from Babylon
H1196J.detail: 1. Baana is a man who belongs to a family of Judeans who returned from exile in Babylon after the decree of Cyrus (around 538 B.C.). He is among the leaders of the people who seal the covenant of Nehemiah to renew their commitment to the Law of God (Nehemiah 10:27).
H1196J.origine: The name Baana literally means "in distress" or "in affliction," composed of the preposition "ba" ("in") and "anah" ("distress, affliction"). This name reflects a difficult situation, perhaps that of the Jewish people during the time of exile and return. Three other men bear this name in Scripture: a Benjaminite murderer (2 Samuel 4), a warrior of David (2 Samuel 23), and this ancestor of a returning family.
H1196J.emploi: Baana is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:27, where he appears among the signatories of the covenant seal. This official document lists the leaders of the families who commit to observing the Law of Moses after the return from exile. His inclusion in this list shows that he held a position of authority within the restored community of Jerusalem and played a role in the religious and civil restructuring of the people.
H1196J.portee: Baana's role in Nehemiah 10 reminds us that the spiritual renewal of God's people comes through the personal commitment of leaders and families. His sealing of the covenant illustrates the necessity of submitting to the Word of God in decisive moments, even after the trial of exile. It is an example of the gradual restoration of the Judean community and its willingness to remain faithful to the divine covenant.

sens: To catch fire, to ignite, to be in flames
To burn, to light, to blaze
To be consumed, reduced to ashes by fire
To be devoured by intense emotion, particularly anger or jealousy
H1197A.detail:
1. To catch fire, to ignite: this is the action of fire that breaks out and spreads. The bush of Moses "was all on fire" (Exodus 3:2), but without being consumed — the image is of flames that appear and shine. At Sinai, the mountain is "all on fire" (Deuteronomy 9:15), visible from afar.

2. To burn, to light: this is to intentionally cause ignition. A bonfire was "lit" before the king (Jeremiah 36:22). It is also the act of consuming, destroying by fire — Samson "burned the grain" of the Philistines (Judges 15:5).

3. To be consumed, reduced to ashes: the fire "burned" the company of the wicked who were "consumed" (Psalms 106:18). The image is one of destruction, of what disappears in smoke.

4. To be devoured by an emotion: "the fervor of God's anger" (Isaiah 42:25) and "the jealousy of your God" are described as a fire that "burns." It is the image of a passion that burns from within, irrepressible and destructive.
H1197A.origine: The Hebrew root bâ'ar primarily denotes the flame and fire that devours. It is very common in biblical Hebrew (62 occurrences) and is used both literally (to light a fire, a bush igniting) and figuratively (the anger of God that "burns"). The verb can take several forms depending on the context: simple form (the fire burns), intensive form (to ignite, to blaze) or passive (to be consumed). It is a very vivid word, appealing to the concrete experience of fire.
H1197A.emploi: The verb "to burn" appears 62 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and the Psalms. It primarily denotes material fire: that which burns wood, consumes sacrifices, destroys cities. But it quickly becomes the image of divine or human anger: "the heat of anger" burns, "jealousy" blazes. The fire of God's judgment on sin is described as a fire that "consumes" — an image of inevitable punishment. In deliverance narratives, God "lights" His fire against the enemies of Israel. The figurative sense eventually dominates: it is less about fire than the destructive passion that "burns."
H1197A.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God is not indifferent to evil: His anger "burns" like a fire that consumes sin. It is also an image of judgment: no one can escape the fire of Judgment, like the burning bush of Moses that continues to burn. But it also speaks of God's passion for His people, a fervor that purifies. Finally, it invites us to examine what "burns" within us: is it jealousy, anger, or zeal for God?

sens: To lack intelligence, discernment, or wisdom
To be insensitive, hardened, closed to reason or truth
To be without common sense, incapable of reflection
To cause damage, devastate (transitive sense)
To graze, to let feed (sense of nourishment)
H1197B.detail:
1. The word describes a person who lacks intelligence and common sense. It is not a question of education, but of willful blindness or inability to understand: "Take heed, you foolish men!" (Psalms 94:8). In Jeremiah 10:14, "Every man becomes stupid by his knowledge," meaning that even those who possess knowledge can lose discernment and fall into the absurdity of worshiping idols.
2. The word characterizes the hardening of the heart, the obstinacy of not seeking God: "The shepherds have been foolish; they have not sought the Lord" (Jeremiah 10:21). It is a moral as well as intellectual foolishness, one that ignores divine wisdom.
3. The word can also emphasize practical absurdity, the lack of common sense in advice or actions: Isaiah 10:11 speaks of the "wise counselors of Pharaoh" forming a "foolish counsel," showing a folly that confuses expertise with the absence of true wisdom.
4. In Exodus 22:5, the verb in the transitive sense means "to cause damage," "to let graze": the livestock left free "grazes" the field of another and devastates it. It is the brute action, without control.
5. The sense of "to graze" or "to let graze" refers to the idea of animal browsing, simple nourishment without reflection: the verb evokes the instinctive behavior of the flock.
H1197B.origine: The Hebrew word בָּעַר (ba'ar) comes from a root expressing the idea of mental brevity, of lack of thinking ability. The nominal form "beasts" or "animals" shares its etymology: human stupidity is thus compared to the lack of reason of animals that feed without reflection. The main nominalizing verb means "to be brutish" or "to act without intelligence." This figurative link between the animal that grazes without awareness and the human who acts without wisdom structures the entire semantic field of the word.
H1197B.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in prophetic and didactic contexts. In the Psalms and Jeremiah, it describes the spiritual folly of those who flee from God or worship idols: humans "become foolish by their knowledge" (Jeremiah 10:14), the shepherd who "does not seek the Lord" (Jeremiah 10:21). In Isaiah 19:11, it characterizes the Egyptian counselors whose counsel is devoid of divine wisdom despite their apparent knowledge. Exodus 22:5 uses it in the transitive sense to denote the damage caused by grazing livestock. The word thus conveys both the idea of severe mental confusion and that of unreasonable destruction, both marked by a lack of discernment.
H1197B.portee: This word calls the reader to ask whether they walk in divine wisdom or fall into spiritual foolishness, even if they possess knowledge or power. Jeremiah uses it to show that those who abandon the search for God become blind to reality, victims of their own idols. It is a call to intellectual humility: true wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, not with the accumulation of knowledge.

sens: To eat grass or foliage (for an animal)
To devour, consume (in terms of destruction)
To make disappear, annihilate
To consume, exhaust (in a figurative sense)
H1197H.detail:
1. Grazing is what animals do: they eat grass or the leaves of trees. This is the primary image of the word. In Isaiah 5:5, the vineyard will be 'grazed' — the animals will devour its fruit and leaves, leaving it barren.
2. The word is also used for brutal destruction that consumes everything: to devastate a region, to plunder it to ruin. In Isaiah 3:14, the elders and leaders have 'grazed' the vineyard of the people — they have devoured its resources and impoverished the poor.
3. To make completely disappear is also a meaning: 'you have made the idols disappear from the land' (2 Chronicles 19:3) means that King Jehoshaphat eliminated them, completely removed them.
4. Figuratively, the word can refer to internal consumption, a destruction from within, like the anger of God that consumes the sinner — the idea of a destruction that burns from the inside until annihilation.
H1197H.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּעַר comes from a root that evokes grazing and the action of eating. Its basic image is that of an animal grazing: it gradually consumes vegetation. From there, the word expands to encompass all forms of destruction and consumption, up to the abstract sense of annihilation. The common idea is one of an action that reduces to nothing, that consumes and exhausts.
H1197H.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the provided usages, in contexts of destruction and consumption. In Isaiah 3:14 and 5:5, it literally describes grazing that devours a vineyard. In 2 Chronicles 19:3, it means to eliminate the idols. In 2 Samuel 4:11, it becomes a threat: God will 'exterminate' the murderers of Bethshan. The meaning evolves from the concrete (grazing) to the destructive (consume, annihilate), passing through political or religious elimination. It is a word of judgment and punishment in the mouth of God.
H1197H.portee: This verb teaches that divine destruction is total and irreversible: it consumes to annihilation. For the believer, it reminds us that God demands the uncompromising destruction of what dishonors Him — the idols — and that He will punish those who devour the heritage of the poor. It is a word that calls for holiness and warns of judgment.

sens: To consume by fire, to burn
To disappear, to be annihilated
To take away, to remove from the midst of a community to purify it
To destroy, to annihilate an evil or a threat
H1197I.detail:
1. To consume by fire, to burn: the literal meaning of the word is the action of fire that devours and reduces to ashes. It is the image of a fire that ignites and consumes wood (Deuteronomy 13:5).
2. To disappear, to be annihilated: by extension, it refers to something that ceases to exist, like something that fades away under the fire of destruction. Evil disappears from the midst of the people when it is eliminated (Deuteronomy 19:19).
3. To take away, to remove from the midst of a community: the Bible often uses this verb to describe the act of removing the guilty from the people of Israel, as one removes what is impure or corrupt. It is to purify the community by removing one who has defiled it through crime or impiety (Deuteronomy 22:22).
4. To destroy, to annihilate an evil: in a broader sense, it is the action of completely eradicating a danger or guilt, by burning it metaphorically so that it no longer exists (Deuteronomy 24:7).
H1197I.origine: The Hebrew verb ba.ar comes from a root that evokes the action of burning and consuming. The basic image is that of a living fire that devours. In Hebrew, related words are found to designate the blaze, the heat. In the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb is often rendered by words that have the same field: to burn, to consume, to destroy. The Bible uses it notably in a figurative sense to speak of the anger of God, which 'burns' against sin, but also for the legal penalty that 'cleanses' the community.
H1197I.emploi: The verb ba.ar appears sixteen times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Deuteronomy and the historical books. It is used mainly in a context of law and purification: when Israel must 'remove the evil from its midst' by executing a criminal (murder, idolatry, rebellion), it is the verb ba.ar that is chosen. It emphasizes that this is not a simple murder, but an action that purifies the community. In 1 Kings 16:3 and 2 Kings 23:24, the verb designates the elimination of idols or things contrary to the law of God. The meaning does not vary much: it is always to consume, to remove, to eradicate what defiles.
H1197I.portee: This verb reminds us that sin is not a mere personal fault: it is something that 'defiles' the entire community and must be removed for the people to live in peace with God. The notion of 'removing the evil' from the midst of Israel reveals a biblical vision of judgment: it is an act of cleansing, not of vengeance. For the Christian, this word speaks of the holiness of God's people and the seriousness with which God treats sin — but also of God's love that wants to preserve His people by eliminating what corrupts them.

sens: lack of intelligence or judgment
moral or spiritual grossness
one who is devoid of sense or reason
H1198.detail:
1. The word first describes a fundamental lack of intelligence or discernment. It is the inability to understand or reflect: the psalmist acknowledges 'I was foolish and without understanding' (Psalms 73:22), admitting that he did not clearly see God's justice. This foolishness is often a spiritual or moral blindness.
2. Beyond intellect, the word denotes a grossness of heart: one who 'hates correction is foolish' (Proverbs 12:1), for he rejects the teaching that could transform him. It is a refusal to improve, a voluntary closing off.
3. The foolish one is sometimes a person, a type of incorrigible man without recourse. In Psalms 49:11, the foolish and the stupid perish, despite the wealth they accumulate: their condition in life changes nothing about their destiny.
4. The underlying image evokes brute stupidity: the psalmist compares his former state to that 'of beasts' (Psalms 73:22), revealing that foolishness lowers man below his dignity.
H1198.origine: The Hebrew word בַעַר (ba'ar) comes from a root evoking the idea of burning or blackening, then spoiling or damaging. The same root is found in words designating sterility or devastation. The image is that of an obscured or damaged intelligence: a 'burned' mind incapable of shining or producing fruit. The word is used to paint not only the absence of intelligence but the absence of all moral and spiritual sense.
H1198.emploi: The word appears five times in Psalms and Proverbs, always to stigmatize one who lacks discernment. In Psalms, it designates one who does not understand divine realities: the psalmist in 73:22 confesses his former foolishness in the face of the mysteries of providence, and that of 92:7 notes that the foolish sees nothing of God's works. In Proverbs, the word characterizes one who rejects correction (12:1) or who is unaware of himself (30:2). In every case, foolishness is not merely a lack of gifts, but an absence of attention, humility, or obedience.
H1198.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to examine his own heart: am I closed to correction? Do I refuse to listen to divine wisdom in the Bible? Biblical foolishness is not so much a matter of intellectual quotient as it is a matter of spiritual docility. It is a call to cultivate humility, to love instruction, and to keep the mind open to warnings and the wisdom of God.

sens: Benjamite woman, wife of Shacharaim
H1199.detail: Baara is a woman from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. She was the wife of Shacharaim, a Benjamite, whom she left (or who sent her away) while he was living in the land of Moab, presumably during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. Her story is part of the genealogy of the Benjaminite families, which the Bible preserves to keep the memory of the descendants of Israel.
H1199.origine: The name Baara means "brutish" (or "coarse, rough") in Hebrew, deriving its meaning from a root that evokes roughness or bestiality. It is a specific proper name, borne by this Benjaminite woman from the royal period of Israel.
H1199.emploi: Baara appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:8. She is mentioned in the genealogical context of the descendants of Shacharaim, a Benjamite leader. The text indicates that she was one of the wives of Shacharaim before he settled in the land of Moab, without providing further details about her life or her role in the history of Israel.
